title: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling
text:
2.1 Runner-to-slot encoding
Let \(w_i\) be the slot assigned to runner \(i\). Then:

\(w_i\) is restricted to the non-impossible slots of runner \(i\);
all runners must receive different slots, normally through all_different(w);
the objective counts the runners whose selected slot is merely acceptable.

Conceptually,
\[
\min \sum_{i=1}^{n}[c_{i,w_i}=1],
\]
where \([P]\) is \(1\) when proposition \(P\) is true and \(0\) otherwise.
crumbs: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling

title: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling
text:
2.2 Boolean-matrix encoding
Let \(A_{i,j}=1\) mean that runner \(i\) receives slot \(j\). The constraints are
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{n}A_{i,j}=1
\quad\text{for every runner }i,
\]
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i,j}=1
\quad\text{for every slot }j,
\]
and
\[
A_{i,j}=0
\]
for every impossible pair. The objective is
\[
\min\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}c_{i,j}A_{i,j},
\]
with forbidden pairs already removed by constraints.
The vector model is compact; the matrix model makes assignment and objective contributions explicit. Both encode the same matching problem.
crumbs: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling

title: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling
text:
3.1 Boolean selection
For a 0-1 knapsack, let \(x_i\in\{0,1\}\) indicate whether object \(i\) is selected:
\[
\sum_i w_i x_i\le C,
\qquad
\max\sum_i p_i x_i.
\]
crumbs: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling

title: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling
text:
3.2 Bounded quantities
If several copies are allowed, let \(x_i\) be the quantity selected, with a domain reflecting the available stock:
\[
x_i\in 0..u_i.
\]
The same capacity and profit expressions apply. The domain now changes the problem from selection to bounded allocation.
The lecture only points to the MiniZinc code; no separate .mzn source was supplied with this deck, so this chapter preserves the mathematical structure without inventing lecturer code.
crumbs: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling

title: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling
text:
5.1 Detection and correction rule
Let \(d\) be the minimum Hamming distance between distinct codewords.

If \(d=2t+1\), the code can always correct up to \(t\) errors.
If \(d=2t\), the code can correct up to \(t-1\) errors and detect \(t\) errors.

The reason is geometric. Correcting \(t\) errors requires the radius-\(t\) Hamming balls around codewords to be disjoint. Two such balls are guaranteed not to overlap when the centres are at least \(2t+1\) apart.
crumbs: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling

title: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling
text:
6.1 Symmetry breaking
The slide explicitly points to symmetry-breaking optimisations. Several transformations preserve all pairwise Hamming distances:

permuting the \(k\) codewords;
permuting the \(n\) bit positions;
complementing one bit position in every codeword.

Therefore, without loss of generality, one may fix the first word to all zeroes:
\[
X_{1,r}=0
\qquad\text{for every }r.
\]
This removes the global bit-complement symmetry. Ordering the binary values represented by the rows can also remove word-permutation symmetry. These constraints do not exclude essentially different codes; they select canonical representatives from symmetric families.






NoteWhat symmetry breaking changes



Symmetry breaking reduces repeated search over equivalent codes. It does not increase the achievable minimum distance and does not change whether a code exists, provided the chosen symmetry-breaking conditions are valid representatives of the true symmetries.
crumbs: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling

title: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling
text:
7.1 Required periods
If course \(c\) requires \(h_c\) periods,
\[
\sum_{p,r}X_{c,p,r}=h_c.
\]
crumbs: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling

title: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling
text:
7.2 Room occupancy
At most one course can use one room in one period:
\[
\sum_c X_{c,p,r}\le1
\qquad\text{for every }p,r.
\]
crumbs: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling

title: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling
text:
7.3 Course conflicts
If conflict[c,d] = 1, the two courses cannot occur simultaneously:
\[
\sum_rX_{c,p,r}+\sum_rX_{d,p,r}\le1
\qquad\text{for every }p.
\]
crumbs: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling

title: Scheduling Models, Hamming Codes, and Timetabling
text:
7.4 Availability
If course \(c\) is unavailable in period \(p\),
\[
X_{c,p,r}=0
\qquad\text{for every room }r.
\]
The precise variable representation may be changed, but every correct model must preserve these four ideas. The deck refers to MiniZinc code, but no authoritative code file accompanies these slides, so no unverified implementation is reproduced.

text:
6.2 Symmetry breaking
The active code contains:
constraint x[1,1] = 1;
constraint forall(i in 1..n)(x[1,i] = i);
The second constraint already implies x[1,1] = 1, so the first is redundant. Redundant does not mean incorrect: the extra constraint does not change the solution set after the first-row condition is imposed.
A stronger, commented option fixes both the first row and the first column:
% constraint
%   forall(i in 1..n)(
%     x[1,i] = i /\
%     x[i,1] = i
%   );
These constraints remove symmetric Latin squares obtained by renaming symbols and permuting rows or columns. The aim is not to alter the essential combinatorial structure but to choose a canonical representative from each symmetric family.

title: MiniZinc Modelling through Classical Constraint Problems
text:
7.2 Version 2: computed magic sum
The total of the numbers \(1,\ldots,n^2\) is
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n^2}i=\frac{n^2(n^2+1)}{2}.
\]
Every row has the same sum and there are \(n\) rows, so the magic sum must be
\[
s=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n^2}i
=\frac{n(n^2+1)}{2}.
\]
The second model computes it:
var int: s;
s = (sum(i in 1..n*n)(i)) div n;
Since s is defined by an expression containing only the parameter n, s is effectively fixed before search even though the source declares it as var int.
The model also adds symmetry breaking:
constraint
  x[1,1] < x[1,n] /\
  x[1,1] < x[n,1] /\
  x[1,1] < x[n,n];
Rotations and reflections map a magic square to other magic squares. Requiring the upper-left corner to be smaller than the other three corners chooses an orientation and removes several symmetric alternatives.








Version
Treatment of \(s\)
Search consequence




unknown-sum version
s is a decision variable constrained by all lines
propagation must also determine s


computed-sum version
s is fixed from \(n\)
the known invariant is exposed before search

section: 11.4 White and black pieces with blocking
text:
11.4 White and black pieces with blocking
Place given white and black queens, rooks, and knights so that pieces of opposite colours do not attack one another. Pieces of the same colour may block rook and queen lines of sight.
The blocking condition is the hard part. It is not enough to forbid two opposite-colour pieces from sharing a row, column, or diagonal: the model must determine whether another piece lies strictly between them on that line.
crumbs: MiniZinc Modelling through Classical Constraint Problems

title: MiniZinc Modelling through Classical Constraint Problems
text:
11.5 Balanced bins with incompatibilities
There are \(n\) weighted objects and \(k\) bins. Each object must be assigned to exactly one bin. For each pair of bins, the difference between their total weights must be less than input threshold \(t\). A Boolean matrix \(c\) additionally requires objects \(i\) and \(j\) to be in different bins when \(c[i,j]=1\).
The model requires assignment variables, bin-weight aggregates, pairwise balance constraints, and incompatibility implications.
crumbs: MiniZinc Modelling through Classical Constraint Problems

title: MiniZinc Modelling through Classical Constraint Problems
text:
11.6 Workers and repeated tasks
There are \(t\) task types with durations given by vector \(d\), and \(n\ge t\) workers. Each worker can perform only a supplied subset of task types. Workers are assigned so that the required work is completed and total time is minimised. A worker performs one task and then stops, while another worker may later perform the same task type.
The repeated occurrence of a task is the difficult part: task types must be distinguished from individual task occurrences or from the amount of repeated work allocated over time.
crumbs: MiniZinc Modelling through Classical Constraint Problems

title: MiniZinc Modelling through Classical Constraint Problems
text:
11.7 Permutation objective
Given vectors \(u\) and \(v\) of length \(n\) with values in \(1..m\), find a permutation \(\pi\) maximising
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}u_i v_{\pi(i)}.
\]
The exercise explicitly asks for a declarative model rather than a specialised algorithm. A permutation may be represented by an array of indices constrained by all_different, after which the objective uses indexed access into \(v\).

title: Global Constraints, Matching-Based Filtering, and Cumulative Scheduling
text:
A global constraint is a constraint over a structured collection of variables with a precise, problem-specific meaning. A global constraint can often be rewritten as a Boolean combination of simpler binary or ternary constraints, but that decomposition may propagate much less information than the global relation considered as a whole.
The difference is not primarily syntactic. It concerns the strength and cost of inference.








Representation
Meaning available to the propagator
Typical consequence




decomposition into small constraints
each local relation is inspected separately
conflicts involving many variables may remain hidden


dedicated global constraint
the complete combinatorial structure is visible
stronger filtering can be performed efficiently



The best-known example is all_different. The lecture develops this constraint in detail and then uses it as a model for understanding why global constraints receive dedicated algorithms.






ImportantEquivalent constraints need not propagate equally



Two formulations may have exactly the same complete solutions while producing different domain reductions during propagation. Logical equivalence therefore does not imply operational equivalence inside a constraint solver.
crumbs: Global Constraints, Matching-Based Filtering, and Cumulative Scheduling

title: Global Constraints, Matching-Based Filtering, and Cumulative Scheduling
text:
2.1 Diff-arc consistency
A CSP is diff-arc consistent when every all_different constraint is hyper-arc consistent. This is a strong, value-by-value support condition.
Consider
\[
C=\operatorname{all\_different}(X_1,\ldots,X_k),
\]
where each variable \(X_i\) has domain \(D_i\). For every variable \(X_i\) and every value \(a_i\in D_i\), diff-arc consistency requires the existence of values
\[
a_j\in D_j
\qquad\text{for every }j\ne i
\]
such that
\[
(a_1,\ldots,a_i,\ldots,a_k)
\in
\operatorname{all\_different}(X_1,\ldots,X_k).
\]
Equivalently, after temporarily fixing
\[
X_i=a_i,
\]
the remaining variables must still be assignable pairwise distinct values from their current domains. The resulting complete tuple is called a support for the value \(a_i\).

2.1.1 What the propagator checks
For every edge between a variable and one of its current values, the propagator asks:

Can this particular variable-value choice be extended to a complete solution of this all_different constraint, using only the current domains?

The possible outcomes are:







Outcome for \(X_i=a_i\)
Propagation consequence




at least one complete all-distinct assignment contains \(X_i=a_i\)
retain \(a_i\) in \(D_i\)


no complete all-distinct assignment contains \(X_i=a_i\)
delete \(a_i\) from \(D_i\)


no complete all-distinct assignment exists for any value
report failure: the constraint is inconsistent



This is stronger than checking whether \(a_i\) is merely different from some value in each other domain separately. The same choices for the other variables must work simultaneously and must be mutually distinct.


2.1.2 A supported value
Suppose
\[
D_1=\{1,2\},
\qquad
D_2=\{1,2\},
\qquad
D_3=\{2,3\}.
\]
To test \(X_1=1\), one complete support is
\[
(X_1,X_2,X_3)=(1,2,3).
\]
All three values belong to the respective domains and are pairwise different. Therefore, value \(1\) remains in \(D_1\).
To test \(X_3=2\), one support is
\[
(X_1,X_2,X_3)=(1,3,2)
\]
only if \(3\in D_2\). In the stated domains, \(3\notin D_2\), so this tuple is unavailable. However, the alternative
\[
(X_1,X_2,X_3)=(1,\text{no available distinct value},2)
\]
shows the issue: after assigning \(X_3=2\), both \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) must draw distinct values from \(\{1,2\}\), but value \(2\) is already used. Only value \(1\) remains for both variables. Hence \(X_3=2\) has no support and can be removed:
\[
D_3:=\{3\}.
\]
Once \(X_3\) is fixed to \(3\), the remaining variables may take \(1\) and \(2\) in either order.

2.1.3 How strong is diff-arc consistency?
For one all_different constraint, diff-arc consistency removes every value that cannot occur in any complete solution of that constraint under the current domains. No stronger domain-filtering operation can delete an additional value using only that single constraint without deleting a value that has a valid support.
This does not mean that the entire CSP is solved. A value may be supported within one all_different constraint but become impossible when other constraints are considered. Propagation therefore alternates among all constraints until a fixed point is reached:

one propagator removes unsupported values;
the reduced domains wake other propagators;
those propagators may remove further values;
all_different is reconsidered with the new domains;
the process stops when no domain changes, or fails when a domain becomes empty.



2.1.4 Hall-set intuition
The strength of the global constraint can also be understood through groups of variables. If a set of \(r\) variables can collectively use only \(r\) values, those values are completely reserved for that group. Every other variable must exclude them.
For example, if
\[
D_1=D_2=\{1,2\},
\qquad
D_3=\{1,2,3\},
\]
then \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) must consume values \(1\) and \(2\) between them. Consequently, \(X_3\) cannot use either value and propagation obtains
\[
D_3:=\{3\}.
\]
If \(r\) variables collectively have fewer than \(r\) available values, no injective assignment exists and the constraint fails. The matching-based algorithm developed later in the lecture detects exactly this global competition for values without explicitly enumerating all complete tuples.






ImportantStrength of diff-arc consistency



Diff-arc consistency is the strongest domain-level filtering for one all_different constraint: every retained value participates in at least one complete injective assignment for that constraint. It is stronger than pairwise arc consistency because support must be global and simultaneous, not assembled from unrelated pairwise witnesses.

title: Global Constraints, Matching-Based Filtering, and Cumulative Scheduling
text:
2.2 Decomposition into pairwise disequalities
The global constraint is logically equivalent to
\[
\bigwedge_{1\le i<j\le k}X_i\ne X_j.
\]
However, hyper-arc consistency for the global constraint is stronger than binary arc consistency for the decomposition.
Consider
\[
D_1=D_2=D_3=\{0,1\}.
\]
Every value of every variable has local support in each pairwise disequality. Therefore,
\[
X_1\ne X_2,
\quad
X_1\ne X_3,
\quad
X_2\ne X_3
\]
can be binary arc consistent. Nevertheless, three variables cannot receive distinct values from a set containing only two values, so the global all_different constraint is inconsistent.








View
What is checked
Result for three domains \(\{0,1\}\)




pairwise disequalities
every value differs from some value in each other domain
arc consistent


global all_different
every value extends to one complete all-distinct tuple
inconsistent

section: 2.3 Why the direct definition is too expensive
text:
2.3 Why the direct definition is too expensive
Let
\[
d_i=|D_i|,
\qquad
d=\max_i d_i.
\]
A propagator that tests supports directly by enumerating combinations may require time on the order of
\[
O(d^{k+1}),
\]
which is unusable for large arity \(k\). The lecture asks an important algorithmic question: is the difficulty intrinsic to the filtering problem, or only a consequence of using a naïve algorithm?
The answer is that stronger filtering can be implemented efficiently by exposing a connection with bipartite matching.

section: 3.2 Proposition: augmenting a matching increases its size
text:
3.2 Proposition: augmenting a matching increases its size






WarningProposition: augmenting along a path



Let \(M\) be a matching in a bipartite graph \(G=\langle X,Y,E\rangle\), and let \(P\) be an augmenting path for \(M\). Then
\[
M' = M\triangle P
   = (M\setminus P)\cup(P\setminus M)
\]
is a matching and
\[
|M'|=|M|+1.
\]


The symmetric difference toggles every edge of the path: edges of \(P\) that belong to \(M\) are removed, while edges of \(P\) that do not belong to \(M\) are inserted.

3.2.1 Proof
Write the matching as
\[
M=
\{(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_k,y_k),
  (x_{k+1},y_{k+1}),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)\},
\]
where, without loss of generality, the first \(k\) edges are exactly the matched edges used by the augmenting path.
Because \(P\) is augmenting, its endpoints are free. Assume that the path starts at free value vertex \(y_0\in Y\) and ends at free variable vertex \(x_0\in X\). The path has the alternating form
\[
P=
\{
(y_0,x_1),
(x_1,y_1),
(y_1,x_2),
(x_2,y_2),
\ldots,
(y_{k-1},x_k),
(x_k,y_k),
(y_k,x_0)
\}.
\]
The edges
\[
(x_1,y_1),\ldots,(x_k,y_k)
\]
belong to \(M\), whereas
\[
(y_0,x_1),
(y_1,x_2),
\ldots,
(y_{k-1},x_k),
(y_k,x_0)
\]
do not belong to \(M\).
After taking the symmetric difference,
\[
\begin{aligned}
M'
={}&(M\setminus P)\cup(P\setminus M)\\
={}&\{
(y_0,x_1),
(y_1,x_2),
\ldots,
(y_{k-1},x_k),
(y_k,x_0),\\
&\qquad
(x_{k+1},y_{k+1}),\ldots,(x_n,y_n)
\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
We must prove two facts.

3.2.1.1 1. \(M'\) is still a matching
Inside the path, every internal vertex was incident to one matched path edge and one unmatched path edge. Toggling the path removes the former and inserts the latter, so every internal vertex is still incident to exactly one selected edge.
The endpoints \(y_0\) and \(x_0\) were free in \(M\) by the definition of augmenting path. Each endpoint becomes incident to exactly one newly inserted edge. No conflict is created with an edge outside the path.
Finally, all edges of \(M\) outside \(P\) are unchanged. Since \(M\) was a matching, their endpoints are pairwise distinct and do not conflict with the path endpoints after the toggle. Therefore, no two edges of \(M'\) share a vertex, and \(M'\) is a matching.


3.2.1.2 2. \(M'\) has one additional edge
The path contains:

\(k\) edges belonging to \(M\);
\(k+1\) edges not belonging to \(M\).

The symmetric difference removes the \(k\) matched edges and inserts the \(k+1\) unmatched edges. Hence
\[
|M'|
=|M|-k+(k+1)
=|M|+1.
\]
Therefore \(M'\) is a matching whose cardinality is one greater than that of \(M\). \(\square\)

title: Global Constraints, Matching-Based Filtering, and Cumulative Scheduling
text:
5.1 Berge’s theorem






WarningBerge’s theorem



Let \(G\) be a graph and let \(M\) be a matching of \(G\). Then
\[
M\text{ is a maximum matching}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{there is no augmenting path with respect to }M.
\]


The theorem gives an exact optimality criterion. It does not merely say that an augmenting path is useful: it says that augmenting paths are the only obstruction to maximum cardinality.

If an augmenting path exists, the current matching can be enlarged.
If no augmenting path exists, no larger matching exists anywhere in the graph.


5.1.1 Proof
The equivalence has two directions.

5.1.1.1 \((\Rightarrow)\) A maximum matching has no augmenting path
Assume that \(M\) is maximum. Suppose, for contradiction, that an augmenting path \(P\) exists with respect to \(M\).
By the previous proposition,
\[
M'=M\triangle P
\]
is a matching and
\[
|M'|=|M|+1.
\]
Thus \(M'\) is strictly larger than \(M\), contradicting the assumption that \(M\) is maximum. Therefore, a maximum matching cannot have an augmenting path.


5.1.1.2 \((\Leftarrow)\) A matching with no augmenting path is maximum
We prove the contrapositive. Assume that \(M\) is not maximum. Then there exists a matching \(M^*\) such that
\[
|M^*|>|M|.
\]
Consider the graph formed by the symmetric difference
\[
H=(V,M\triangle M^*).
\]
An edge belongs to \(H\) exactly when it belongs to one of the two matchings but not to both.
Because both \(M\) and \(M^*\) are matchings, every vertex of \(H\) is incident to:

at most one edge from \(M\);
at most one edge from \(M^*\).

Therefore every vertex in \(H\) has degree at most two. Each connected component of \(H\) is consequently one of the following:

an isolated vertex;
an alternating path;
an alternating cycle.

Along every nontrivial component, edges alternate between \(M\) and \(M^*\).

    end

    Y0 --- X1

 Structure of the symmetric difference M triangle M*. Every nontrivial component is an alternating path or an alternating even cycle because each vertex is incident to at most one edge from each matching. 



In the diagram, blue edges belong to \(M\) and orange dashed edges belong to \(M^*\). The displayed component contains one more edge from \(M^*\) than from \(M\).
Now compare the number of edges contributed by the two matchings in each component.

In an alternating cycle, the numbers are equal because the cycle has even length.
In an even alternating path, the numbers are equal when the first and last edges belong to different matchings.
In an odd alternating path, one matching contributes exactly one more edge than the other.

Since
\[
|M^*|>|M|,
\]
it is impossible for every component to contain at least as many edges from \(M\) as from \(M^*\). Therefore, at least one path component contains one more edge from \(M^*\) than from \(M\).
Such a component must begin and end with edges of \(M^*\). Let its endpoints be \(u\) and \(v\).
Neither endpoint can be matched by \(M\) outside the component. If, for example, \(u\) were incident to an edge of \(M\) outside the component, that edge would also belong to \(M\triangle M^*\) and the component would not be maximal. Hence \(u\) and \(v\) are free with respect to \(M\).
The component is therefore:

alternating with respect to \(M\);
acyclic, because it is a path;
starting and ending at free vertices of \(M\).

It is an augmenting path for \(M\).
Thus, whenever \(M\) is not maximum, an augmenting path exists. Taking the contrapositive, if no augmenting path exists, \(M\) is maximum. \(\square\)






NoteWhy Berge’s theorem is algorithmically decisive



The theorem transforms maximum matching into a search problem with a certificate:

an augmenting path certifies that the current matching is not maximum;
the absence of any augmenting path certifies that the current matching is maximum.

This is why the basic algorithm repeatedly searches for augmenting paths and stops exactly when none can be found.

title: Global Constraints, Matching-Based Filtering, and Cumulative Scheduling
text:
5.2 Naïve maximum-matching algorithm
Starting from the empty matching, repeatedly find and augment along an augmenting path:
M := empty matching
while an augmenting path P for M exists:
    M := M symmetric-difference P
return M
Let
\[
n=\min\{|X|,|Y|\},
\qquad
m=|E|.
\]
At most \(n\) augmentations are possible. If each augmenting path is found in \(O(m)\) time with a depth-first search, the total cost is
\[
O(nm).
\]
The lecture contrasts this with the Hopcroft-Karp bound
\[
O(m\sqrt n),
\]
which finds several shortest augmenting paths per phase rather than increasing the matching only once per full scan.



Method
Augmentation strategy
Complexity stated in the lecture




naïve algorithm
one augmenting path at a time
\(O(nm)\)


Hopcroft-Karp
batches of shortest augmenting paths
\(O(m\sqrt n)\)

text:
7.1 Proof
We prove both directions.

7.1.1 \((\Rightarrow)\) Diff-arc consistency implies matching support for every edge
Assume that \(P\) is diff-arc consistent. Consider an arbitrary all_different constraint
\[
C=\operatorname{all\_different}(X_1,\ldots,X_k)
\]
and an arbitrary edge
\[
(X_i,a_i)\in E_C.
\]
By the definition of the value graph,
\[
a_i\in D_i.
\]
Because \(P\) is diff-arc consistent, \(C\) is hyper-arc consistent. Therefore the value \(a_i\) has a complete support: there exist values
\[
a_j\in D_j
\qquad\text{for every }j\ne i
\]
such that
\[
(X_1,\ldots,X_k)=(a_1,\ldots,a_k)
\]
satisfies \(C\). Since \(C\) is all_different, these values are pairwise distinct:
\[
a_r\ne a_s
\qquad\text{whenever }r\ne s.
\]
Now consider the edge set
\[
M=\{(X_1,a_1),\ldots,(X_k,a_k)\}.
\]
Every edge belongs to \(E_C\) because \(a_j\in D_j\). Moreover:

every variable vertex \(X_j\) occurs exactly once in \(M\);
every value vertex \(a_j\) occurs at most once because the values are pairwise distinct.

Hence \(M\) is a matching of size \(k\). It contains the original edge \((X_i,a_i)\). Since the edge was arbitrary, every edge of \(G_V(C)\) belongs to at least one matching of size \(k\).

 Forward direction of Régin’s theorem. A complete support for Xi = ai supplies one distinct value for every variable, and the corresponding edges form a size-k matching containing the tested edge. 



The red edge is the tested assignment \(X_i=a_i\). Hyper-arc consistency provides all the other blue edges needed to complete it to a matching that covers every variable.


7.1.2 \((\Leftarrow)\) Matching support for every edge implies diff-arc consistency
Assume now that every edge of \(G_V(C)\) belongs to at least one matching of size \(k\). We must prove that every value in every variable domain has a complete support.
Take an arbitrary variable \(X_i\) and an arbitrary value
\[
a_i\in D_i.
\]
By the definition of \(E_C\), the edge
\[
(X_i,a_i)
\]
belongs to the value graph. By hypothesis, there exists a matching \(M\) of size \(k\) containing this edge.
There are exactly \(k\) variable vertices in \(X_C\). A matching of size \(k\) can use each variable vertex at most once, so it must cover all variables. Thus, for every \(X_j\), the matching contains exactly one edge
\[
(X_j,a_j).
\]
Because \(M\) is a matching, no two selected edges share a value endpoint. Therefore
\[
a_r\ne a_s
\qquad\text{for every }r\ne s.
\]
The assignment
\[
X_1=a_1,
\ldots,
X_i=a_i,
\ldots,
X_k=a_k
\]
is consequently a solution of the all_different constraint \(C\). In particular, it is a support for the arbitrarily chosen value \(a_i\).
Since both \(X_i\) and \(a_i\in D_i\) were arbitrary, every value in every domain has a support. Hence \(C\) is hyper-arc consistent. Repeating the argument for every all_different constraint in \(\mathcal C\) gives that \(P\) is diff-arc consistent. \(\square\)

ImportantMeaning for propagation



Régin’s theorem changes the support test for all_different from tuple enumeration into graph analysis:
\[
\text{retain }a\in D_i
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
(X_i,a)\text{ belongs to at least one size-}k\text{ matching}.
\]
Therefore, enforcing diff-arc consistency means deleting exactly the edges that belong to no matching covering all variables.

section: 7.2 Why one maximum matching is not yet sufficient
text:
7.2 Why one maximum matching is not yet sufficient
Let
\[
d_i=|D_i|,
\qquad
d=\max_i d_i,
\qquad
e=\sum_{i=1}^{k}d_i\le kd.
\]
The value graph contains \(k\) variable vertices, \(\left|\bigcup_iD_i\right|\) value vertices, and \(e\) edges. A maximum matching can be found within the complexity bound used in the lecture:
\[
O(\sqrt{k}\,e)=O(k^{3/2}d).
\]
If the maximum matching has size smaller than \(k\), the constraint is inconsistent. If its size is \(k\), it proves that at least one solution exists. However, that single matching supports only the edges that it uses directly. Other unmatched edges may still belong to different size-\(k\) matchings.
Consequently, filtering requires one additional question:

Which edges belong to at least one maximum matching, even if they do not belong to the particular maximum matching currently stored?

The next sections answer this question through even alternating paths from free value vertices and alternating cycles.

section: 8.3 Why every optional edge has this form
text:
8.3 Why every optional edge has this form
Suppose edge \(e\) belongs to maximum matching \(M\) but not to another maximum matching \(M'\). In
\[
M\triangle M',
\]
every vertex has degree at most two. Starting from \(e\), the connected component is therefore an alternating path or an alternating cycle.

If the component closes, \(e\) lies on an alternating cycle.
If it does not close, maximality rules out an odd augmenting component; the component is an even alternating path with a free endpoint.

Thus paths and cycles are not merely convenient sufficient conditions. They characterize all changes that transform one maximum matching into another without decreasing its cardinality.
crumbs: Global Constraints, Matching-Based Filtering, and Cumulative Scheduling

text:
9.1 Step 1: check feasibility
Find a maximum matching \(M\) in the value graph.

If \(|M|<k\), at least one variable cannot be matched, so no all-distinct assignment exists and the constraint fails.
If \(|M|=k\), the matching is one complete support, but unmatched edges still need classification.

text:
9.2 Step 2: find exchangeable edges
Starting from every free value vertex in the right partition, retain edges reachable through even alternating paths. Then detect alternating cycles using strongly connected components in the directed alternating graph.

9.3 Step 3: prune domains
Retain:

every edge of the current maximum matching;
every edge on a retained even alternating path;
every edge on an alternating cycle.

Delete every other edge. Deleting edge \((X_i,a)\) means
\[

text:
3.1 Variable-choice annotations
A variable-choice heuristic attempts to select the variable whose assignment is expected to expose useful propagation or failure early.







Annotation
Choice made




input_order
select variables in the order supplied to int_search


occurrence
select the variable participating in the largest number of constraints


first_fail
select a variable with the smallest current domain


anti_first_fail
select a variable with the largest current domain


most_constrained
select a smallest-domain variable, breaking ties by the number of attached constraints


dom_w_deg
use a domain-size to weighted-degree criterion, where failures increase constraint weights


impact
select the variable with the largest measured impact on the remaining search space


max_regret
select the variable with the largest difference between the two smallest values in its domain


smallest
select the variable whose domain currently contains the smallest value


largest
select the variable whose domain currently contains the largest value



The first-fail principle tries to branch on the variable most likely to become impossible. If the current partial assignment is inconsistent, discovering that inconsistency near the top of the tree avoids constructing a much larger doomed subtree. most_constrained refines this idea by using constraint participation as a tie-breaker.
anti_first_fail makes the opposite choice. It is therefore not a generally interchangeable spelling of first_fail; it deliberately favours the variable with the largest domain.

3.2 Domain-choice annotations
After selecting a variable, a domain-choice annotation determines the next branch. Some annotations assign a value; others split the domain or remove one value.







Annotation
Effect on the selected domain




indomain
try values in ascending order


indomain_interval
if the domain has several contiguous intervals, keep the first interval; otherwise bisect it


indomain_max
assign the largest value


indomain_median
assign a middle value of the domain


indomain_middle
assign the domain value closest to the mean of the current lower and upper bounds


indomain_min
assign the smallest value


indomain_random
assign a randomly selected value


indomain_reverse_split
bisect the domain and exclude the lower half first


indomain_split
bisect the domain and exclude the upper half first


indomain_split_random
bisect the domain and randomly decide which half to exclude first


outdomain_max
exclude the largest value


outdomain_median
exclude a middle value


outdomain_min
exclude the smallest value


outdomain_random
exclude a randomly selected value



The distinction between indomain_median and indomain_middle matters. The former is based on the ordered values actually present in the domain. The latter uses the mean of the current bounds and then chooses the available value closest to that mean. The results can differ when the domain has holes.

7.1 Propagation through a minimum constraint
Consider
\[
X=\min(A,B,C,D)
\]
with domains
\[
D_X=2..10,
\quad
D_A=4..20,
\quad
D_B=4..5,
\quad
D_C=5..23,
\quad
D_D=7..20.
\]
The minimum cannot be below \(4\), because every argument is at least \(4\). It cannot exceed \(5\), because \(B\) is guaranteed to be at most \(5\). Therefore propagation infers
\[
D_X=4..5.
\]
Furthermore, \(D\) cannot be the variable attaining the minimum, since its lower bound is \(7\), whereas the minimum is at most \(5\). The example illustrates why an aggregate is a genuine constraint: information flows from the argument domains to \(X\) and can also rule out roles for individual arguments.

9.1 Restart schedules



Annotation
Node budget before the next restart




restart_constant(n)
always \(n\) nodes


restart_linear(n)
\(nk\) nodes for run \(k\)


restart_geometric(\omega,n)
\(n\omega^k\) nodes for run \(k\)


restart_luby(n)
\(nL[k]\) nodes, where \(L\) is the Luby sequence


restart_none
no restart



The schedules express different trade-offs. A constant schedule repeatedly gives the same budget. A linear schedule increases it steadily. A geometric schedule increases it multiplicatively. The Luby schedule repeatedly returns to short runs while also allocating runs of increasing length.

title: MiniZinc Search Annotations and Constraint Modelling
text:
9.2 The Luby sequence
The sequence shown in the lecture begins
\[
1,1,2,1,1,2,4,1,1,2,1,1,2,4,8,\ldots
\]
All run lengths are powers of two. After two runs of a given length have been completed in the recursive pattern, a run of twice that length appears.
One recursive definition is
\[
t_i=
\begin{cases}
2^{k-1}, & \text{if } i=2^k-1,\\[4pt]
t_{i-2^{k-1}+1}, & \text{if }2^{k-1}\le i<2^k-1.
\end{cases}
\]
For example, \(i=14\) lies in the block associated with \(k=4\), so
\[
t_{14}=t_{14-8+1}=t_7=4.
\]
The purpose is not to predict the ideal restart length in advance. The schedule systematically tries short and progressively longer runs.

title: Computational Complexity, Machine Models, and Cost Criteria
text:
In an algorithms course, the usual starting point is an algorithm, whose use of resources is then analysed. Computational complexity changes the focus: the central object is the problem itself.
A problem can be viewed abstractly as a mapping
\[
D : \text{inputs} \longrightarrow \text{outputs}.
\]
The goal is not merely to determine the cost of one chosen algorithm, but to classify the intrinsic difficulty of the problem. This requires considering the best possible algorithm under a specified resource measure and, when possible, proving lower bounds showing that no algorithm can solve the problem with fewer resources.
In the first part of the course, the principal resources are:

time, measured through the number or cost of executed operations;
space, measured through the amount of memory used during the computation.

The optimal algorithm for time need not be the optimal algorithm for space. An algorithm can save memory by reusing storage while performing additional computation, so reducing one resource may increase the other. Consequently, time and space complexity must be analysed separately.


Three broad forms of computational problem are useful.








Problem form
Required output
Graph-colouring version




Decision
a yes-or-no answer
decide whether \(G\) is colourable with at most three colours


Functional
a concrete output object
produce a valid colouring of \(G\)


Optimization
an optimal feasible solution
minimize the number of colours used



This course concentrates mainly on decision problems, which provide the basic framework for complexity classes.



Let
\[
G=(V,E)
\]
be a finite undirected graph, where \(V\) is the set of vertices and \(E\) is the set of edges. A colouring assigns a colour to every vertex. Formally, a colouring can be represented by a function
\[
c:V\longrightarrow \{1,2,\ldots,|V|\}.
\]
It is valid when adjacent vertices receive different colours:
\[
\{u,v\}\in E \implies c(u)\neq c(v).
\]
The same underlying graph-colouring task can be formulated in different ways.

Functional version: given \(G\), produce a valid colouring.
Decision version: given \(G\) and a fixed number of colours, decide whether a valid colouring exists using at most that many colours.
Optimization version: given \(G\), find the minimum number of colours needed for a valid colouring.

The lecture used the decision problem 3-COLOURING:

Given a graph \(G\), decide whether there exists a valid colouring of \(G\) using at most three colours.

A positive instance requires only the answer yes. The algorithm is not required to return the colouring itself. In a complete graph, every pair of distinct vertices is adjacent, so each vertex needs a different colour; in the worst case, as many as \(|V|\) colours may therefore be necessary.

title: Computational Complexity, Machine Models, and Cost Criteria
text:
4.1 Primitive instructions
The basic URM instructions introduced in the lecture are:

Successor \(S(i)\):
\[
r_i\gets r_i+1.
\]
Zero \(Z(i)\):
\[
r_i\gets 0.
\]
Transfer \(T(i,j)\):
\[
r_j\gets r_i.
\]
Conditional jump \(J(i,j,q)\): if \(r_i=r_j\), continue from instruction \(q\); otherwise continue with the next instruction.

A program is a finite sequence of labelled instructions. A program counter identifies the instruction currently being executed. The input is initially stored in \(R_0\), while the other registers initially contain \(0\). At termination, the output is read from \(R_0\). If several integer inputs are required, they may be placed in consecutive registers.
The jump instruction supplies both comparison and control flow. An unconditional jump can be implemented as
\[
J(i,i,q),
\]
because every register is equal to itself.



Instruction
Effect
Role




\(S(i)\)
\(r_i\gets r_i+1\)
increment


\(Z(i)\)
\(r_i\gets 0\)
reset


\(T(i,j)\)
\(r_j\gets r_i\)
copy


\(J(i,j,q)\)
jump to \(q\) if \(r_i=r_j\)
comparison and control flow

title: Computational Complexity, Machine Models, and Cost Criteria
section: 8.1 Repeated squaring in linear URM time
text:
8.1 Repeated squaring in linear URM time
Suppose the input is \(x\) in \(R_0\). Copy \(x\) to \(R_1\), use \(R_2\) as a loop counter, and repeat the following actions until \(R_2\) reaches the saved value \(x\):

square the content of \(R_0\);
increment \(R_2\);
jump back to the comparison.

A schematic version is:
1. T(0,1)          # preserve the input x
2. J(1,2,6)        # stop when the counter reaches x
3. P(0)            # r0 <- r0^2
4. S(2)
5. J(3,3,2)        # unconditional jump
6. ...             # termination
After \(k\) squarings,
\[
r_0=x^{2^k}.
\]
Therefore, after a number of iterations linear in \(x\), the output has magnitude on the order of
\[
x^{2^x}.
\]
The exact exponent can vary by one squaring depending on whether the loop test is placed before or after the body; this does not affect the complexity argument.
The growth caused by repeated squaring is visible immediately:



Squarings \(k\)
Content of \(R_0\)




\(0\)
\(x\)


\(1\)
\(x^2\)


\(2\)
\(x^4\)


\(3\)
\(x^8\)


\(k\)
\(x^{2^k}\)









flowchart LR
 X0["x"] -->|"square"| X1["x^2"] -->|"square"| X2["x^4"] -->|"square"| X3["x^8"] -->|"continue"| XK["x^(2^k)"]
 classDef value fill:#e8f1ff,stroke:#2f6fb0,stroke-width:2px; class X0,X1,X2,X3,XK value;


 Repeated squaring: the number of machine instructions grows linearly, but the represented value grows extremely rapidly. 



Under uniform cost, the extended URM performs only \(\Theta(x)\) instructions. A Turing machine, however, must explicitly write the output on its tape. The binary length of the output is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\ell\!\left(x^{2^x}\right)
&= \left\lfloor\log_2\!\left(x^{2^x}\right)\right\rfloor+1\\
&= \left\lfloor 2^x\log_2 x\right\rfloor+1\\
&= \Theta\!\left(2^x\log x\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Writing that many bits already requires
\[
\Omega\!\left(2^x\log x\right)
\]
Turing-machine steps, regardless of how efficiently the arithmetic is organized. Thus the uniform-cost extended URM appears to finish in linear time, while a Turing machine requires exponential time merely to materialize the output. The two cost measures are not polynomially related.
This does not refute the Extended Church–Turing Thesis. It shows instead that uniform cost is not a reasonable accounting method for a machine whose primitive instructions can manipulate exponentially growing integers in one step.

title: Operational Semantics and Time Complexity of Turing Machines
text:
The lecture begins by recalling three points from the preceding discussion:

the logarithmic and uniform cost criteria;
the restriction to decision problems;
the Extended Church–Turing Thesis.

The logarithmic cost criterion is necessary for computational models whose primitive operations may manipulate values whose size grows during the computation. Charging every such operation one unit could hide the cost of handling increasingly long representations. For a Turing machine, however, one transition reads and modifies only one tape symbol, so the uniform and logarithmic criteria coincide at the level considered here.
A decision problem asks for a yes/no answer. Equivalently, it is represented by a language \(L \subseteq \Sigma^*\): the strings in \(L\) are precisely the yes-instances.
The class \(\mathrm{P}\), also called \(\mathrm{PTIME}\), contains the decision problems solvable in polynomial time by a deterministic Turing machine. Its importance is not simply that every polynomial is practically small. For example, an \(n^{100}\) algorithm is polynomial but already infeasible for modest \(n\). The deeper point is invariance under a change of reasonable deterministic computational model.


Extended Church–Turing Thesis and the invariance of P

All reasonable deterministic models of computation are polynomially related. Consequently, changing from deterministic Turing machines to another reasonable deterministic model, such as a URM or an ordinary programming language, does not change the class \(\mathrm{P}\).

The thesis is a statement about the relationship among reasonable models, not a theorem derived from the formal definitions in this lecture. Its consequence is nevertheless central: \(\mathrm{P}\) lets us discuss polynomial-time solvability without fixing every detail of the machine model.
A narrower class, such as the problems solvable in time \(n^3\) on one chosen model, need not be invariant. A simulation on another model may introduce overhead and move the same problem outside that exact bound. The union over all polynomial bounds is stable even when individual bounds are not.






flowchart LR
  A[Deterministic Turing machine] -->|polynomial simulation| B[URM or program model]
  B -->|polynomial simulation| A
  A --> C[Polynomial-time problems]
  B --> C
  classDef model fill:#2f6f9f,color:#fff,stroke:#173f5f
  classDef classNode fill:#8f3f71,color:#fff,stroke:#5d2549
  class A,B model
  class C classNode


 Changing a reasonable deterministic model may alter a precise polynomial bound, but not membership in P. 



This part of complexity theory is especially relevant to symbolic AI, automated reasoning, and verification. Rule-based procedures can establish that a property holds for every possible execution of a system, but the algorithms needed to prove such guarantees may be computationally expensive. This contrasts with the earlier information-theoretic material, which is particularly relevant to sub-symbolic AI such as machine learning and neural networks.

title: Operational Semantics and Time Complexity of Turing Machines
text:
3.1 Configurations
A configuration must contain all information required to determine the next step. For a one-tape Turing machine it is a triple
\[
(q,x,y),
\]
where \(q\) is the current internal state and \(x,y\in\Sigma^*\). The string \(x\) contains the tape from the left-end marker through the cell currently scanned; therefore its last symbol is under the head. The string \(y\) is the significant tape content strictly to the right of the head. Unwritten trailing cells are implicitly blank, and the first symbol of \(x\) is \(\triangleright\).

  
    ▷x₁…xⱼy₁…yₖ□□
  
  The head scans the last symbol of the left component.

Configuration \((q,x,y)\), where \(x=\triangleright x_1\cdots x_j\) and \(y=y_1\cdots y_k\). The head scans the last symbol of \(x\).
The initial configuration on input \(w\in\Sigma^*\) is
\[
(s,\triangleright,w).
\]
Initially the head scans \(\triangleright\), the machine is in state \(s\), and the input lies to the right.

title: Operational Semantics and Time Complexity of Turing Machines
text:
3.2 One computation step
Write
\[
(q,x,y)\longrightarrow_M(q',x',y')
\]
when \(M\) transforms the first configuration into the second in one transition. The relation is defined by cases according to \(\delta\) and the head movement.
The lecture develops the right-move case. Suppose
\[
x=x_1\cdots x_j,\qquad y=y_1\cdots y_k,
\]
and
\[
\delta(q,x_j)=(q',z,\rightarrow).
\]
The machine replaces the scanned symbol \(x_j\) by \(z\), moves right, and enters \(q'\). Hence
\[
(q,x,y)\longrightarrow_M(q',x',y'),
\]
with
\[
x'=x_1\cdots x_{j-1}zy_1,
\qquad
y'=y_2\cdots y_k.
\]
The symbol \(y_1\) moves into the left component because it becomes the newly scanned symbol. The left-move and stay cases are defined analogously, with separate boundary cases when the significant right suffix is empty.
The same step can be read directly in the parenthesised notation used in the notes. If
\[
\delta(q,0)=(q',1,\rightarrow),
\]
then
\[
(q,\triangleright 10,011)
\longrightarrow_M
(q',\triangleright 110,11).
\]
The scanned \(0\) is replaced by \(1\); after the right move, the first symbol of the former right part becomes the scanned symbol and therefore joins the new left part.

  Before the transition
  ▷10011□
  After the transition
  ▷11011□
  The machine writes 1, moves right and changes state.

Before the transition, the configuration is \((q,\triangleright 10,011)\). After the transition, it is \((q',\triangleright 110,11)\).






Note



The lecture distinguishes the internal state \(q\) from the complete configuration \((q,x,y)\). In broader operational-semantics terminology, the full configuration may also be called the state of the transition system.
crumbs: Operational Semantics and Time Complexity of Turing Machines

title: Operational Semantics and Time Complexity of Turing Machines
text:
3.3 Final configurations and computation shapes
A final configuration has the form
\[
(h,x,y),
\qquad
h\in\{\mathsf{yes},\mathsf{no},\mathsf{halt}\}.
\]
No transition is defined from a halting state. For a decision problem, the relevant outcomes are \(\mathsf{yes}\) and \(\mathsf{no}\).
Because \(M\) is deterministic, each non-final configuration has at most one successor. Starting from a fixed input, the reachable computation therefore has no branching. Three shapes are possible:






flowchart TB
  I[Initial configuration] --> Q{Evolution}
  Q -->|finite| H[Halting configuration]
  Q -->|repeated configuration| L[Infinite loop]
  Q -->|always new configurations| D[Infinite divergence]
  classDef start fill:#2f6f9f,color:#fff,stroke:#173f5f
  classDef halt fill:#347a4a,color:#fff,stroke:#20512f
  classDef nonterm fill:#8f3f71,color:#fff,stroke:#5d2549
  class I,Q start
  class H halt
  class L,D nonterm


 A deterministic computation either halts, repeats a configuration, or continues forever through new configurations. 











Case
Shape
What can be concluded?




Termination
A finite path reaches \(\mathsf{yes}\), \(\mathsf{no}\), or \(\mathsf{halt}\)
The computation has a finite running time.


Repeating loop
A configuration already seen is reached again
Determinism forces the same future behaviour, so the loop is infinite and detectable once repetition occurs.


Divergence without repetition
Every reached configuration is new
The run is infinite, but no finite observation certifies that it will never halt.



The course restricts attention to machines proved to halt on every input. No general algorithm can inspect an arbitrary Turing machine and decide whether it always terminates. For decision problems, a terminating machine decides a language \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\) by satisfying
\[
M(w)=\mathsf{yes}\Longleftrightarrow w\in L,
\qquad
M(w)=\mathsf{no}\Longleftrightarrow w\notin L.
\]

title: Operational Semantics and Time Complexity of Turing Machines
text:
5.1 Counting the steps
For an unprocessed substring of length \(n\):



Phase
Steps recorded in the lecture




Scan from left to right and reach the boundary
\(n+2\)


Return from right to left
\(n\)


Recurse on the remaining substring
\(T(n-2)\)



The notes state the recurrence, up to a possible additive constant that the lecturer explicitly flagged for checking,
\[
T(n)=
\begin{cases}
2, & n=0,\\
2n+2+T(n-2), & n>0.
\end{cases}
\]
Repeated substitution adds a decreasing arithmetic sequence:
\[
T(n)
=
(2n+2)+(2(n-2)+2)+(2(n-4)+2)+\cdots.
\]
There are about \(n/2\) iterations, and the sum of the linear terms is quadratic. Therefore the solution has the form
\[
T(n)=an^2+bn+c,
\]
for suitable constants \(a,b,c\), and consequently the machine has quadratic running time. The lecture intentionally postpones the formal introduction of asymptotic notation, so the key conclusion here is the explicit quadratic form rather than a formal \(\Theta\)-classification.

title: Multitape Simulation, Time Complexity, and Linear Speed-Up
text:
The lecture begins by comparing the running time of a \(k\)-tape Turing machine with that of a standard single-tape Turing machine. The purpose is not merely to show that the two models decide the same languages: it is to quantify the time overhead introduced by the simulation.
Let \(M\) be a \(k\)-tape Turing machine deciding a language \(L \subseteq \Sigma^*\). On an input \(x\) of length \(n=|x|\), assume that \(M\) halts after at most \(f(n)\) steps, with
\[
f(n) \ge n.
\]
The lower bound \(f(n)\ge n\) is used later to simplify \(O(n+kf(n))\) to \(O(f(n))\), because the number \(k\) of tapes is fixed for the machine.


Multitape-to-single-tape simulation

If a \(k\)-tape Turing machine \(M\) decides \(L \subseteq \Sigma^*\) in at most \(f(n)\) steps, where \(f(n)\ge n\), then there exists a single-tape Turing machine \(M'\) deciding the same language in at most \(\widehat f(n)\) steps, with
\[
\widehat f(n) \in O\!\left((f(n))^2\right).
\]
Equivalently, for every input \(x\),
\[
M'(x)=\mathrm{yes}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
M(x)=\mathrm{yes}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
x\in L.
\]



The tape alphabet of \(M'\) must represent both the symbols written by \(M\) and the positions of the \(k\) tape heads. If \(\Gamma\) is the tape alphabet of \(M\), the simulator uses an enriched alphabet containing unmarked and marked versions of its symbols. A marked symbol records that the simulated head is currently scanning that tape cell.
The contents of the \(k\) tapes are stored consecutively on the single tape of \(M'\), separated by delimiters. Thus, one tape contains a complete instantaneous representation of all the tapes of \(M\).

  
    Tape 1
    ▷x₁…xₙ□□…
  
  
    Tape 2
    ▷□□□□□…
  
  
    ⋮
  
  
    Tape k
    ▷□□□□□…
  
  Initial configuration of M: tape 1 contains the input x, while tapes 2 through k contain only blank symbols. Every head starts on the first data cell.



  
    Tape of M′
    ⊢x₁x₂…xₙ
    #a₁a₂a₃…
    #…#b₁b₂…bᵣ□
  
  The simulator stores the k tape contents one after another. Delimiters separate tape blocks, and the red markers encode the k simulated head positions.

The logical content of the handwritten tape drawing is captured by the following compact representation:
The construction in the notes compares the original machine and its simulator as follows.








Component
Original machine \(M\)
Simulating machine \(M'\)




Number of tapes
\(k\) tapes
One tape


Initial tape contents
Tape 1 contains \(x=x_1\cdots x_n\); tapes \(2,\ldots,k\) contain only blanks
The input is initially \(x=x_1\cdots x_n\); during the simulation, one tape stores the \(k\) tape contents of \(M\) consecutively


Language decided
\(M(x)=\mathrm{yes}\Longleftrightarrow x\in L\)
\(M'(x)=\mathrm{yes}\Longleftrightarrow x\in L\)


Running time
At most \(f(|x|)\)
\(O((f(|x|))^2)\)


Tape alphabet
\(\Gamma\)
An extended alphabet \(\Gamma'\) containing the symbols of \(\Gamma\), marked copies used to record head positions, and dedicated separator/blank markers



The marked copy of a symbol is not new simulated data. It records that the corresponding head of \(M\) is scanning that cell. The separator symbols identify where one simulated tape block ends and the next begins.



To simulate one step of \(M\), the single-tape machine \(M'\) performs two conceptual passes.

Read pass. It scans the encoded tape, finds the \(k\) marked symbols currently read by the heads of \(M\), and stores those \(k\) symbols in its finite control.
Update pass. It returns across the encoding and performs the writes, head movements and state change prescribed by the transition function of \(M\).

  C[Encoded configuration] --> R[Scan all tape blocks]
  R --> S[Store k scanned symbols in the state]
  S --> B[Return across the encoding]
  B --> U[Write symbols and move head markers]
  U --> N[Next encoded configuration]

  classDef action fill:#198754,color:#fff,stroke:#0f5132;
  class C,N data;
  class R,S,B,U action;


 One simulated transition requires a scan to collect the read symbols and a second pass to apply the transition. 



The expensive case occurs when a simulated head moves beyond the represented end of one of its tapes. The corresponding tape block must grow, so \(M'\) may need to shift the remainder of its physical tape one cell to the right. Therefore, the cost of one simulated transition is proportional to the total length of the current encoding.



Initially, the input contributes \(n\) cells. During one transition, each of the \(k\) simulated heads can extend its tape content by at most one cell. Hence, after \(t\) steps of \(M\), the sum of the represented tape lengths is at most
\[
O(n+kt).
\]
Since \(t\le f(n)\),
\[
O(n+kt)
\subseteq O(n+kf(n))
=O(f(n)),
\]
where the last equality uses the facts that \(k\) is constant and \(f(n)\ge n\).






flowchart LR

 The represented tape content grows by at most k cells per simulated step. 






In the worst case, \(M'\) scans or shifts an encoding of length \(O(f(n))\) in order to simulate one step of \(M\). The constant number of passes and the fixed number \(k\) of tapes are absorbed into the asymptotic notation:
\[
\text{cost of one simulated step}=k\cdot O(f(n))=O(f(n)).
\]
Machine \(M'\) must simulate at most \(f(n)\) steps. Therefore,
\[
\underbrace{f(n)}_{\text{simulated steps}}
\cdot
\underbrace{O(f(n))}_{\text{cost per step}}
=
O\!\left((f(n))^2\right).
\]



Quantity
Upper bound




Length of the complete one-tape encoding
\(O(f(n))\)


Cost of simulating one step of \(M\)
\(O(f(n))\)


Number of steps simulated
\(f(n)\)


Total running time of \(M'\)
\(O((f(n))^2)\)



The quadratic bound is a worst-case upper bound. It reflects repeated full scans and possible shifts of the encoded tapes, not a claim that every simulated step necessarily takes the maximum time.

title: Multitape Simulation, Time Complexity, and Linear Speed-Up
text:
3.1 Example
Suppose that
\[
L\in\operatorname{TIME}(100n^2).
\]
Choose \(\varepsilon=\frac{1}{100}\). The theorem gives
\[
f'(n)
=
\frac{1}{100}(100n^2)+n+2
=
n^2+n+2,
\]
and consequently
\[
L\in\operatorname{TIME}(n^2+n+2).
\]
This does not change the quadratic order of growth. It shows that the leading constant can be reduced, at the cost of a linear input-conversion term.

title: Multitape Simulation, Time Complexity, and Linear Speed-Up
section: 3.2 Proof idea: grouping cells into macro-symbols
text:
3.2 Proof idea: grouping cells into macro-symbols
Let \(M\) decide \(L\) in at most \(f(n)\) steps. Denote its components schematically by
\[
M=(K,\Sigma,\delta,s),
\]
where \(K\) is its finite set of states, \(\Sigma\) is its tape alphabet, \(\delta\) is its transition function and \(s\) is its initial state.
Construct a machine \(M'\) whose larger tape alphabet groups blocks of \(m\) symbols of \(M\) into one macro-symbol. Thus a symbol of the new alphabet represents an element of \(\Sigma^m\). The block size \(m\) will be chosen as a function of the desired constant \(\varepsilon\).

  
    Tape of M
    aᵢaᵢ₊₁…aᵢ₊ₘ₋₁
    
    aᵢ₊ₘ…aᵢ₊₂ₘ₋₁
  
  
    Tape of M′
    [aᵢ … aᵢ₊ₘ₋₁][aᵢ₊ₘ … aᵢ₊₂ₘ₋₁]
  
  Each cell of the faster machine stores a block of m consecutive symbols of the original tape. Two adjacent macro-cells expose at most 2m original cells.

During one macro-step, \(M'\) reads and modifies at most two adjacent macro-symbols, corresponding to at most \(2m\) cells of the original tape. This local information is enough to reproduce \(m\) consecutive steps of \(M\): in \(m\) steps, the original head cannot move farther than \(m\) cells from its starting position.
The lecture’s construction assigns at most six elementary steps of \(M'\) to one macro-step. Therefore, \(m\) steps of \(M\) are simulated in at most six steps of \(M'\).








Machine action
Amount handled
Cost in the construction




Read/modify local macro-region
At most \(2\) macro-symbols of size \(m\)
At most \(6\) steps of \(M'\)


Simulate original computation
\(m\) steps of \(M\)
At most \(6\) steps of \(M'\)


Simulate \(f(n)\) steps of \(M\)
\(f(n)/m\) macro-steps
At most \(6f(n)/m\) steps of \(M'\)



Hence the simulation phase takes at most
\[
\frac{6}{m}f(n)
\]
steps. To make this coefficient no larger than the prescribed \(\varepsilon\), choose \(m\) so that
\[
\frac{6}{m}\le\varepsilon,
\qquad\text{for example}\qquad
m\ge\left\lceil\frac{6}{\varepsilon}\right\rceil.
\]
The computation then has two phases.






flowchart LR
  X["Input of length n"] --> C["Convert the input"]
  C --> E["Grouped tape encoding"]
  E --> S["Simulate blocks of m steps"]
  S --> H["Accept or reject"]
  C -. "cost: n plus 2" .-> E
  S -. "cost: at most epsilon times f(n)" .-> H
  classDef input fill:#0d6efd,color:#ffffff,stroke:#084298
  classDef preprocess fill:#6f42c1,color:#ffffff,stroke:#432874
  classDef simulate fill:#198754,color:#ffffff,stroke:#0f5132
  class X input
  class C,E preprocess
  class S,H simulate


 The total running time consists of input conversion followed by accelerated simulation. 




Input conversion. Read the input and encode it using the grouped alphabet \(\Sigma^m\). According to the lecture construction, this needs \(n+2\) steps and uses a second tape.
Accelerated simulation. Simulate groups of \(m\) transitions of \(M\), using at most \[
\frac{6}{m}f(n)\le\varepsilon f(n)
\] steps.

Adding the two costs yields
\[
f'(n)
=
\varepsilon f(n)+n+2.
\]
The result concerns constant-factor speed-up. The extra \(n+2\) term remains because the input must still be read and reorganised before the grouped simulation begins.

title: Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Relation to Entropy
text:
Kolmogorov complexity measures the descriptive complexity of an individual string. To define it, a program must itself be represented as a finite string that can be supplied to a universal Turing machine.
Let a Turing machine be described schematically by
\[
m=(K,\Sigma,\delta,s),
\]
where:








Component
Meaning
Role in the finite description




\(K\)
finite set of states
determines the control states that must be encoded


\(\Sigma\)
finite tape alphabet
determines the symbols that may be read and written


\(\delta\)
transition function
returns a next state or special outcome, a symbol to write, and a head movement


\(s\in K\)
initial state
identifies where execution begins



The tape is unbounded, but the machine description is finite. A configuration consists of the current state, the finite non-blank portion of the tape, and the head position.






flowchart TB
    C["Finite control: current state q"] -->|"read current symbol a"| H["Read/write head"]
    H --> T["... | blank | 1 | 0 | a | 1 | blank | ..."]
    C --> D["delta(q,a) = (q',b,d)"]
    D -->|"write b"| H
    D -->|"enter q'"| C
    D --> M["move d in {-1,0,+1}"]

    classDef control fill:#fff2cc,stroke:#b38600,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef tape fill:#e8f1ff,stroke:#2f6fb0,stroke-width:2px;
    class C,D control;
    class H,T,M tape;


 Schematic Turing-machine configuration. The finite control reads one tape cell, applies the transition function, writes a symbol, changes state, and moves the head. 



A universal Turing machine \(U\) receives an encoding of another machine \(m\) and simulates it. When the simulated machine halts with a string \(x\) on its output tape, write
\[
U(m)=x.
\]
The notation \(m(x)\) can likewise be read as the result produced by machine \(m\) on the relevant input.


The universal Turing machine is written as
\[
U=(\mathbb Z_U,\Sigma_U,\delta_U,s_U),
\]
and its tape alphabet must contain at least the symbols needed to write binary descriptions and control the tape representation. In the notation used in the lecture,
\[
\Sigma_U \supseteq \{0,1,\sqcup,\triangleright\}.
\]
where \(\sqcup\) is the blank symbol and \(\triangleright\) is the left-end or start marker. The first two symbols, \(0\) and \(1\), are the symbols from which the binary encoding is constructed.






NoteStatus of the separator symbol



The notes explicitly write \(\Sigma_U\supseteq\{0,1,\sqcup,\triangleright\}\), without including a semicolon. The tape drawing nevertheless uses ; between variable-length fields. The chapter preserves both facts without silently modifying the stated alphabet: ; is treated as a separator in the schematic representation. For ; to be an actual symbol written on the tape, it would also have to belong to \(\Sigma_U\); alternatively, the separator must be implemented through a binary self-delimiting encoding. The lecture notes do not resolve which interpretation is intended at this point.


The machine to be encoded is
\[
m=(K,\Sigma,\delta,s),
\]
with transition function
\[
\delta:
K\times\Sigma
\longrightarrow
\bigl(K\cup\{\mathrm{yes},\mathrm{no},\mathrm{halt}\}\bigr)
\times\Sigma\times\{\rightarrow,\leftarrow,-\}.
\]
The movement component uses \(\rightarrow\) to move one tape cell to the right, \(\leftarrow\) to move one tape cell to the left, and \(-\) to leave the head on the current cell. The three special outcomes in the codomain are not members of \(K\). Consequently, the encoding must assign numbers not only to the states in \(K\) and the symbols in \(\Sigma\), but also to \(\mathrm{yes}\), \(\mathrm{no}\), and \(\mathrm{halt}\).


Let
\[
K=\{s,q_0,\ldots,q_{|K|-2}\}.
\]
There are \(|K|\) states in total: the initial state \(s\) plus the remaining \(|K|-1\) states. The lecture assigns consecutive integers as follows:
\[
\nu(s)=0,
\]
\[
\nu(q_i)=i+1
\qquad
\text{for }i=0,\ldots,|K|-2.
\]
Thus the ordinary states use exactly the integers
\[
0,1,\ldots,|K|-1.
\]
The three special results appearing in the codomain of \(\delta\) are placed immediately after the ordinary states:
\[
\nu(\mathrm{yes})=|K|,
\qquad
\nu(\mathrm{no})=|K|+1,
\qquad
\nu(\mathrm{halt})=|K|+2.
\]



Object
Assigned integer or range




initial state \(s\)
\(0\)


remaining states \(q_0,\ldots,q_{|K|-2}\)

title: Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Relation to Entropy
text:
2.1 Conditional Kolmogorov complexity
For strings \(x\) and \(y\), the conditional Kolmogorov complexity of \(x\) given \(y\) is
\[
K_U(x\mid y)=\min_{m:U(m,y)=x}|m|.
\]
The auxiliary string \(y\) is supplied to the universal machine and is not counted as part of the program length. The quantity measures the additional description needed to produce \(x\) once \(y\) is already known.

2.1.1 Example: a long string of zeros
Let
\[
x=0^n=\underbrace{00\cdots0}_{n\text{ zeros}}.
\]
If the value of \(n\) must be included in the program, the program needs both:

instructions that print a zero repeatedly;
a representation of the number \(n\).

The two situations in the notes are visually different:






flowchart LR
    subgraph A["Unconditional description"]
      P1["program: loop and encoded value n"] --> U1["universal machine U"]
      U1 --> X1["0 repeated n times"]
    end
    subgraph B["Conditional description"]
      P2["fixed loop program"] --> U2["universal machine U"]
      N["auxiliary input n"] --> U2
      U2 --> X2["0 repeated n times"]
    end

    classDef prog fill:#fff2cc,stroke:#b38600,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef machine fill:#e8f1ff,stroke:#2f6fb0,stroke-width:2px;
    class P1,P2,N prog;
    class U1,U2 machine;


 Producing a long all-zero string with and without the length supplied as auxiliary input. 



If \(n=|x|\) is instead supplied as conditional information, a fixed loop suffices:
for i = 1 to |x|:
    print(0)
The corresponding tape picture has a fixed program followed by the auxiliary input \(n\):

  
    ▷
    Print(0)
    ;
    bin(n)
    □□
  

Figure: the program is fixed; only the auxiliary input \(n=|x|\) varies. The output is \(0^n\).
The loop has constant size, independently of \(n\). Consequently,
\[
K_U(0^n\mid n)=O(1).
\]
The important distinction is between receiving \(n\) as an external input and hard-coding \(n\) inside the program. In the latter case, the bits used to represent \(n\) contribute to the program length.

title: Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Relation to Entropy
text:
4.1 A direct upper bound
Consider a universal machine with two behaviours selected by its first bit:

if the first bit is \(0\), it interprets the rest of the input as a machine description and performs universal simulation;
if the first bit is \(1\), it prints the remaining input verbatim.

Then \(1x\) is a program that outputs \(x\). For this particular machine,
\[
K_U(x)\le |x|+1.
\]
By the invariance property, for any fixed reference universal machine,
\[
K(x)\le |x|+c.
\]
The book’s binary-only model has no separate delimiter. Repeating the bits so that a reserved binary stop sequence remains available gives the weaker direct estimate
\[
K(x)\le 2|x|+c.
\]
The factor \(2\) is an encoding overhead, not an intrinsic property of the string. The lecture’s machine model with a separator avoids it.
A binary-only description can also reduce the overhead by first encoding \(|x|\) in a self-delimiting way and then writing \(x\) without repetition. This changes the dominant term from approximately \(2|x|\) to \(|x|\) plus a logarithmic description of the length. Iterating the same idea pushes the remaining overhead into progressively smaller iterated logarithmic terms. The lecture used this observation only to explain the role of separators and did not develop a new complexity notion from it.

title: Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Relation to Entropy
text:
4.2 Existence of incompressible strings
For every integer \(k\), fewer than \(2^k\) binary programs have length strictly less than \(k\):
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}2^i=2^k-1.
\]
Each terminating program produces at most one output string. Therefore, fewer than \(2^k\) strings can have Kolmogorov complexity less than \(k\).
There are exactly \(2^k\) binary strings of length \(k\). By the pigeonhole principle, at least one length-\(k\) string is not produced by any program shorter than \(k\). Hence, for every \(k\), there exists a string \(x\in\{0,1\}^k\) such that
\[
K(x)\ge k=|x|.
\]
This is an existence statement. It does not provide an algorithm for identifying a particular incompressible string.







Objects counted
Number




binary programs of length \(i\)
\(2^i\)


binary programs of length less than \(k\)
\(\sum_{i=0}^{k-1}2^i=2^k-1\)


binary strings of length exactly \(k\)
\(2^k\)



Since there are more length-\(k\) strings than shorter programs, at least one length-\(k\) string cannot be named by a program of length below \(k\).
crumbs: Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Relation to Entropy

title: Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Relation to Entropy
text:
4.3 Non-computability
Kolmogorov complexity is mathematically well defined but not computable. To determine \(K(x)\) exactly, an algorithm would need to decide whether each shorter candidate program eventually outputs \(x\) or runs forever. Non-termination prevents such a general decision procedure.
The difficulty is stronger than merely not knowing a shortest program: in general, even the length of that shortest program cannot be computed algorithmically. This is why useful results about Kolmogorov complexity are commonly expressed as upper and lower bounds.

title: Kolmogorov Complexity and Its Relation to Entropy
text:
7.1 Choosing the Shannon code
Let \(\varphi_S\) be the Shannon code for the distribution \(P^m\). Its expected length satisfies
\[
\mathbb E_{P^m}[|\varphi_S(X^m)|]
< H(P^m)+1
= mH(P)+1.
\]
The Shannon decoder is determined by the distribution \(P\). A shortest effective description of \(P\) can therefore be used as part of a program implementing that decoder. Absorbing fixed implementation details into the machine-dependent constant, the lecture writes this decoder cost as \(K(P)\). Hence
\[
\mathbb E_{P^m}[K(X^m)]
\le
K(P)+mH(P)+1.
\]
After division by \(m\),
\[
\frac{1}{m}\mathbb E_{P^m}[K(X^m)]
\le
H(P)+\frac{K(P)+1}{m}.
\]
The two directions can be compared directly:








Direction
Construction used
Result




entropy lower-bounds expected algorithmic description length
treat shortest machine descriptions as a uniquely decodable code
\(H(P^m)\le \mathbb E[K(X^m)]\)


entropy upper-bounds the normalized expectation asymptotically
turn a Shannon codeword and its decoder into a program
\(\mathbb E[K(X^m)]\le K(P)+mH(P)+1\)



Combining the lower and upper bounds gives
\[
H(P)
\le
\frac{1}{m}\mathbb E_{P^m}[K(X^m)]
\le
H(P)+\frac{K(P)+1}{m}.
\]
The term \(K(P)+1\) does not depend on the block length \(m\). Therefore,
\[
\lim_{m\to\infty}
\frac{1}{m}\mathbb E_{P^m}[K(X^m)]
=H(P).
\]
The conclusion concerns the expected Kolmogorov complexity of strings generated by the source, normalized per symbol. It does not claim that every individual length-\(m\) string has complexity exactly \(mH(P)\).

title: The Deterministic Time Hierarchy Theorem
text:
The lecture begins with a question about the usefulness of proper time bounds: could substantially different proper functions nevertheless define the same deterministic time class? The time hierarchy theorem gives a precise separation result. It does not say that every pair of distinct functions gives different classes; rather, it constructs a language that can be decided within one bound but cannot be decided within a sufficiently smaller one.

Notation note. The opening question includes an illustrative equality involving an exponential-looking time bound. The handwritten exponent is not unambiguous enough to reproduce as a formula, so the chapter preserves the question it motivates rather than guessing its exact expression.

The starting point is the halting problem. Its undecidability is familiar, but its formulation through encoded Turing machines is also the model needed for the quantitative result.


Write a deterministic Turing machine as
\[
M=(K,\Sigma,\delta,s),
\]
where:

\(K\) is the finite set of states;
\(\Sigma\) is the tape alphabet;
\(\delta\) is the transition function;
\(s\) is the initial state.

A machine can be represented by a finite binary string, denoted by \(\langle M\rangle\). The lecture’s encoding assigns distinct integer codes to the objects used by the machine. One possible assignment, following the notes, is:







Object
Assigned codes




Ordinary states
\(1,2,\ldots,|K|\)


Accepting and rejecting outcomes
\(|K|+1\) and \(|K|+2\)


Tape symbols
\(|K|+3,\ldots,|K|+|\Sigma|+2\)


Moves right, left and stay
\(|K|+|\Sigma|+3\), \(|K|+|\Sigma|+4\) and \(|K|+|\Sigma|+5\)



The transition function is encoded as a sequence of tuples. Each component of a tuple is replaced by its assigned integer code, and the resulting description is written in binary. The encoding therefore contains enough information to recover the states, tape symbols, head moves and transition rules of \(M\).
The exact integer codes are a convention. What matters is that the representation is finite, unambiguous and effectively decodable.



A universal Turing machine \(U\) takes an encoded machine and an input string. It simulates the encoded machine on that input:
\[
U(\langle M\rangle,x)\text{ simulates }M(x).
\]
In the simulation, one tape contains the description of \(M\), another contains the input \(x\), and working tape space is used to keep track of the current simulated configuration. A configuration records the current state, the tape contents and the head positions. To simulate one transition, the universal machine reads the current configuration, consults the encoded transition function \(\delta\), and updates the configuration.
The halting language is
\[
H=\{\langle M,x\rangle\mid M(x)\downarrow\},
\]
where \(M(x)\downarrow\) means that \(M\) eventually halts on \(x\), either by accepting or by rejecting.


Halting Theorem

The halting language \(H\) is enumerable (Turing-recognizable), but it is not decidable.

To recognize \(H\), simulate \(M\) on \(x\) and accept as soon as the simulation halts. This procedure accepts every pair in \(H\). If \(M\) never halts, the simulation also continues forever, so it does not provide a decision procedure for non-members. The halting theorem states that no alternative Turing machine can decide all such pairs.
This distinction motivates the next step. For an unbounded computation, a simulator may run forever. If a time limit is supplied, however, the simulator can stop when the limit is reached and return a negative answer. The bounded version is therefore decidable.
