title: The Deterministic Time Hierarchy Theorem
text:
2.1 The bounded halting language
For a proper function \(f\), define
\[
H_f=\left\{\langle M,x\rangle\;\middle|\;
M(x)\text{ accepts within at most }f(|x|)+5|x|+4\text{ steps}\right\}.
\]
Here, acceptance means that the simulated machine enters its accepting, or yes, state within the stated number of transitions. A computation that rejects, does not halt before the limit, or accepts only after the limit does not put the pair in \(H_f\).
The input to the language is the encoded pair \(\langle M,x\rangle\). When a time class is written for this language, its input length \(n\) is the length of the whole pair encoding; the clock in the definition of \(H_f\) is based on the length \(|x|\) of the simulated input.
The additive term \(5|x|+4\) is a deliberate technical allowance. The diagonal machine constructed later has to copy its input in order to form a pair of the form \(\langle M,M\rangle\). In the encoding used in the lecture, this copy takes at most \(5|M|+4\) steps. The allowance makes the diagonal machine’s own computation fit inside the acceptance bound. A different encoding or copying routine could require a different fixed linear overhead; the proof would then use that overhead consistently.
A bounded simulator can decide \(H_f\):






flowchart TD
  A["Input: encoded pair (M, x)"] --> B["Compute the step limit"]
  B --> C["Write the initial configuration of M on x"]
  C --> D["Simulate one transition of M"]
  D --> E{"Has M accepted?"}
  E -- "Yes" --> F["Accept the pair"]
  E -- "No" --> G{"Has M rejected or reached the limit?"}
  G -- "Yes" --> H["Reject the pair"]
  G -- "No" --> D


 The bounded simulator stops when the simulated machine accepts, rejects, or reaches the prescribed time limit. 



The machine always halts: it either observes an accepting or rejecting configuration, or completes the prescribed number of simulated steps. This is exactly what was missing in the unbounded halting problem.

title: The Deterministic Time Hierarchy Theorem
section: 3.1 Corollary: a strict separation between time classes
text:
3.1 Corollary: a strict separation between time classes
The theorem gives the following consequence, also recorded in the lecture:


Corollary: strict time-class separation

For a proper function \(f\) with \(f(n)\geq n\),
\[
\mathrm{TIME}(f(n))\subsetneq
\mathrm{TIME}\bigl((f(2n+1))^3\bigr).
\]

The idea is to apply the theorem to the rescaled proper function \(g(n)=f(2n+1)\). Its upper bound is
\[
g(n)^3=(f(2n+1))^3,
\]
while its lower-bound exclusion is based on
\[
g(\lfloor n/2\rfloor)
=f\bigl(2\lfloor n/2\rfloor+1\bigr).
\]
The argument of \(f\) here is \(n\) when \(n\) is odd and \(n+1\) when \(n\) is even. Using the monotonicity of the proper bound, this is at least \(f(n)\). Consequently, the witness supplied by the theorem is not in \(\mathrm{TIME}(f(n))\), even though it belongs to the larger class with the cubic bound.

title: The Deterministic Time Hierarchy Theorem
section: 4.1 What this says about P versus NP
text:
4.1 What this says about P versus NP
The inclusions established in earlier lectures are
\[
\mathrm{P}\subseteq\mathrm{NP}\subseteq\mathrm{EXP}.
\]
Together with \(\mathrm{P}\neq\mathrm{EXP}\), they imply that at least one of the two inclusions must be strict:
\[
\mathrm{P}\neq\mathrm{NP}
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\mathrm{NP}\neq\mathrm{EXP}.
\]
The “or” is not exclusive: both inequalities may hold. The time hierarchy theorem does not determine which inclusion is strict, and therefore does not settle whether \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).
The lecture uses SAT to make the significance of the open question concrete. SAT is NP-complete. If a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for SAT were found, then every language in NP could be decided in polynomial time by reducing it to SAT. This would imply
\[
\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}.
\]
A faster-than-exponential algorithm is not necessarily a polynomial-time algorithm. The lecture’s brief remark about the Exponential Time Hypothesis (ETH) and a claimed improvement for SAT is not recoverable unambiguously. The handwritten annotation says that ETH is false, but the adjoining sentence and the spoken explanation do not consistently establish whether SAT was said to be solvable or not solvable in less than an exponential bound. The chapter therefore does not present a refutation of ETH as an established fact. The point that can be retained without assuming a particular claim about its status is that being faster than an exponential-time bound does not, by itself, mean being polynomial-time, and therefore does not by itself imply \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

title: The Deterministic Time Hierarchy Theorem
text:
5.1 Part 1: deciding \(H_f\) in cubic time
We construct a machine \(M_f\) that decides \(H_f\). On input \(\langle M,x\rangle\), it performs the following steps:

Copy the input data needed for the simulation.
Compute the bound \(f(|x|)+5|x|+4\) in unary.
Store the initial configuration of \(M\) on input \(x\).
Simulate at most that many transitions of \(M\).
Accept if the simulated machine reaches its yes state within the limit; otherwise reject.

The initial configuration has the start state \(s\), the input string \(x\) on the appropriate tape, and blank symbols in the other tape cells. During the simulation, the working tape stores the current encoded configuration. At each macro-step, \(M_f\) reads that configuration, consults the transition table encoded in \(\langle M\rangle\), applies the corresponding change, and writes the next configuration.
The tape organization is schematic: it distinguishes the fixed machine description, the simulated input and the working record of the simulated machine’s configuration.


<span class="tape-label">Description tape</span>
<div class="tape-cells"><span class="tape-cell">encoded M</span></div>


<span class="tape-label">Input tape</span>
<div class="tape-cells"><span class="tape-cell">x</span><span class="tape-cell">blank</span><span class="tape-cell">blank</span></div>


<span class="tape-label">Working tape</span>
<div class="tape-cells"><span class="tape-cell">current state</span><span class="tape-cell">tape contents</span><span class="tape-cell">head positions</span></div>



Schematic of the simulator’s records. The working tape stores the encoded configuration that is updated at each macro-step.


5.1.1 Counting the steps
Let \(n\) be the length of the encoded input pair. Since \(|x|\leq n\), the number of simulated transitions is at most
\[
f(|x|)+5|x|+4=O(f(n)),
\]
using the growth condition \(f(n)\geq n\) and the properness assumptions on \(f\).
It remains to count the cost of one macro-step. If \(M\) has \(k\) tapes, then during a computation of \(O(f(n))\) transitions, each simulated tape can use at most \(O(f(n))\) cells. The encoded configuration therefore has length
\[
O(k f(n)).
\]
The simulator may need to scan this record, as well as the encoded transition information, to find the appropriate transition and update the configuration. The number \(k\) is not a fixed constant here: \(M\) is part of the input, so the number of tapes of the machine being simulated may vary. Its encoding is part of the input of length \(n\), and hence \(k\leq n\leq f(n)\). Therefore, the cost of one macro-step is bounded by
\[
O(k f(n))=O(f(n)^2).
\]
There are \(O(f(n))\) macro-steps, so the total simulation time is
\[
O(f(n))\cdot O(f(n)^2)=O(f(n)^3).
\]
The initial copying and the computation of the unary time limit fit within this bound. Thus
\[
H_f\in\mathrm{TIME}(f(n)^3).
\]
The cubic estimate is a convenient upper bound for this uniform simulation. The lecture notes that a more careful analysis can improve the estimate, but does not need a sharper bound for the hierarchy theorem.

title: The Deterministic Time Hierarchy Theorem
text:
5.2 Part 2: diagonalization
We prove that
\[
H_f\notin\mathrm{TIME}\bigl(f(\lfloor n/2\rfloor)\bigr)
\]
by contradiction. Suppose that there is a deterministic machine \(M_{H_f}\) deciding \(H_f\) within at most \(f(\lfloor n/2\rfloor)\) steps on inputs of length \(n\).

5.2.1 Constructing the diagonal machine
Construct a machine \(D\) that, on input an encoded machine \(M\):

copies \(M\) to form the pair \(\langle M,M\rangle\);
runs \(M_{H_f}\) on this pair;
returns the opposite answer.

In particular,
\[
\begin{aligned}
D(M)&=\text{yes} &&\Longleftrightarrow&& M_{H_f}(\langle M,M\rangle)=\text{no},\\
D(M)&=\text{no}  &&\Longleftrightarrow&& M_{H_f}(\langle M,M\rangle)=\text{yes}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The length of the encoded pair is \(2|M|+1\) in the encoding used in the lecture. By the assumed time bound for \(M_{H_f}\), its computation on this pair takes at most
\[
f\left(\left\lfloor\frac{2|M|+1}{2}\right\rfloor\right)
=f(|M|)
\]
steps. Copying \(M\) takes at most \(5|M|+4\) steps. Consequently, the entire computation of \(D(M)\) takes at most
\[
f(|M|)+5|M|+4
\]
steps. Since \(M_{H_f}\) is assumed to be a decider, \(D\) always halts.


5.2.2 Running \(D\) on its own encoding
Now consider the pair \(\langle D,D\rangle\). By definition of \(H_f\),
\[
M_{H_f}(\langle D,D\rangle)=\text{yes}
\]
if and only if \(D(D)\) accepts within at most
\[
f(|D|)+5|D|+4
\]
steps. But the running-time calculation above shows that \(D(D)\) always halts within precisely this allowed bound. Thus
\[
M_{H_f}(\langle D,D\rangle)=\text{yes}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
D(D)=\text{yes}.
\]
On the other hand, the construction of \(D\) says that it returns the opposite of the answer of \(M_{H_f}\) on the same pair. Therefore,
\[
D(D)=\text{yes}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
M_{H_f}(\langle D,D\rangle)=\text{no},
\]
which contradicts the preceding equivalence.
The same contradiction can be seen by considering the two possible outputs:

If \(D(D)=\text{no}\), then \(M_{H_f}(\langle D,D\rangle)=\text{yes}\). The definition of \(H_f\) would then say that \(D(D)\) accepts within the allowed bound, contradicting its output.
If \(D(D)=\text{yes}\), then \(M_{H_f}(\langle D,D\rangle)=\text{no}\). This is impossible: \(D(D)\) halts because \(M_{H_f}\) is a decider; it does not reject; and it cannot accept after the allowed bound because its running time was shown to be at most that bound.

Both possibilities lead to a contradiction. Hence no such decider \(M_{H_f}\) exists, and
\[
H_f\notin\mathrm{TIME}\bigl(f(\lfloor n/2\rfloor)\bigr).
\]
This diagonal argument is the quantitative counterpart of the reasoning in the halting theorem: the constructed machine examines the answer of a purported decider on its own encoding and reverses that answer. Here, the additional time calculation ensures that the reversal takes place within the very time limit used to define \(H_f\).

title: Introduction to Information Theory
text:
The course carries 6 CFU and consists of 48 hours. The lecture introduces separate references for the two main parts of the course.
For Information Theory, the indicated references are:

Thomas M. Cover and Joy A. Thomas, Elements of Information Theory;
David J. C. MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms.

For Complexity Theory, the indicated reference is:

Christos H. Papadimitriou, Computational Complexity.

The first lecture begins the Information Theory part and refers to Claude Shannon’s 1948 paper A Mathematical Theory of Communication.

title: Introduction to Information Theory
text:
3.1 Limiting cases
The two extreme cases make this relationship clear.

3.1.1 A certain message
If
\[
p(m)=1,
\]
then the message was already certain. Receiving the message removes no uncertainty and therefore provides no new information:
\[
I(m)=0.
\]


3.1.2 An increasingly unlikely message
As
\[
p(m)\to 0^+,
\]
the occurrence of \(m\) becomes increasingly surprising. The corresponding information should grow without bound:
\[
I(m)\to +\infty.
\]
The limit is written as \(p(m)\to0^+\) because the lecture defines the information of messages with positive probability. A message assigned probability zero is treated as impossible by the model, so observing it would reveal a problem in that model rather than merely an extremely large but ordinary surprise.

title: Introduction to Information Theory
text:
4.1 Why use a logarithm?
The logarithm is used because separate independent pieces of information should combine additively.
Suppose that two independent messages \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) occur. Independence means that their joint probability is
\[
p(m_1,m_2)=p(m_1)p(m_2).
\]
If the two observations are independent, the information obtained from observing both should be the information from the first plus the information from the second:
\[
I(m_1,m_2)=I(m_1)+I(m_2).
\]
Therefore, an information measure \(f\) based on probability should satisfy
\[
f(pq)=f(p)+f(q).
\]
The logarithm has precisely this property:
\[
\log(pq)=\log p+\log q.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\begin{aligned}
I(m_1,m_2)
&=-\log_2\bigl(p(m_1)p(m_2)\bigr)\\
&=-\log_2p(m_1)-\log_2p(m_2)\\
&=I(m_1)+I(m_2).
\end{aligned}
\]
Under the natural requirements that the measure varies continuously with probability and that independent information adds, the logarithmic form is not an arbitrary choice: it is the form that fulfils those requirements, up to a positive multiplicative constant.

title: Introduction to Information Theory
section: 4.2 Why is there a minus sign?
text:
4.2 Why is there a minus sign?
For every probability \(p\in(0,1]\),
\[
\log_2p\leq0.
\]
The minus sign makes the information non-negative:
\[
-\log_2p\geq0.
\]
It also ensures that smaller probabilities correspond to larger information values.

title: Introduction to Information Theory
text:
4.3 Why use base 2?
The base determines the unit of measurement. Base \(2\) measures information in bits.
For example,
\[
I(m)=-\log_2\left(\frac12\right)=1\text{ bit}.
\]
An event with probability \(1/2\) therefore carries one bit of self-information. Similarly,
\[
I(m)=-\log_2\left(\frac14\right)=2\text{ bits},
\]
and
\[
I(m)=-\log_2\left(\frac18\right)=3\text{ bits}.
\]
Every halving of probability adds one bit of information. This gives the logarithmic measure a direct interpretation in terms of binary distinctions.

title: Introduction to Information Theory
text:
6.1 Compressing messages
Compression seeks a more compact representation of a message while preserving the information required for its recovery.
Compression is possible when the original representation contains redundancy. If some messages or patterns are more predictable than others, a coding method can exploit that predictability instead of representing every possibility in the same way.
The lecture associates entropy with the fundamental limit on message compression. At this point, entropy is introduced only through this role: it expresses how far a source can be compressed on average without losing the information needed to recover its messages. The mathematical definition of entropy is left to a later lecture.
The statement written in the lecture notes as “entropy is the maximum message compression” should therefore be read as follows:

Entropy determines the theoretical limit of lossless compression for a source.

It is the achievable compactness that is limited; entropy is not itself a compression algorithm.

title: Introduction to Information Theory
text:
6.2 Correcting transmission errors
A transmitted representation may be altered while passing through the channel. Error-correcting methods add carefully designed structure that enables the receiver to detect or correct some transmission errors.
Compression and error correction address different problems:

compression removes redundancy that is unnecessary for representing the source efficiently;
error correction introduces useful redundancy to protect the encoded message during transmission.

title: Time and Space Complexity Classes
text:
The lecture begins by completing the interpretation of the linear speed-up theorem from the preceding lesson. If
\[
L\in\operatorname{TIME}(f(n)),
\]
then, for every constant \(\varepsilon>0\),
\[
L\in\operatorname{TIME}(\varepsilon f(n)+n+2).
\]
The additive term \(n+2\) accounts for the initial processing of the input and is linear in the input length. Therefore, when \(f(n)\ge n\), constant multiplicative factors do not change the asymptotic time class: a language in \(\operatorname{TIME}(f(n))\) can be decided in \(O(f(n))\) steps.
This motivates grouping running-time bounds by their order of growth rather than by their exact leading constant.


For each fixed \(k\in\mathbb{N}\), \(\operatorname{TIME}(n^k)\) contains the languages decidable within a polynomial bound of degree \(k\). The class of all polynomial-time languages is
\[
\mathrm{P}
=
\mathrm{PTIME}
=
\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\operatorname{TIME}(n^k).
\]
The union means that a language belongs to \(\mathrm{P}\) when some fixed polynomial bounds its worst-case running time. The exponent \(k\) may depend on the machine or language, but it is not allowed to grow with the input length.



The notes next introduce increasingly larger deterministic time classes:
\[
\mathrm{EXP}
=
\mathrm{EXPTIME}
=
\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}
\operatorname{TIME}\!\left(2^{n^k}\right),
\]
and
\[
\mathrm{DEXP}
=
\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}
\operatorname{TIME}\!\left(2^{2^{n^k}}\right).
\]
The elementary-time class permits any fixed finite tower of exponentials. For \(h\ge 1\), define the tower functions recursively by
\[
\operatorname{tower}_1(t)=2^t,
\qquad
\operatorname{tower}_{h+1}(t)=2^{\operatorname{tower}_h(t)}.
\]
Then the class written in the notes as ELEMENTARY can be expressed robustly as
\[
\mathrm{ELEMENTARY}
=
\bigcup_{h\in\mathbb{N},\,h\ge 1}
\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}
\operatorname{TIME}\!\left(\operatorname{tower}_h(n^k)\right).
\]
The important restriction is that the tower height \(h\) is fixed. A bound whose tower height itself grows with \(n\) is not included merely by this definition.

title: Time and Space Complexity Classes
text:
3.1 Read-only input
The input tape can be read but not modified. If the scanned symbols are \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_k\), an ordinary transition may change the symbols on the non-input tapes, but it must preserve the symbol \(\sigma_1\) on the first tape.
When the input head scans the left-end marker, the marker is likewise preserved and the head cannot cross the left boundary. Thus the input remains available throughout the computation without being counted as writable workspace.

title: Time and Space Complexity Classes
text:
3.2 Write-only output
The output tape can only be written, and its head moves in the output direction prescribed by the model. The notes express this by restricting the output-head movement to
\[
M_k\in\{\rightarrow,-\}.
\]
In other words, the output head may move to the right or remain stationary, but it does not move left to reread or reuse previously written output as working memory.

title: Time and Space Complexity Classes
text:
3.3 What is counted as space
For an I/O Turing machine, the input tape and output tape are excluded from the space measure. Only the \(k-2\) working tapes contribute. If their finite contents are represented by \(u_i\) and \(v_i\), then
\[
\operatorname{space}_M(x)
=
\max_{C\text{ reached on }x}
\sum_{i=2}^{k-1}
\left(|u_i|+|v_i|\right).
\]
This definition permits meaningful sublinear bounds. A machine may inspect an input of length \(n\) while using only logarithmic or even constant working space, because the \(n\) input cells are not counted.








Tape
Permitted role
Included in space measure?




Input tape
Read the original input; do not modify it
No

Read, write and revisit temporary data
Yes


Output tape
Write the result without using it as reusable memory
No





Worst-case space bound

A language \(L\) is decided in space \(f(n)\) if there exists an I/O Turing machine \(M\) such that, for every \(x\in\Sigma^*\),
\[
M(x)=\mathrm{yes}
\Longleftrightarrow
x\in L,
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{space}_M(x)
\le
f(|x|).
\]
The bound is a worst-case bound over all inputs of each length.

title: Time and Space Complexity Classes
section: 4.1 Time classes and the I/O model
text:
4.1 Time classes and the I/O model
The notes state that time-complexity classes defined using I/O Turing machines agree with the corresponding classes defined using the previous Turing-machine model, under the standing assumption \(f(n)\ge n\). Separating input and output is therefore essential for expressing small space bounds, but it does not change the time classes being studied at this level.

title: Time and Space Complexity Classes
text:
4.2 From time to space
A machine running for \(t(n)\) steps cannot use more than \(O(t(n))\) working cells, because every transition can visit only a constant number of new cells. Therefore,
\[
\mathrm{L}
\subseteq
\mathrm{PTIME}
\subseteq
\mathrm{PSPACE}.
\]
The first containment is justified in the notes by the fact that a logarithmic-space machine has only polynomially many relevant configurations. Because the machine is a decider, it cannot repeat a nonhalting configuration indefinitely; hence its running time is polynomial. The second containment follows directly from the observation that polynomial time allows at most polynomially many visited cells.

title: Information, Probability, and Random Variables
text:
The lecture begins from the surprise effect: observing an unlikely outcome is more informative than observing an outcome that was already expected.
Let \(m\) be a possible message and let \(p(m)\) be its probability before it is observed. The information carried by the observation of \(m\) is
\[
I(m)=-\log_2 p(m)
     =\log_2\left(\frac{1}{p(m)}\right).
\]
The quantity \(I(m)\) is also called the self-information or surprisal of \(m\).


If \(p(m)\) is close to \(1\), the message was almost certain and its observation changes very little. If \(p(m)\) is small, the message rules out many alternatives that were considered more likely and therefore changes the receiver’s knowledge much more.
The formula has the required limiting behaviour:
\[
p(m)=1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad I(m)=0,
\]
whereas
\[
p(m)\to0^+ \quad\Longrightarrow\quad I(m)\to+\infty.
\]
A certain message carries no new information. An increasingly improbable message has increasingly large surprisal.



Suppose two independent messages \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) are observed. Independence gives
\[
p(m_1,m_2)=p(m_1)p(m_2).
\]
The information obtained from the two independent observations should add:
\[
I(m_1,m_2)=I(m_1)+I(m_2).
\]
Therefore, a probability-based information measure \(f\) should satisfy
\[
f(pq)=f(p)+f(q).
\]
The logarithm converts a product into a sum:
\[
\log(pq)=\log p+\log q.
\]
Under the natural additional requirement of continuity, this additive requirement leads to a logarithmic measure, up to a constant that fixes the unit. The minus sign is necessary because \(\log p\leq0\) for \(0<p\leq1\), whereas information should be non-negative.
Base \(2\) measures information in bits. For example,
\[
-\log_2\frac12=1,
\qquad
-\log_2\frac14=2,
\qquad
-\log_2\frac18=3.
\]
Each halving of the probability adds one bit of surprisal.






NoteSingle-outcome information versus entropy contribution



For one observed outcome, the surprisal is \(-\log_2p\), not \(-p\log_2p\). The quantity \(-p\log_2p\) is the probability-weighted contribution of that outcome to the average entropy.

title: Information, Probability, and Random Variables
text:
2.1 Fair coin
For a fair coin,
\[
P(H)=P(T)=\frac12.
\]
Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(M)
&=-\frac12\log_2\frac12
  -\frac12\log_2\frac12\\
&=1\text{ bit}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The two outcomes are equally likely, so the result is maximally uncertain for a binary source.

title: Information, Probability, and Random Variables
text:
2.2 Biased coin
For a biased coin with
\[
P(H)=\frac14,
\qquad
P(T)=\frac34,
\]
we obtain
\[
H(M)
=-\frac14\log_2\frac14
-\frac34\log_2\frac34
\approx0.811\text{ bits}.
\]
The entropy is lower because one outcome is easier to predict.
For a source with \(s\) possible outcomes,
\[
0\leq H(M)\leq\log_2s.
\]
The minimum is reached when one outcome is certain. The maximum is reached by the uniform distribution, because uncertainty is largest when no outcome is preferred over the others.

title: Information, Probability, and Random Variables
text:
3.1 Unions of events
For arbitrary events \(A\) and \(B\),
\[
P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B).
\]
The intersection is subtracted because its probability is included once in \(P(A)\) and once in \(P(B)\).
If \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint, then \(A\cap B=\varnothing\) and
\[
P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B).
\]
More generally, for pairwise disjoint events \(A_1,\ldots,A_k\),
\[
P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}A_i\right)
=\sum_{i=1}^{k}P(A_i).
\]

title: Information, Probability, and Random Variables
text:
3.2 Animal example
Let
\[
\Omega=\{c,d,f,w\},
\]
where the symbols denote cat, dog, fox and wolf. The lecture uses
\[
P(c)=\frac12,
\qquad
P(d)=\frac14,
\qquad
P(f)=P(w)=\frac18.
\]
Consider the event
\[
A=\{d,f,w\},
\]
meaning that the animal is not a cat. Since the three elementary outcomes are disjoint,
\[
P(A)=\frac14+\frac18+\frac18=\frac12.
\]

title: Information, Probability, and Random Variables
text:
4.1 Conditional probability
If \(P(B)>0\), the conditional probability of \(A\) given \(B\) is
\[
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}.
\]
Conditioning means that \(B\) is now known to have occurred. Outcomes outside \(B\) are removed, and the probabilities of the outcomes remaining inside \(B\) are renormalised so that they sum to \(1\).
Rearranging the definition gives the product rule:
\[
P(A\cap B)=P(A\mid B)P(B).
\]
Because \(A\cap B=B\cap A\), the same joint event may also be written as
\[
P(A\cap B)=P(B\mid A)P(A).
\]
Therefore,
\[
P(A\mid B)P(B)=P(B\mid A)P(A).
\]

title: Information, Probability, and Random Variables
text:
4.2 Partitions
Events \(B_1,\ldots,B_r\) form a partition of \(\Omega\) when they are mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive:
\[
B_i\cap B_j=\varnothing
\quad\text{for }i\neq j,
\]
and
\[
\bigcup_{i=1}^{r}B_i=\Omega.
\]
A partition provides a complete list of non-overlapping cases.

title: Information, Probability, and Random Variables
text:
4.3 Law of total probability
Since the events \(A\cap B_1,\ldots,A\cap B_r\) form a disjoint decomposition of \(A\),
\[
P(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{r}P(A\cap B_i).
\]
Using the product rule in each case gives
\[
P(A)=\sum_{i=1}^{r}P(A\mid B_i)P(B_i).
\]
The law of total probability therefore computes an overall probability by:

calculating the probability inside each possible case;
weighting that conditional probability by how often the case occurs;
adding the weighted terms.

title: Information, Probability, and Random Variables
text:
4.4 Dangerous-animal signal
Let \(R=1\) mean that the animal is dangerous, and let \(S_1,\ldots,S_r\) denote the possible observed signals. If the signal events form a partition, then
\[
P(R=1)
=\sum_{i=1}^{r}P(R=1\mid S_i)P(S_i).
\]
The conditional danger probabilities alone do not determine the overall danger probability. The frequency of each signal, \(P(S_i)\), is also required.

title: Information, Probability, and Random Variables
text:
6.1 Indicator variables
For an event \(A\), its indicator variable is
\[
\mathbf{1}_A(\omega)
=
\begin{cases}
1, & \omega\in A,\\
0, & \omega\notin A.
\end{cases}
\]
The indicator translates a yes-or-no event into a numerical random variable. Its distribution is
\[
P(\mathbf{1}_A=1)=P(A),
\qquad
P(\mathbf{1}_A=0)=1-P(A).
\]
In the animal example, one may define a variable \(T\) that equals \(1\) when the observed animal belongs to a chosen target category, such as fox or wolf, and equals \(0\) otherwise. The probability that \(T=1\) is then the probability of the corresponding event.

title: Information, Probability, and Random Variables
text:
7.1 Joint distribution
The joint probability mass function is
\[
p_{X,Y}(x,y)=P(X=x,Y=y).
\]
It assigns a probability to each possible pair \((x,y)\) and satisfies
\[
p_{X,Y}(x,y)\geq0,
\qquad
\sum_x\sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y)=1.
\]

title: Information, Probability, and Random Variables
text:
7.2 Marginal distributions
If only \(X\) is of interest and \(Y\) is ignored, all joint probabilities compatible with \(X=x\) must be added:
\[
p_X(x)=\sum_y p_{X,Y}(x,y).
\]
Similarly,
\[
p_Y(y)=\sum_x p_{X,Y}(x,y).
\]
These are called marginal distributions because, in a joint probability table, the sums are traditionally displayed in the table margins.

title: Information, Probability, and Random Variables
text:
7.3 Conditional distribution
If \(p_Y(y)>0\), the conditional distribution of \(X\) given \(Y=y\) is
\[
p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)
=\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,y)}{p_Y(y)}.
\]
For a fixed observed value \(y\), this conditional distribution satisfies
\[
\sum_x p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)=1.
\]
The product rule becomes
\[
p_{X,Y}(x,y)
=p_{X\mid Y}(x\mid y)p_Y(y)
=p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)p_X(x).
\]
This is the random-variable version of
\[
P(A\cap B)=P(A\mid B)P(B).
\]

title: Information, Probability, and Random Variables
text:
8.1 Disjointness is different from independence
Two events are disjoint when they cannot occur together:
\[
P(A\cap B)=0.
\]
If both events have positive probability, then
\[
P(A)P(B)>0,
\]
so the independence equation cannot hold. Disjoint positive-probability events are therefore dependent: observing one makes the other impossible.

title: Learning Automata and Sequential Transducers
text:
The deck introduces automata learning as a supervised-learning problem in which the examples are structured objects, typically words \(w\in\Sigma^*\), and the target is a regular language. A regular language can be represented by its characteristic function
\[
f:\Sigma^*\longrightarrow\{0,1\}.
\]
The comparison with neural networks is conceptual. A neural network is presented as learning a complex function over comparatively simple numerical data while its architecture is fixed in advance. In automata learning, inputs such as words are structurally rich, the target function is regular, and the learner must infer the automaton’s states and transitions. The learned result is therefore an explicit behavioural model rather than only a classifier.








Aspect
Neural-network example in the deck
Automata-learning example




Input
vector \(\bar x\in\mathbb R^k\)
word \(w\in\Sigma^*\)


Target
complex classifier, such as recognising dogs
regular language \(L\subseteq\Sigma^*\)


Structure
architecture fixed before training
states and transitions inferred






In passive learning, the learner receives labelled examples chosen in advance. In active learning, the learner chooses queries and uses the answers to decide what information to request next. Active learning can be more efficient because each query can target a current uncertainty, but it can be less practical because it requires an entity capable of answering those queries.
The historical path shown in the deck starts with Moore’s 1956 thought experiments on sequential machines, continues with Gold’s learning in the limit and Angluin’s 1987 active query framework, and then branches into PAC learning and cryptographic hardness, regular \(\omega\)-languages, word and tree transformations, weighted automata, infinite alphabets, timed languages, and spectral techniques. These later entries establish the breadth of the area; the chapter follows the deck by concentrating on active learning of regular languages and its extension to sequential transducers.

title: Learning Automata and Sequential Transducers
text:
2.1 Teacher, learner, and query types
The teacher has a secret regular language \(L_0\subseteq\Sigma^*\), represented conceptually by a target DFA \(A_0\). The learner initially knows only the alphabet \(\Sigma\) and may ask two kinds of questions.








Query
Learner asks
Teacher returns




Membership
“Is \(w\in L_0\)?”
yes or no


Equivalence
“Is \(L(A)=L_0\)?”
yes, or a counterexample in the symmetric difference



For an incorrect hypothesis \(A\), the counterexample belongs to

\[
(L_0\setminus L(A))\cup(L(A)\setminus L_0).
\]

It is therefore a word on which the target and the candidate disagree. The slides allow the teacher to return a shortest counterexample, which is particularly informative because it localises the earliest observable failure of the candidate.






flowchart LR
  L["Learner"] -->|"membership query w"| T["Teacher for L0"]
  T -->|"yes or no"| L
  L -->|"equivalence query A"| T
  T -->|"yes"| D["Learning terminates"]
  T -->|"counterexample w"| L


 Active automata learning as an interaction between learner and teacher. 



Membership queries alone cannot guarantee exact identification after finitely many questions: any finite set of observed words leaves infinitely many unqueried words on which another regular language might differ. Equivalence queries force global progress by returning a discrepancy whenever the hypothesis is wrong. Angluin’s result states that the learner has a winning strategy whose number of query rounds is polynomial in the size of the target automaton \(A_0\). The deck identifies this strategy with the \(L^*\) algorithm.

title: Learning Automata and Sequential Transducers
section: 2.2 Minimally adequate teachers and black-box learning

title: Learning Automata and Sequential Transducers
text:
3.1 The true equivalence
For the target language \(L_0\), define

\[
u\sim_{L_0}v
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall t\in\Sigma^*\;
(ut\in L_0\iff vt\in L_0).
\]

Two prefixes are equivalent when every continuation gives the same membership result. They therefore have the same future behaviour and may be represented by the same DFA state.
The relation has three properties emphasised in the deck:

it refines the coarse partition into words inside and outside \(L_0\) because the empty continuation \(\varepsilon\) is permitted;
it is right-invariant: \[u\sim_{L_0}v\Longrightarrow ua\sim_{L_0}va;\]
it has finite index exactly when \(L_0\) is regular.

The states of the minimal DFA correspond to the equivalence classes \([u]_{\sim_{L_0}}\). Its transition on \(a\) sends \([u]\) to \([ua]\), and right invariance makes this definition independent of the chosen representative.

title: Learning Automata and Sequential Transducers
section: 3.2 Approximation by a finite test set
text:
3.2 Approximation by a finite test set
The learner cannot quantify over all continuations. It maintains a finite test set \(T\subseteq\Sigma^*\) and uses

\[
u\approx_{L_0,T}v
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall t\in T\;
(ut\in L_0\iff vt\in L_0).
\]

Because \(T\) contains only some continuations, \(\approx_{L_0,T}\) is coarser than \(\sim_{L_0}\): distinct true states may initially appear equal. Adding tests can split an approximate class, but it cannot merge classes already distinguished.
The learner also maintains a finite set \(S\subseteq\Sigma^*\) of state representatives.

\(S\) is \(T\)-minimal when different representatives have different rows over \(T\):
\[
\forall s\ne s'\in S\qquad s\not\approx_{L_0,T}s'.
\]
\(S\) is \(T\)-complete when every one-letter extension is represented:


\[
\forall s\in S\;\forall a\in\Sigma\;\exists s'\in S
\qquad s'\approx_{L_0,T}sa.
\]

Minimality guarantees uniqueness of the representative \(s'\); completeness guarantees existence. Together, they make the candidate transition function well-defined.

title: Learning Automata and Sequential Transducers
text:
4.1 Candidate construction
Start from
\[
S=T=\{\varepsilon\}.
\]
While \(S\) is not \(T\)-complete, choose \(s\in S\) and \(a\in\Sigma\) whose extension \(sa\) has no equivalent representative, and add \(sa\) to \(S\). Once the table is minimal and complete, construct the DFA \(A\) as follows:

state set: \(S\);
initial state: \(\varepsilon\);
accepting states: those \(s\in S\) for which the membership query on \(s\) returns yes;
transition: \[
\delta(s,a)=s',
\] where \(s'\) is the unique representative satisfying \(s'\approx_{L_0,T}sa\).

The candidate is then submitted in an equivalence query. If the answer is yes, learning terminates. If the teacher returns a counterexample \(w\), the algorithm adds all suffixes of \(w\) to \(T\) and restores completeness.
S := {ε}; T := {ε}
repeat
  while S is not T-complete do
    choose s in S and a in Σ with no representative for sa
    S := S ∪ {sa}
  construct candidate DFA A from (S,T)
  if Equivalence(A) then return A
  else
    obtain counterexample w
    T := T ∪ {suffixes of w}

title: Learning Automata and Sequential Transducers
text:
4.2 Why a counterexample forces progress
Let
\[
w=a_1\cdots a_n
\]
be a counterexample, let \(t_i=a_{i+1}\cdots a_n\) be its suffixes, and let \(s_i\) be the candidate state reached after reading the prefix \(a_1\cdots a_i\). Assume, for contradiction, that adding all \(t_i\) leaves \(S\) complete. Using the definition of transitions and the new tests, one proves inductively that
\[
w\in L_0\iff s_i t_i\in L_0
\]
for each \(i\), and ultimately that
\[
w\in L_0\iff w\in L(A).
\]
This contradicts the fact that \(w\) is a counterexample. Hence the refined test set makes the current state set incomplete, so the next iteration adds a new representative. Since distinct representatives correspond to distinct true Myhill-Nerode classes, \(S\) cannot grow beyond the index of \(\sim_{L_0}\). When that index is reached, the target minimal DFA has been recovered.






Important



The counterexample is not simply stored as another labelled sample. Its suffixes are added as experiments that reveal which previously merged prefixes have different futures.

title: Learning Automata and Sequential Transducers
section: 5.1 Rows as behaviours and columns as tests
text:
5.1 Rows as behaviours and columns as tests
The language Hankel matrix is the infinite Boolean matrix
\[
H\in\{0,1\}^{\Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*}
\]
with
\[
H(s,t)=\operatorname{Membership}(st).
\]
Rows are indexed by prefixes and columns by continuation tests. Two complete rows are equal exactly when their prefixes are Myhill-Nerode equivalent. Restricting a row to the columns in \(T\) yields the approximate equivalence \(\approx_{L_0,T}\).



Matrix object
Learning interpretation




row indexed by \(s\)
future behaviour after prefix \(s\)


column indexed by \(t\)
continuation experiment \(t\)


equal full rows
same \(\sim_{L_0}\) class


equal subrows over \(T\)
same \(\approx_{L_0,T}\) class


selected rows \(S\)
candidate states


selected columns \(T\)
current distinguishing tests



The algorithm can therefore be read geometrically. It chooses enough rows to make the observed table closed under one-letter extensions, constructs a hypothesis from those rows, and uses counterexamples to add columns. New columns split rows that were falsely identified.
The progressive example begins with \(S=T=\{\varepsilon\}\), expands \(S\) to obtain completeness, and builds an initial automaton. The counterexample \(w=aba\) adds
\[
\{\varepsilon,a,ba,aba\}
\]
to the test set. These columns reveal another distinct row, so \(S\) grows to include a new representative such as \(ab\). The rebuilt automaton then reflects the finer behavioural partition.






flowchart LR
  ST["Finite table (S,T)"] --> C{"T-complete?"}
  C -->|"no"| R["Add a representative to S"]
  R --> ST
  C -->|"yes"| A["Build candidate automaton"]
  A --> E{"Equivalent to target?"}
  E -->|"yes"| F["Return learned DFA"]
  E -->|"no"| X["Add counterexample suffixes to T"]
  X --> ST


 Mutual refinement of representatives and experiments in the Hankel table.

title: Learning Automata and Sequential Transducers
text:
6.1 Sequential transducers
Automata can also represent functions
\[
f:\Sigma^*\longrightarrow\Gamma^*.
\]
The deck uses a sequential transducer
\[
A=(\Sigma,\Gamma,Q,q_0,\delta)
\]
with
\[
\delta:Q\times\Sigma\longrightarrow Q\times\Gamma^*.
\]
A transition consumes one input letter, changes state, and appends a finite output word. Concatenating transition outputs along the unique run gives the value of the function.
The functions considered are total and monotone with respect to the prefix order:
\[
w\preceq w'\Longrightarrow f(w)\preceq f(w').
\]
A sequential transducer cannot retract output already emitted. Extending the input therefore only extends the output.

title: Learning Automata and Sequential Transducers
text:
6.2 The active-learning protocol for functions
The teacher now has a secret monotone function \(f_0:\Sigma^*\to\Gamma^*\) computed by a sequential transducer \(A_0\). The learner may ask:

an evaluation query: “What is \(f_0(w)\)?”;
an equivalence query: “Does candidate transducer \(A\) compute \(f_0\)?”

An incorrect candidate produces a shortest word \(w\) satisfying
\[
f_0(w)\ne A(w).
\]
The protocol is the functional analogue of membership and equivalence learning for languages.

title: Learning Automata and Sequential Transducers
text:
7.1 Residual output
If \(x\) is a prefix of \(y\), write \(y-x\) for the unique suffix \(z\) such that \(y=xz\). Monotonicity guarantees that \(f_0(u)\) is a prefix of \(f_0(ut)\), so the residual
\[
f_0(ut)-f_0(u)
\]
is defined. It represents the additional output produced after continuation \(t\) from the state reached by \(u\).
The functional Myhill-Nerode equivalence is

\[
u\sim_{f_0}v
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall t\in\Sigma^*\;
\bigl(f_0(ut)-f_0(u)=f_0(vt)-f_0(v)\bigr).
\]

Prefixes are equivalent when every future input produces the same future output, after removing output already produced. The relation is right-invariant, and its finite index characterises functions computable by the sequential transducers considered in the deck.

title: Learning Automata and Sequential Transducers
text:
7.2 The separator-insertion example
The example function inserts \(c\) between successive input positions. The slides give values such as
\[
f_0(\varepsilon)=\varepsilon,
\qquad f_0(a)=a,
\qquad f_0(aa)=aac,
\qquad f_0(aaa)=aaca.
\]
The apparent ordering reflects when the transducer can emit the separator while reading incrementally. The residual behaviour distinguishes the empty prefix from nonempty prefixes, but all nonempty prefixes have the same future mode. Hence the relation has two classes, represented by \([\varepsilon]_{\sim_{f_0}}\) and \([a]_{\sim_{f_0}}\).

title: Learning Automata and Sequential Transducers
text:
7.3 Functional Hankel matrix and learning
The Hankel matrix now has word-valued entries:
\[
H\in(\Gamma^*)^{\Sigma^*\times\Sigma^*},
\qquad
H(s,t)=f_0(st)-f_0(s).
\]
The finite-test approximation is

\[
u\approx_{f_0,T}v
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall t\in T\;
\bigl(f_0(ut)-f_0(u)=f_0(vt)-f_0(v)\bigr).
\]

As before, the learner maintains \(T\)-minimal and \(T\)-complete sets of representatives. For a transition from representative \(s\) on input \(a\), the successor is the representative equivalent to \(sa\), while the transition output is the incremental output exposed by the corresponding table entries.
In the progressive example, the learner starts from \(S=T=\{\varepsilon\}\) and builds a one-state candidate. The counterexample \(w=ab\) expands the tests to include \(\varepsilon\), \(b\), and \(ab\). The new observations distinguish the empty and nonempty residual modes, so \(S\) expands to \(\{\varepsilon,a\}\) and the resulting two-state transducer implements the separator-insertion behaviour.

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
text:
Propositional logic is the first classical logic considered in the deck. Its vocabulary contains a set
\[
\Sigma=\{p,q,r,\ldots\}
\]
of Boolean variables, also called propositional letters, together with the Boolean connectives
\[
\lor,\quad \land,\quad \neg,\quad \rightarrow,\quad \leftrightarrow.
\]
The syntax is defined inductively. Every propositional letter is a formula; if \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are formulas, then so are \(\varphi\lor\psi\), \(\varphi\land\psi\), \(\neg\varphi\), \(\varphi\rightarrow\psi\), and \(\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi\). This inductive definition matters because algorithms can follow the same recursive structure.
A structure, or valuation, is a function
\[
S:\Sigma\longrightarrow\{\mathit{true},\mathit{false}\}.
\]
The satisfaction relation \(S\models\varphi\) says that \(\varphi\) holds under \(S\). It is defined recursively:
\[
\begin{aligned}
S\models p &\iff S(p)=\mathit{true},\\
S\models\varphi\lor\psi &\iff S\models\varphi\text{ or }S\models\psi,\\
S\models\varphi\land\psi &\iff S\models\varphi\text{ and }S\models\psi,\\
S\models\neg\varphi &\iff S\not\models\varphi.
\end{aligned}
\]
Implication and equivalence have their usual Boolean meanings. Syntax determines which expressions are formulas; semantics determines whether a formula is true in a given valuation.



The propositional model-checking problem receives a formula \(\varphi\) and a valuation \(S\) and asks whether \(S\models\varphi\). The algorithm evaluates the syntax tree recursively. At a leaf it reads \(S(p)\); at a connective it recursively evaluates the immediate subformulas and combines their truth values.
Model-check(φ, S):
  if φ = p, return S(p)
  if φ = φ₁ ∨ φ₂, return Model-check(φ₁,S) or Model-check(φ₂,S)
  if φ = φ₁ ∧ φ₂, return Model-check(φ₁,S) and Model-check(φ₂,S)
  if φ = ¬φ₁, return not Model-check(φ₁,S)
  treat → and ↔ according to their Boolean semantics
The running time is polynomial, in fact linear in the size of the represented formula when each node is visited once. The deck records the sharper complexity statement that propositional model checking is P-complete.



A formula is satisfiable if some valuation makes it true:
\[
\varphi\text{ is satisfiable}\iff \exists S\;(S\models\varphi).
\]
A direct algorithm enumerates the \(2^n\) valuations of the \(n\) propositional letters occurring in \(\varphi\) and invokes model checking on each one. The search is therefore exponential in the number of variables. The decision problem SAT is NP-complete.
The following table separates the two algorithmic questions.









Problem
Input
Question
Complexity stated in the deck




Model checking
\(S,\varphi\)
Does \(S\models\varphi\)?
P-complete


Satisfiability
\(\varphi\)
Is there an \(S\) such that \(S\models\varphi\)?
NP-complete



The difference is the valuation. Model checking receives it; satisfiability must find one.

crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
text:
2.1 Eliminating implication and equivalence
The first economy-of-syntax result states that every formula is equivalent to one not using \(\rightarrow\) or \(\leftrightarrow\). The rewritings are
\[
\varphi\rightarrow\psi\equiv\neg\varphi\lor\psi
\]
and

\[
\varphi\leftrightarrow\psi
\equiv
(\neg\varphi\lor\psi)\land(\neg\psi\lor\varphi).
\]

These identities show that the two connectives are convenient abbreviations rather than essential additions to expressive power.
crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
text:
2.2 Negation normal form
A formula is in negation normal form (NNF) when it uses only \(\land\), \(\lor\), and negation applied directly to propositional letters. After removing implication and equivalence, negations are pushed inward with De Morgan’s laws and double-negation elimination:
\[
\neg(\varphi\land\psi)\equiv\neg\varphi\lor\neg\psi,
\qquad
\neg(\varphi\lor\psi)\equiv\neg\varphi\land\neg\psi,
\qquad
\neg\neg\varphi\equiv\varphi.
\]
The transformation follows the syntax tree and preserves equivalence.
crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
text:
2.3 Conjunctive and disjunctive normal form
A literal is a propositional letter \(p\) or its negation \(\neg p\). A formula is in conjunctive normal form (CNF) if it is a conjunction of clauses, where each clause is a disjunction of literals. It is in disjunctive normal form (DNF) if it is a disjunction of terms, where each term is a conjunction of literals.



Normal form
Outer operation
Inner components




CNF
conjunction
disjunctions of literals


DNF
disjunction
conjunctions of literals



Distributivity converts NNF formulas to CNF or DNF, but a direct equivalence-preserving conversion can cause an exponential increase in formula size. The deck therefore introduces a more economical construction for satisfiability.
crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
text:
2.4 Tseitin transformation
The Tseitin transformation introduces a fresh variable for selected subformulas and constrains that variable to represent the subformula’s truth value. For example, if \(x\) names \(\alpha\land\beta\), the defining equivalence is
\[
x\leftrightarrow(\alpha\land\beta).
\]
It can be expressed in CNF as
\[
(\neg x\lor\alpha)\land(\neg x\lor\beta)\land(x\lor\neg\alpha\lor\neg\beta).
\]
Analogous local constraints are produced for disjunction and negation. A final unit clause requires the variable naming the whole formula to be true. The result is linear in the original syntax tree and is equisatisfiable with the original formula.






Important



Equivalent formulas have the same truth value under every valuation of the same variables. Equisatisfiable formulas need only agree on whether some satisfying valuation exists. Tseitin variables make the latter relation sufficient for SAT solving.
crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
text:
2.5 Circuits and shared subformulas
A formula is a tree: repeated subformulas are copied. A Boolean circuit is a directed acyclic graph: a subcomputation may feed several later gates. This sharing can represent the same Boolean function more succinctly.






flowchart LR
  P["p"] --> A["p ∧ q"]
  Q["q"] --> A
  A --> O["(p ∧ q) ∨ r"]
  R["r"] --> O
  A --> N["¬(p ∧ q)"]


 A shared Boolean subexpression represented once in a circuit. 



The shared node \(p\land q\) is computed once and reused. Tseitin variables provide a logical encoding of such gate-by-gate structure.
crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
text:
4.1 Syntax and semantics
Quantified Boolean formulas (QBF) extend propositional logic with quantifiers \(\exists p\) and \(\forall p\). Their semantics modifies the value assigned to the quantified variable:
\[
S\models\exists p\,\varphi
\iff
S[p:=\mathit{true}]\models\varphi
\text{ or }
S[p:=\mathit{false}]\models\varphi,
\]
\[
S\models\forall p\,\varphi
\iff
S[p:=\mathit{true}]\models\varphi
\text{ and }
S[p:=\mathit{false}]\models\varphi.
\]
An occurrence of \(p\) under the scope of \(\exists p\) or \(\forall p\) is bound; otherwise it is free. A formula with no free variables is a sentence. Its truth no longer depends on an external valuation.
The recursive model-checking algorithm branches existentially for \(\exists p\) and universally for \(\forall p\). Although the recursion explores exponentially many assignments in the worst case, it needs to keep only the current branch and valuation. QBF model checking is PSPACE-complete.
crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
text:
4.2 Satisfiability and quantifier structure
A QBF with free variables \(p_1,\ldots,p_k\) is satisfiable precisely when its existential closure is true:
\[
\varphi(p_1,\ldots,p_k)\text{ satisfiable}
\iff
\models\exists p_1\cdots\exists p_k\,\varphi.
\]
Quantifier order is semantically significant. In general,
\[
\forall p\,\exists q\,\varphi
\not\equiv
\exists q\,\forall p\,\varphi.
\]
In the first formula, the choice of \(q\) may depend on \(p\); in the second, one choice of \(q\) must work for both values of \(p\). This dependence explains the game-like character of alternating quantifiers and the increased complexity from SAT to QBF.
crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
text:
5.1 Vocabulary and structures
First-order logic (FO) replaces Boolean variables with variables ranging over a domain and introduces relation, function, and constant symbols. A vocabulary records the arities of its symbols. A structure \(S\) supplies:

a nonempty universe \(U^S\);
a relation \(R^S\subseteq(U^S)^k\) for every \(k\)-ary relation symbol \(R\);
a function \(f^S:(U^S)^k\to U^S\) for every \(k\)-ary function symbol \(f\);
an element \(c^S\in U^S\) for every constant symbol \(c\).

Terms are built from variables, constants, and function applications. Atomic formulas compare terms or apply relation symbols. Formulas are then constructed using Boolean connectives and the quantifiers \(\exists x\) and \(\forall x\).
A variable assignment maps free variables to elements of \(U^S\). The satisfaction relation for quantifiers is
\[
S,\eta\models\exists x\,\varphi
\iff
\text{for some }a\in U^S,
\ S,\eta[x:=a]\models\varphi,
\]
\[
S,\eta\models\forall x\,\varphi
\iff
\text{for every }a\in U^S,
\ S,\eta[x:=a]\models\varphi.
\]
The deck illustrates how formulas acquire meaning only after the corresponding symbols are interpreted. A unary relation may express a property such as “drinks,” while a binary relation can express an association between two elements.
crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
text:
5.2 Translating statements
The sentence “There is a man such that, when he drinks, everybody drinks” is represented by a formula of the form
\[
\exists x\bigl(R(x)\rightarrow\forall y\,R(y)\bigr),
\]
where \(R\) is unary. Since the formula has no free variables, a structure either satisfies it or does not.
Properties of a binary relation can also be stated internally. For example, that \(R\) represents a total function can be written by requiring every \(x\) to have exactly one \(R\)-successor:

\[
\forall x\,\exists y\left(
R(x,y)\land
\forall z\,(R(x,z)\rightarrow z=y)
\right).
\]

For a binary function symbol \(+\), commutativity is
\[
\forall x\,\forall y\;(x+y=y+x).
\]
The existence of a neutral element and inverses requires quantifier order that reflects dependence: first choose a common neutral element, then allow each \(x\) to have its own inverse.
crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
text:
5.3 Model checking and satisfiability
FO model checking recursively evaluates atomic formulas, Boolean connectives, and quantifiers. For \(\exists x\,\varphi\), it tries elements of the finite domain until one succeeds; for \(\forall x\,\varphi\), every element must succeed. With a finite structure this is an effective algorithm, although its cost depends strongly on formula size, quantifier nesting, and domain size.
The satisfiability question is fundamentally different:
\[
\text{Does there exist a structure }S\text{ such that }S\models\varphi?
\]
The deck states Trakhtenbrot’s theorem: finite satisfiability of first-order logic is undecidable. The proof strategy is a reduction from an undecidable domino-tiling problem.








Logic
Model checking
Satisfiability




Propositional logic
P-complete
NP-complete


QBF
PSPACE-complete
reducible to truth of an existential closure


First-order logic over finite structures
decidable for a supplied finite structure
undecidable
crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
text:
6.1 The source problem
The domino problem receives finitely many four-sided tile types and asks whether copies of them can form a finite rectangle with a prescribed white border and matching adjacent colours. The variant used in the deck is undecidable by reduction from the Halting Problem. A computation can be represented row by row: each row describes a machine configuration, while local colour constraints force the next row to represent a valid transition.
crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
section: 6.2 Encoding a rectangle in first-order logic
text:
6.2 Encoding a rectangle in first-order logic
Given a domino set, the reduction constructs an FO sentence \(\varphi_D\) such that

\[
\varphi_D\text{ is finitely satisfiable}
\iff
D\text{ tiles a white-bordered rectangle}.
\]

The encoding has three conceptual layers:

Grid structure. Binary relations \(H(x,y)\) and \(V(x,y)\) describe the horizontal and vertical successor relations. They are constrained as partial functions or partial bijections and must commute where both paths exist, so moving right then up reaches the same cell as moving up then right.
Tile assignment. Unary predicates identify which domino type labels each cell, with exactly one type assigned to each grid position.
Local compatibility and border. FO formulas require matching colours across \(H\)- and \(V\)-adjacent cells and enforce the prescribed border condition.







flowchart LR
  X["x"] -->|"H"| Y["y"]
  X -->|"V"| Z["z"]
  Y -->|"V"| W["w"]
  Z -->|"H"| W


 Local square condition used in the first-order encoding of a rectangular grid. 



The commuting-square requirement is expressed by a formula of the form

\[
\forall x\,\forall y\,\forall z\,
\bigl(H(x,y)\land V(x,z)
\rightarrow
\exists w\,(V(y,w)\land H(z,w))\bigr).
\]

Because all constraints are local, FO can state them even though the global rectangle may be arbitrarily large. If finite satisfiability were decidable, the domino problem would be decidable, contradicting its undecidability. This is the purpose of the construction.
crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
text:
7.1 Ordered natural numbers
The theory \(\mathrm{FO}[\mathbb N,<]\) includes statements expressing that every natural number has a larger one, that no element is smaller than itself, and that the order is total. The point is that familiar order properties become sentences whose truth is evaluated in the single structure \((\mathbb N,<)\).
crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
text:
7.2 Presburger arithmetic
Presburger arithmetic is the first-order theory of natural numbers with addition, written in the deck as \(\mathrm{FO}[\mathbb N,+]\). It is decidable. The slides connect it with constraint solving, theorem provers such as Coq and Isabelle, and models of distributed systems such as Petri nets.
Multiplication by a fixed natural number can be represented through repeated addition, but multiplication of two variables is not available as a primitive relation in this theory. This expressive restriction is central to decidability.
crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
text:
7.3 Peano arithmetic
The deck contrasts Presburger arithmetic with the theory of natural numbers equipped with both addition and multiplication, written \(\mathrm{FO}[\mathbb N,+,\times]\). This theory is undecidable. The stated proof route is a reduction from Hilbert’s tenth problem, the problem of deciding whether a Diophantine equation has a solution in natural numbers.
crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
text:
7.4 Tarski arithmetic
The first-order theory of real closed fields, represented in the deck by the real numbers with addition, multiplication, and order, is referred to as Tarski arithmetic. Unlike the corresponding natural-number theory, it is decidable through quantifier elimination. The applications listed in the slides include computer graphics, invariants and abstractions, kinematics and motion planning, combinatorics on words, grammar equivalence, coding theory, and cryptography.
The contrast is worth keeping explicit:

\((\mathbb N,+)\)

crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic
section: 7.5 Random graphs and the zero-one law
text:
7.5 Random graphs and the zero-one law
The deck also considers FO over finite random graphs. For a fixed FO sentence \(\varphi\), examine the probability that a random graph with \(n\) vertices satisfies it. The zero-one law for FO states that, as \(n\) tends to infinity, this probability tends to either \(0\) or \(1\).
This does not mean that every finite graph agrees on \(\varphi\). It says that asymptotically almost all large finite graphs satisfy the sentence or asymptotically almost none do. The limiting theory is associated with the countable Rado graph, which explains its appearance beside the arithmetic theories.
crumbs: Classical Logics: Propositional Logic, QBF, and First-Order Logic

title: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability
text:
The deck begins by recalling the role of first-order logic (FO). FO is expressive, model checking over a supplied finite universe is decidable and can be performed in polynomial space, while satisfiability, validity, and equivalence over finite structures are undecidable through reductions from the domino problem. For a fixed infinite structure one can instead study its FO theory; some such theories are decidable and others are not. Logical interpretations can transfer questions from one FO theory to another.
The new question is not whether a given formula is true, but which properties are expressible by some FO formula. The slides use three guiding examples:

Is “the universe has even cardinality” definable in FO?
Is strong connectivity of a directed graph definable in FO using only the edge relation?
Is the word language \((AA)^*\) definable in FO using the order relation on positions?

A direct search through all formulas is not a workable method for proving non-definability. Games provide a semantic technique: instead of attempting to enumerate formulas, one compares structures and asks whether a player can expose a difference visible to formulas of bounded quantifier rank.
crumbs: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability

title: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability
text:
2.1 Positions and players
The evaluation game is a warm-up that turns the recursive semantics of FO into a two-player game. Its purpose is to determine whether
\[
S\models\varphi.
\]
Assume that \(\varphi\) is in negation normal form, so negation occurs only in front of atomic formulas. The players are:

Eve, who tries to establish that the formula is true;
Adam, who tries to establish that it is false.

A position is a pair \((\alpha,\lambda)\), where \(\alpha\) is a subformula of \(\varphi\) and
\[
\lambda:\operatorname{FreeVars}(\alpha)\longrightarrow U^S
\]
assigns elements of the universe to the free variables of \(\alpha\). The initial position consists of the complete formula and the binding of its free variables. For a sentence, the initial binding is empty.
crumbs: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability

title: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability
text:
2.2 Moves and terminal positions
The game follows the outermost connective or quantifier of the current subformula.








Current subformula
Player who chooses
Next position




\(\alpha_1\lor\alpha_2\)
Eve
\((\alpha_i,\lambda)\) for a chosen disjunct


\(\alpha_1\land\alpha_2\)
Adam
\((\alpha_i,\lambda)\) for a chosen conjunct


\(\exists x\,\alpha'(x)\)
Eve
\((\alpha',\lambda[x:=u])\) for a chosen \(u\in U^S\)


\(\forall x\,\alpha'(x)\)
Adam
\((\alpha',\lambda[x:=u])\) for a chosen \(u\in U^S\)



At an atom \(R(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\), play ends. Eve wins exactly when
\[
(\lambda(x_1),\ldots,\lambda(x_k))\in R^S.
\]
At a negated atom \(\neg R(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\), the winner is reversed: Eve wins exactly when the tuple is not in \(R^S\).






flowchart TD
  P["Position (α, λ)"] --> K{"Outermost form of α"}
  K -->|"α1 ∨ α2"| E1["Eve chooses a disjunct"]
  K -->|"α1 ∧ α2"| A1["Adam chooses a conjunct"]
  K -->|"∃x α'"| E2["Eve chooses u in the universe"]
  K -->|"∀x α'"| A2["Adam chooses u in the universe"]
  K -->|"atom or negated atom"| T["Truth in S determines the winner"]
  E1 --> P2["Continue with a smaller subformula"]
  A1 --> P2
  E2 --> P2
  A2 --> P2


 Recursive structure of the first-order evaluation game. 



Every move descends to a proper subformula, so the game is finite. The central lemma is
\[
S\models\varphi
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{Eve has a winning strategy in }G_{S,\varphi}.
\]
The correspondence mirrors semantics exactly. At disjunction and existential quantification, truth requires one successful choice, so Eve chooses. At conjunction and universal quantification, truth must survive every choice, so Adam selects the challenge. The evaluation game therefore does not change the semantics; it reorganises it as strategic interaction.
crumbs: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability

title: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability
text:
3.1 Definability and elementary equivalence
A property \(P\), understood as a class of structures, is defined by an FO sentence \(\varphi\) when
\[
\forall S\qquad S\in P\iff S\models\varphi.
\]
Two structures \(S\) and \(S'\) are elementarily equivalent when they agree on every FO sentence:
\[
S\equiv S'
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall\varphi\in\mathrm{FO}\qquad
S\models\varphi\iff S'\models\varphi.
\]
Thus no FO sentence can distinguish elementarily equivalent structures. Consequently, if \(S\in P\), \(S'\notin P\), and \(S\equiv S'\), then \(P\) is not FO-definable. For finite structures, however, non-isomorphic structures can eventually be distinguished by an FO sentence. To prove non-definability over finite structures, the deck therefore introduces a bounded notion.
crumbs: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability

title: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability
text:
3.2 Quantifier rank and n-equivalence
The quantifier rank \(\operatorname{qr}(\varphi)\) is the maximum number of nested quantifiers in \(\varphi\). It is not the total number of quantifiers. For example,

\[
\forall x\,\forall y\,
\bigl(\neg E(x,y)\lor(\exists z\,E(x,z))\lor(\exists t\,E(t,y))\bigr)
\]

has quantifier rank \(3\): along a deepest branch, the two outer universal quantifiers are followed by one existential quantifier.
Structures \(S\) and \(S'\) are \(n\)-equivalent, written \(S\equiv_n S'\), when they agree on all FO sentences of quantifier rank at most \(n\):
\[
S\equiv_n S'
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\forall\varphi\,
\bigl(\operatorname{qr}(\varphi)\le n
\Rightarrow
(S\models\varphi\iff S'\models\varphi)\bigr).
\]
Elementary equivalence means \(n\)-equivalence for every \(n\). The useful non-definability criterion is weaker and better suited to finite structures:

\[
\left[
\forall n\in\mathbb N\ \exists S_n,S'_n:
S_n\in P,
S'_n\notin P,
S_n\equiv_n S'_n
\right]
\Longrightarrow
P\text{ is not FO-definable}.
\]

If a sentence \(\varphi\) defined \(P\), choose \(n=\operatorname{qr}(\varphi)\). The corresponding \(S_n\) and \(S'_n\) would have to agree on \(\varphi\), even though exactly one belongs to \(P\), a contradiction.
crumbs: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability

title: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability
text:
4.1 Rules of the game
The \(n\)-round Ehrenfeucht-Fraïssé game \(G^n_{S,S'}\) is played by Spoiler and Duplicator on two structures with the same vocabulary.
At round \(i\):

Spoiler chooses an element from either \(U^S\) or \(U^{S'}\).
Duplicator responds with an element from the other structure.
The chosen elements form paired tuples \((u_1,\ldots,u_i)\) and \((v_1,\ldots,v_i)\).

Duplicator survives the current round when the correspondence \(u_j\mapsto v_j\) is a partial isomorphism. This means that equality, constants, and every relation in the vocabulary agree on the selected elements. For a graph vocabulary with edge relation \(E\), for example,
\[
u_j=u_k\iff v_j=v_k
\]
and
\[
E^S(u_j,u_k)\iff E^{S'}(v_j,v_k)
\]
must hold for every selected pair of indices. Duplicator wins the \(n\)-round game if the partial isomorphism is preserved after all \(n\) rounds; Spoiler wins as soon as it fails.






flowchart LR
  H["Current paired tuples"] --> S["Spoiler selects in either structure"]
  S --> D["Duplicator answers in the other structure"]
  D --> C{"Selected correspondence is a partial isomorphism?"}
  C -->|"yes"| N["Proceed to the next round"]
  C -->|"no"| W["Spoiler wins"]


 One round of an Ehrenfeucht-Fraïssé game. 



Spoiler tries to reveal a structural distinction. Duplicator does not need to construct a global isomorphism; she needs only to preserve all atomic information about the finitely many selected elements.
crumbs: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability

title: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability
text:
4.2 The Fraïssé-Ehrenfeucht theorem
The fundamental theorem is
\[
S\equiv_n S'
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{Duplicator can survive }n\text{ rounds in }G^n_{S,S'}.
\]
This is the soundness-and-completeness bridge between games and logic.

Soundness: if Duplicator survives \(n\) rounds, no FO sentence of quantifier rank at most \(n\) distinguishes the structures.
Completeness: if the structures agree on all formulas of quantifier rank at most \(n\), Duplicator has a strategy for surviving \(n\) rounds.

The theorem converts a syntactic universal quantification over formulas into a strategic problem on structures.
crumbs: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability

title: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability
text:
4.3 Why soundness holds
Suppose Duplicator has a strategy for \(n\) rounds. The proof proceeds by induction on formulas of quantifier rank at most \(n\), with already selected elements interpreting their free variables.

Atomic and negated atomic formulas agree because the selected correspondence is a partial isomorphism.
Boolean combinations agree by the induction hypothesis.
For \(\exists x\,\psi\), a witness chosen in one structure can be viewed as Spoiler’s next move. Duplicator’s response supplies a matching element in the other structure, and the induction hypothesis applies to \(\psi\).
Universal quantification follows dually, or through negation normal form and the evaluation-game interpretation.

The connection with the evaluation game is direct: Duplicator uses her EF strategy to transfer a winning evaluation-game strategy from one structure to the other.
crumbs: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability

title: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability
text:
4.4 Why completeness holds
For completeness, suppose Duplicator has no winning response at some stage. The possible responses in the other structure can then be separated by formulas of smaller quantifier rank. Combining these formulas under a quantifier produces a formula that distinguishes the current tuples. Repeating this argument backwards constructs a distinguishing sentence of quantifier rank at most \(n\).
The finite-vocabulary assumption ensures that, at the atomic level, only finitely many relevant atomic facts must be combined. The argument establishes that failure of a Duplicator strategy is not merely intuitive evidence: it yields an FO formula witnessing the difference.
crumbs: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability

title: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability
section: 5.1 Finite linear orders and interval sizes
text:
5.1 Finite linear orders and interval sizes
Several progressive slides ask how many rounds Duplicator can survive on finite ordered structures. The key observation is that selected points divide each order into intervals. Duplicator preserves the relative order of selected points and answers so that corresponding intervals remain either equally small or both sufficiently large for the remaining number of rounds.
This explains the exponential threshold used later in the deck: with \(r\) rounds remaining, Spoiler can repeatedly choose near the middle of an interval, approximately halving the unresolved distance. Duplicator therefore maintains the invariant that corresponding intervals have equal length or both have length at least a power of two determined by the remaining rounds.
The same “distance budget” appears in the comparison between
\[
S=(\mathbb Z,<)
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
S'=(\mathbb R,<).
\]
The orders are not isomorphic: one is discrete and the other dense. Spoiler can expose discreteness by creating a pair with no integer strictly between them while the corresponding real interval contains another point. The progressive moves illustrate how a local order difference becomes visible through selected witnesses.
crumbs: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability

title: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability
section: 5.2 Non-isomorphic structures with arbitrarily long finite survival
text:
5.2 Non-isomorphic structures with arbitrarily long finite survival
The deck contrasts finite and infinite structures. On non-isomorphic finite structures, Spoiler eventually wins: after enough rounds, every element can be selected and the resulting total correspondence would have to be an isomorphism.
For infinite structures, Duplicator may survive every prescribed finite number of rounds without there being one strategy that survives an actual infinite game. The example compares
\[
(\mathbb Z,<)
\qquad\text{with}\qquad
(\{1,2\}\times\mathbb Z,<_{\mathrm{lex}}).
\]
The second structure consists of two lexicographically ordered copies of the integers. They are not isomorphic, but for each fixed \(n\), Duplicator can maintain the invariant stated in the slides: after round \(i\), corresponding marked points are at equal distance or both at distance at least \(2^{n-i}\). The threshold decreases as the game progresses. Any distinction beyond that threshold remains invisible in the remaining rounds.






Important



“For every \(n\), Duplicator has an \(n\)-round strategy” does not automatically mean that Duplicator has one strategy for an infinite game. The deck explicitly separates arbitrary finite survival from survival forever.
crumbs: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability

title: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability
text:
6.1 A reusable method
The deck distils EF games into a standard proof pattern for showing that a property \(P\) is not FO-definable:

Fix an arbitrary quantifier-rank bound \(n\).
Choose structures \(S_n\in P\) and \(S'_n\notin P\).
Give Duplicator a strategy for surviving \(n\) rounds in \(G^n_{S_n,S'_n}\).
Apply the Fraïssé-Ehrenfeucht theorem to obtain \(S_n\equiv_n S'_n\).
Since this works for every \(n\), conclude that no FO sentence defines \(P\).

The structures are allowed, and usually required, to depend on \(n\).
crumbs: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability

title: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability
text:
6.2 Connectivity of finite graphs
To show that connectivity is not definable in FO, the slides choose highly symmetric graphs whose components are long cycles. For a given \(n\), take:

\(S_n\): one sufficiently long cycle, hence connected;
\(S'_n\): two sufficiently long cycles of the same local form, hence disconnected.







flowchart LR
  C1["S_n: one long cycle\nconnected"]
  C2["S'_n: two long cycles\ndisconnected"]
  C1 <-->|"same bounded local view"| C2


 EF-game comparison used for non-definability of graph connectivity. 



Duplicator responds in the corresponding local neighbourhood while maintaining distances between selected vertices up to the threshold visible in the remaining rounds. If the cycles are sufficiently long, Spoiler cannot traverse enough of them in \(n\) rounds to establish globally that one structure has one component and the other has two. FO of bounded quantifier rank therefore sees the same local configurations while connectivity is different.
The argument also applies to strong connectivity for directed variants when the chosen cycles and edge orientations match the vocabulary used in the property.
crumbs: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability

title: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability
text:
6.3 Even cardinality
For the property “the universe has even cardinality,” the vocabulary may be empty, so only equality between selected elements matters. Given \(n\), choose two finite sets with at least \(n\) elements, one of even size and one of odd size. Duplicator answers a previously selected element with its paired partner and a new element with a fresh element.
After at most \(n\) rounds, the equality pattern is identical in both structures. Thus Duplicator survives \(n\) rounds even though one universe is even and the other odd. Since this can be done for every \(n\), parity of finite cardinality is not FO-definable in the empty vocabulary.
crumbs: Games in Logic and First-Order Definability

title: Modelling and Verification in UPPAAL
text:
UPPAAL combines two ingredients introduced in the deck:

networks, or products, of automata, used to model concurrent timed systems;
a monitorable fragment of CTL, used to state properties that the model checker verifies.

The models are timed because real-valued clocks measure elapsed time. They are concurrent because several templates execute as one network and can communicate through shared state or synchronous channels.


A network is built from automata whose ordinary locations and edges are enhanced with:

bounded-range variables, such as int[0,100] i;
real-valued clocks, such as clock x;
shared memory, such as bool flag;
synchronous send and receive actions, such as ack! and ack?.

A channel send and its matching receive occur together. In the introductory example, one component emits inc!, another receives inc?, and the receiver updates count++. The same pattern applies to dec! and dec?.



A global state records:

one current location for every automaton;
values of local and global variables;
values of all clocks;
satisfaction of the relevant invariants.

The state is therefore not just a location name. Two executions can occupy the same tuple of locations but represent different global states because variables or clock values differ.



The transition relation contains both discrete changes and the passage of time.







Transition aspect
Meaning




Location change
an automaton follows an edge to another location


Update
local/global variables change or clocks are reset


Delay
time elapses uniformly on all clocks


Synchronisation
two automata jointly take matching ! and ? edges


Guard
an edge may be taken only when its condition holds



The distinction between a location invariant and a transition guard is essential. An invariant such as \(y\le 1\) limits how long the system may remain at the location. When \(y=1\), time may not advance further there. A guard such as \(y\ge 1\) only specifies when an outgoing edge becomes enabled; by itself, it does not force the edge to occur, so the system may continue delaying if the current location allows it.






Important



An enabled edge need not be taken immediately. Preventing delay requires an invariant, an urgent location, or another urgency mechanism. This distinction explains both modelling defects found in the train example.
