title: Modelling and Verification in UPPAAL
section: 3.1 The process template and required properties
text:
3.1 The process template and required properties
The first case study instantiates a process template twice, with identifiers \(0\) and \(1\). Each process repeatedly performs non-critical work, calls lock(pid), enters a critical location, and then invokes unlock(pid).
Mutual exclusion requires that at most one distinct process is critical at any moment:

\[
AG\,\neg\bigvee_{i\ne j}
\bigl(p_i.\mathit{critical}\land p_j.\mathit{critical}\bigr).
\]

Deadlock-freeness requires an enabled non-delay transition, possibly after some delay, unless all processes have legitimately halted. The deck writes this in the form

\[
AG\left(\neg\mathit{deadlock}\lor\bigwedge_i p_i.\mathit{halt}\right).
\]

The halt exception separates an intended terminated state from an unintended global deadlock.

title: Modelling and Verification in UPPAAL
Modelling and Verification in UPPAAL
Modelling and Verification in UPPAAL
text:
3.4 Algorithm 3: flags and victim
The third proposal combines the two ideas:
flags[pid] := true;
victim := pid;
while (flags[1-pid] == true && victim == pid) {}
A process waits only if the other process is interested and the current process is the designated victim. If both processes compete, the last assignment to victim breaks the symmetry: one waits and the other enters. On leaving, a process clears its flag. UPPAAL verifies both requirements for this model.



Algorithm 3 combines interest flags with the victim variable and verifies both mutual exclusion and deadlock-freeness.

title: Modelling and Verification in UPPAAL
text:
4.1 Informal timing requirements
The second case study consists of three communicating timed automata.

Train: sends request!, waits for ack?, starts crossing within \(30\) seconds of the acknowledgement, and completes crossing within \(10\) seconds.
Controller: receives train requests, sends lower! to the gate, and sends acknowledgements exactly \(10\) seconds after lowering starts. A counter records pending requests.
Gate: receives lower?, reaches the safe state within \(10\) seconds, and returns to start after \(60\) seconds from the beginning of lowering.

The automata communicate through the channels request, lower, and ack.

title: Modelling and Verification in UPPAAL
text:
4.2 Train automaton
The train moves through start, waiting, approaching, and crossing.



Train timed automaton.


From start, the train emits request! and enters waiting. The ack? edge resets clock \(x\) and enters approaching. The invariant \(x\le 30\) bounds the time before crossing begins. Entering crossing resets \(x\) again, and \(x\le 10\) bounds the crossing duration.

title: Modelling and Verification in UPPAAL
text:
4.3 Controller automaton
The controller uses locations start, transient, lowering, and granting, a pending-request counter, and clock \(y\).



Controller timed automaton before the urgency correction.


Receiving request? increments count. The controller emits lower!, resets \(y\), and remains in lowering under invariant \(y\le 10\). The edge to granting is enabled at \(y=10\). From granting, ack! is sent while count>0, and count is decremented. When count==0, the controller returns to start.

title: Modelling and Verification in UPPAAL
text:
4.4 Gate automaton
The gate moves from start to lowering on lower?, resetting clock \(z\). It must leave lowering before \(10\) seconds and enters safe. The invariant \(z\le 60\) bounds its stay in safe, and the edge at \(z=60\) returns to start.



Gate timed automaton.

title: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin
text:
Strong cryptographic primitives such as RSA, DSA, ElGamal, AES, and SHA-3 do not by themselves guarantee a secure distributed application. E-commerce, e-banking, electronic voting, mobile communication, and digital contract signing combine primitives into communication protocols. Errors can arise from the order of messages, omitted identities, replayed values, or incorrect assumptions about what a received message proves.
A protocol is a set of rules governing the exchange of messages between two or more principals. It is a distributed algorithm with particular emphasis on communication. A cryptographic protocol employs cryptographic mechanisms to achieve goals such as secrecy, authentication, integrity, key establishment, freshness, or non-repudiation under an explicit threat model.
In a concrete execution, abstract roles are instantiated by agents. One agent may even occupy different roles in different concurrent sessions. The protocol specification therefore describes permitted role behaviour, whereas an execution combines instantiated roles, network activity, and adversarial interference.



Protocol roles and a concrete execution with several role instances.


The central questions are semantic. What does it mean for a key to be known only to two agents? How can an agent know that a key is fresh? What evidence authenticates the peer? Formal verification requires a precise model of messages, agents, adversarial knowledge, executions, and goals.
crumbs: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin

title: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin
section: 2.1 First attempt: the key in clear text
text:
2.1 First attempt: the key in clear text
Assume an honest server \(S\) assists initiator \(A\) and responder \(B\):
A -> S : A, B
S -> A : k_AB
A -> B : k_AB, A
The construction fails immediately because \(k_{AB}\) is transmitted in clear text. The first threat assumption is that an adversary can eavesdrop on every network message.
crumbs: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin

title: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin
text:
2.2 Second attempt: long-term symmetric keys
Assume that \(S\) shares a long-term key \(k_S(A)\) with each agent \(A\):

\[
\begin{aligned}
A&\rightarrow S: A,B,\\
S&\rightarrow A: \{k_{AB}\}_{k_S(A)},\{k_{AB}\}_{k_S(B)},\\
A&\rightarrow B: \{k_{AB}\}_{k_S(B)},A.
\end{aligned}
\]

The encrypted messages resist passive eavesdropping under the perfect cryptography assumption: ciphertext can be deciphered only by an agent possessing the required key. The threat model is then strengthened. The adversary may capture, modify, drop, replay, and inject messages.
crumbs: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin

title: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin
section: 2.3 The Dolev-Yao adversary and a binding attack
text:
2.3 The Dolev-Yao adversary and a binding attack
In the Dolev-Yao model, the adversary completely controls the network. The adversary can intercept any message and send any term constructible from currently available information, under any apparent sender identity. Cryptographic operations remain ideal: the adversary cannot break encryption but may apply legitimate constructors and destructors when the required material is known.
The adversary may also be a legitimate participant. If intruder \(I\) changes \(A\)’s request from \((A,B)\) to \((A,I)\), the server creates \(k_{AI}\). Because the reply to \(A\) does not cryptographically bind the intended peer identity to the key, \(A\) can mistake this key for one shared with \(B\). This is a binding attack: a message valid in one context is accepted in another.
The repair is to include peer identities inside the protected data:

\[
\begin{aligned}
A&\rightarrow S: A,B,\\
S&\rightarrow A:
\{k_{AB},B\}_{k_S(A)},\{k_{AB},A\}_{k_S(B)},\\
A&\rightarrow B:\{k_{AB},A\}_{k_S(B)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
crumbs: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin

title: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin
text:
2.4 Replay and key compromise
The third attempt identifies peers correctly, but old encrypted tickets can be replayed. If an old session key \(k_{AB}\) is later compromised, an adversary can replay the old server response. The agents may accept a known, stale key, allowing the adversary to decrypt, modify, or inject traffic protected under it.
Even without learning the old key, forcing acceptance of an old key is harmful because previous ciphertexts can be replayed. Freshness therefore cannot be inferred solely from successful decryption.
A nonce is a random value intended for one use. A challenge-response exchange returns a nonce, or a function of it, to demonstrate that a response belongs to the current run.
crumbs: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin

title: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin
text:
2.5 Needham-Schroeder with conventional keys
The fourth attempt is the Needham-Schroeder protocol with conventional keys:

\[
\begin{aligned}
A&\rightarrow S: A,B,N_A,\\
S&\rightarrow A:
\{k_{AB},B,N_A,\{k_{AB},A\}_{k_S(B)}\}_{k_S(A)},\\
A&\rightarrow B:\{k_{AB},A\}_{k_S(B)},\\
B&\rightarrow A:\{N_B\}_{k_{AB}},\\
A&\rightarrow B:\{N_B-1\}_{k_{AB}}.
\end{aligned}
\]

\(N_A\) ties the server response to \(A\)’s current request. The final exchange provides key confirmation: each response demonstrates possession of \(k_{AB}\). Nevertheless, the Denning-Sacco attack replays an old ticket for \(B\) after the corresponding session key has been compromised. The challenge-response then succeeds because the adversary knows that old key.
crumbs: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin

title: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin
section: 2.6 Final design and remaining interpretation issue
text:
2.6 Final design and remaining interpretation issue
The final design begins with a fresh responder nonce:

\[
\begin{aligned}
B&\rightarrow A:A,B,N_B,\\
A&\rightarrow S:A,B,N_A,N_B,\\
S&\rightarrow A:
\{k_{AB},B,N_A\}_{k_S(A)},
\{k_{AB},A,N_B\}_{k_S(B)},\\
A&\rightarrow B:\{k_{AB},A,N_B\}_{k_S(B)}.
\end{aligned}
\]

Each recipient checks a nonce it generated, so the server-protected key is linked to the current run. The protocol avoids the attacks shown under perfect cryptography and server honesty. However, the slides stress that “correct” must still be defined. Unlike the previous protocol, the final design does not give either side explicit key confirmation that the peer actually possesses \(k_{AB}\).








Attack
Root problem
Defence used in the sequence




Eavesdropping
session key sent in clear
encrypt under long-term keys


Binding
peer identity not cryptographically tied to key
include names in encrypted payloads


Replay
old protected values remain syntactically valid
use fresh nonces and challenge-response


Masquerading after compromise
old key enables a valid response
bind freshness to the current session



Other attack forms listed in the deck include intruder-in-the-middle, reflection, oracle, and type-flaw attacks. The engineering guidance is correspondingly explicit: every message should say what it means; names essential to interpretation should be present; conditions for acting on a message should be clear; the purpose of encryption and all assumptions should be stated; and timestamp-based designs must account for clock variation.
crumbs: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin

title: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin
text:
5.1 Sorted term algebra
Messages are represented as well-sorted terms over a signature. The signature shown in the deck includes encryption and decryption, hashing, multiplication and inverses in an exponent group, exponentiation, the unit element, pairing, and projections:

\[
\Sigma_{DH}=
\{\operatorname{enc},\operatorname{dec},h,*,{}^{-1},{}^{\_},1,
\langle\_,\_\rangle,\operatorname{fst},\operatorname{snd}\}.
\]

The sorts include messages, fresh names, and public names. Fresh and public names are constants; variables are available for each sort. Terms are generated inductively: variables are terms, and applying an \(n\)-ary function symbol to \(n\) terms produces another term. Ground terms contain no variables.
A substitution maps variables to terms and extends homomorphically. If \(\sigma(x)=i(y)\) and \(\sigma(y)=e\), then applying \(\sigma\) replaces every occurrence consistently throughout a term.
crumbs: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin

title: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin
text:
5.2 Equational theories
An equation \(t\simeq u\) identifies two terms. Important examples are
\[
\operatorname{dec}(\operatorname{enc}(m,k),k)\simeq m
\]
and the Diffie-Hellman equality
\[
(g^x)^y\simeq(g^y)^x.
\]
A set \(E\) of equations induces a congruence \(=_E\) and a quotient term algebra. Equality modulo \(E\) means that terms belong to the same equivalence class.
The Diffie-Hellman theory in the deck also contains pairing projections, associativity and commutativity of multiplication, neutral and inverse laws, and exponent laws. For example,

\[
((g^a)^b)^{a^{-1}}
=_E g^{(a*b)*a^{-1}}
=_E g^b.
\]

Unification asks whether substitutions can make two terms equal modulo the equational theory. Syntactic unification, with no equations, is decidable and has a most general unifier. Unification modulo unrestricted theories is undecidable, motivating restrictions on supported theories.
A rewrite system is terminating when every reduction sequence reaches a normal form, and confluent when diverging reductions can be joined. A convergent system is both. It is subterm-convergent when each right-hand side is a proper subterm of the left-hand side, or a ground normal form. This provides a controlled extension mechanism for primitives such as asymmetric encryption and signatures.
crumbs: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin

title: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin
text:
6.1 Linear and persistent facts
A Tamarin state is a finite multiset of facts. Linear facts model resources that can be consumed once. Persistent facts, written with ! in Tamarin notation, remain available and can be used arbitrarily often.



Special fact
Kind
Meaning




\(K(m)\)
persistent
message \(m\) is known to the adversary


\(Out(m)\)
linear
the protocol placed \(m\) on the network


\(In(m)\)
linear
the adversary supplied \(m\) to the protocol


\(Fr(n)\)
linear
fresh value \(n\) was generated uniquely



User-defined facts represent protocol-local state.
crumbs: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin

title: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin
text:
6.2 Labelled rules and transitions
A rule has the form
\[
L\xrightarrow{A}R,
\]
where \(L\), \(R\), and \(A\) are multisets of facts. For a ground instance \(l\xrightarrow{a}r\) applicable in state \(S\), linear premises are removed, conclusions are added, persistent premises remain, and action facts \(a\) are appended to the trace:
\[
S'=S-\operatorname{lin}(l)+r.
\]
For example,
\[
F(x)\xrightarrow{A(x)}G(h(x))
\]
applied with \(x=a\) consumes \(F(a)\), produces \(G(h(a))\), and appends \(A(a)\) to the trace.
Built-in rules generate unique fresh names and model adversary deduction. Representative rules are
\[
Out(x)\longrightarrow K(x)
\]
and
\[
K(x)\xrightarrow{K(x)}In(x).
\]
The adversary can learn public names, create fresh values under its control, and apply public function symbols to known messages. Protocol rules cannot mention \(K\) directly; Out appears only in conclusions, while In and Fr appear only in premises. Non-public variables in conclusions must already occur in premises.
crumbs: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin

title: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin
text:
6.3 Traces
A trace is the sequence
\[
\langle a_1,\ldots,a_n\rangle
\]
of action multisets produced during execution. Empty action sets can be removed to obtain the observable trace. The examples show why persistent facts matter: a persistent fact such as \(!C(a)\) can justify multiple later applications, whereas a linear fact \(D(y)\) is consumed and replaced by \(D(h(y))\).
crumbs: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin

title: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin
text:
8.1 Secrecy with compromise exceptions
The NAXOS secrecy statement begins:

\[
\forall A,B,ek,k,i,j.
\ Accept(A,B,ek,k)@i\land K(k)@j
\rightarrow \text{an authorised compromise occurred}.
\]

The right-hand side may allow that the accepted session key was revealed, that the key of a matching session was revealed, or that a relevant long-term secret was compromised. This illustrates an important point: secrecy is not simply “the attacker never knows \(k\).” It is conditional on the compromise model stated by the protocol analysis.
crumbs: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin

title: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin
text:
10.1 Guarded trace properties
The verification fragment uses formulas in negation normal form. Quantified variables must be guarded by an action atom containing all of them:

existential form: \(\exists\vec x.\ G\land\psi\);
universal form: \(\forall\vec x.\ G\rightarrow\psi\).

Terms may be built only from quantified variables and public names. The set of guarded properties is closed under negation and invariant under trace normalisation. Thus verification in multiset-rewriting semantics modulo the Diffie-Hellman theory agrees with verification over normalised dependency graphs modulo \(AC\).
The freshness example states that two consumptions of the same fresh value must occur at the same time point:

\[
\forall n{:}\mathit{fresh},i,j.\
FreshConsumed(n)@i\land FreshConsumed(n)@j
\rightarrow i\doteq j.
\]
crumbs: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin

title: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin
text:
10.2 Backward reachability
Tamarin negates the property and searches for a model of the negation. A constraint system contains dependency-graph constraints and guarded trace formulas. A solution is a normal dependency graph, together with a valuation, satisfying all constraints.



Backward-reachability verification strategy.








flowchart TD
  N["Negate φ and rewrite to NNF"] --> O["Initial multiset Ω of constraint systems"]
  O --> C{"Solved system exists?"}
  C -->|"yes"| A["Construct attack dependency graph"]
  C -->|"no"| E{"Ω empty?"}
  E -->|"yes"| V["Verification successful"]
  E -->|"no"| R["Choose Γ and apply a reduction rule"]
  R --> O


 Constraint-refinement loop used to search for an attack. 



The reduction relation refines a constraint system into alternatives. The slides present rules for trace formulas, graph constraints, and message deduction. Soundness and completeness mean that the solution set of a parent system equals the union of the solution sets of its children, and that every solved system yields a concrete protocol solution.
crumbs: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin

title: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin
text:
10.3 Reading the backward example
To prove that no Rev(k) action is reachable, Tamarin starts from the negated goal
\[
\exists k,i.\ Rev(k)@i.
\]
Free variables are treated existentially, so the initial constraint can be represented as Rev(k)@i. Because only one rule emits Rev, any satisfying dependency graph must contain an instance of that rule. Its Key(k) premise must be justified by an incoming edge from a rule producing Key(k). Repeating this reasoning constructs earlier causal requirements until a solved graph is obtained or a contradiction is exposed.
In the illustrated example, the procedure reaches a solved system and therefore a counterexample to unreachability. The final sequence of slides performs a more detailed reduction for a uniqueness property: two Fin actions using the same key must occur at the same time and with the same message. Equalities are unified where possible; incompatible action symbols generate contradictory branches; and the remaining constraints are progressively expanded into rule instances and edges.






Important



A successful Tamarin proof is relative to the symbolic model, equational theory, compromise rules, and guarded property supplied. A counterexample is a trace admitted by that model. The model assumptions are therefore part of the security claim.
crumbs: Symbolic Verification of Security Protocols with Tamarin

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
text:
Verification and validation techniques provide formal methods for specifying systems and establishing whether relevant properties hold. The course focuses especially on reactive programs and systems and on the environments with which they interact or that they control. Properties are expressed through suitable logical formalisms, particularly temporal logics, and are analysed with mathematical models and algorithms.
The course develops three connected kinds of resources:

techniques, such as satisfiability checking and model checking;
methodologies, which organise the construction of models and specifications;
tools, which mechanise analysis, verification, learning, and synthesis.

Formal methods support several distinct tasks. They can be used to check that a specification is internally consistent, to determine whether a program or system satisfies an expected property, and to synthesise a controller that is correct by construction. These tasks should not be conflated. Consistency concerns whether the requirements can hold together. Verification compares a model against a property. Synthesis constructs behaviour from a formal requirement.
The broader course progression begins with background in logic, finite automata, regular languages, and games; it then considers fair transition systems, automata on infinite objects, temporal logics, and algorithms for satisfiability checking, model checking, automata learning, and synthesis. Applications concern artificial intelligence and cybersecurity. This chapter, however, remains within the introductory material and the first deck on logic.



A transformational program receives an input, performs a computation, terminates, and returns an output. Its correctness is usually described as a relation between initial and final states.
A reactive program or system, by contrast, is intended to maintain an appropriate interaction with its environment over time, potentially indefinitely. Its purpose is not simply to terminate with a final value. Operating systems, concurrent and real-time programs, process-control software, embedded systems, monitors, and control protocols for cyber-physical systems are representative examples.
This distinction changes what correctness means. For a reactive system, it is not enough to inspect a final result. One must reason about an entire execution, often an infinite sequence of states or events. Typical requirements say that something bad never occurs, that a requested service is eventually provided, or that the system continues to react correctly whenever its environment produces new inputs.



Concurrency is a distinctive feature of reactive systems. It appears in two closely related forms:

a system operates concurrently with its environment;
several component processes execute concurrently within the system.

The two views can be unified by treating both the system and its environment as interacting components. Formal analysis must therefore describe not only the local behaviour of each component but also their interactions.
Concurrent processes communicate and synchronise primarily through:

shared variables, where processes access common state;
message passing, where processes exchange explicit messages.

The course seeks a uniform account that does not depend on one particular communication mechanism. Fundamental patterns such as mutual exclusion and the producer/consumer schema can be implemented using either shared variables or message passing.
A further distinction is between true concurrency and interleaving. True concurrency means that processes physically execute at the same time. Interleaving models concurrency by arranging atomic actions from different processes into a sequence, selecting one action at a time. Interleaving can faithfully represent relevant aspects of true concurrency only under suitable syntactic restrictions and fairness assumptions. Without such assumptions, an interleaving model may admit unrealistic computations in which an enabled component is postponed forever.



The computational models announced in the introductory deck include fair transition systems and automata over infinite words, trees, or graphs. Temporal logic provides the corresponding specification language.
The introductory classification of properties distinguishes:

safety: bad situations must never occur;
liveness: good situations must eventually occur;
reactivity: ongoing interaction combines obligations to avoid failures and to continue producing appropriate responses.

Safety has a universal flavour: every relevant point of every execution must avoid the forbidden situation. Liveness has an eventuality flavour: an execution must not postpone the required good event forever.
Algorithms then connect models and specifications. The course mentions tableau systems, automata, and logical games as foundations for satisfiability checking, model checking, and synthesis. Model checking is considered for temporal logics such as LTL, CTL, CTL*, and the modal \(\mu\)-calculus. A central practical obstacle is state explosion, where the number of system states grows extremely rapidly with the number of components and variables. Approaches named in the introduction include symbolic model checking, ordered binary decision diagrams (OBDDs), partial-order reduction, automata-based model checking, bounded and SAT-based methods, and IC3-style invariant checking.
The introductory tool landscape includes NuSMV for symbolic model checking and ProVerif and Tamarin for symbolic analysis of cryptographic protocols. These names establish the later application context; their detailed operation is outside this chapter.
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
text:
A transformational program receives an input, performs a computation, terminates, and returns an output. Its correctness is usually described as a relation between initial and final states.
A reactive program or system, by contrast, is intended to maintain an appropriate interaction with its environment over time, potentially indefinitely. Its purpose is not simply to terminate with a final value. Operating systems, concurrent and real-time programs, process-control software, embedded systems, monitors, and control protocols for cyber-physical systems are representative examples.
This distinction changes what correctness means. For a reactive system, it is not enough to inspect a final result. One must reason about an entire execution, often an infinite sequence of states or events. Typical requirements say that something bad never occurs, that a requested service is eventually provided, or that the system continues to react correctly whenever its environment produces new inputs.
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
text:
Concurrency is a distinctive feature of reactive systems. It appears in two closely related forms:

a system operates concurrently with its environment;
several component processes execute concurrently within the system.

The two views can be unified by treating both the system and its environment as interacting components. Formal analysis must therefore describe not only the local behaviour of each component but also their interactions.
Concurrent processes communicate and synchronise primarily through:

shared variables, where processes access common state;
message passing, where processes exchange explicit messages.

The course seeks a uniform account that does not depend on one particular communication mechanism. Fundamental patterns such as mutual exclusion and the producer/consumer schema can be implemented using either shared variables or message passing.
A further distinction is between true concurrency and interleaving. True concurrency means that processes physically execute at the same time. Interleaving models concurrency by arranging atomic actions from different processes into a sequence, selecting one action at a time. Interleaving can faithfully represent relevant aspects of true concurrency only under suitable syntactic restrictions and fairness assumptions. Without such assumptions, an interleaving model may admit unrealistic computations in which an enabled component is postponed forever.
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
text:
The computational models announced in the introductory deck include fair transition systems and automata over infinite words, trees, or graphs. Temporal logic provides the corresponding specification language.
The introductory classification of properties distinguishes:

safety: bad situations must never occur;
liveness: good situations must eventually occur;
reactivity: ongoing interaction combines obligations to avoid failures and to continue producing appropriate responses.

Safety has a universal flavour: every relevant point of every execution must avoid the forbidden situation. Liveness has an eventuality flavour: an execution must not postpone the required good event forever.
Algorithms then connect models and specifications. The course mentions tableau systems, automata, and logical games as foundations for satisfiability checking, model checking, and synthesis. Model checking is considered for temporal logics such as LTL, CTL, CTL*, and the modal \(\mu\)-calculus. A central practical obstacle is state explosion, where the number of system states grows extremely rapidly with the number of components and variables. Approaches named in the introduction include symbolic model checking, ordered binary decision diagrams (OBDDs), partial-order reduction, automata-based model checking, bounded and SAT-based methods, and IC3-style invariant checking.
The introductory tool landscape includes NuSMV for symbolic model checking and ProVerif and Tamarin for symbolic analysis of cryptographic protocols. These names establish the later application context; their detailed operation is outside this chapter.
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
section: 2.2 A model-checking example: the vending machine
text:
2.2 A model-checking example: the vending machine
The deck introduces a vending machine as a transition system. Its states represent stages of operation, and edges are labelled by events such as insertion of \(5\,\text{¢}\) or \(10\,\text{¢}\), coffee, refund, and kick. An execution is a path through this graph. Because the property concerns continuing behaviour, the question is posed over infinite executions.
The intended requirement is:

Whenever a \(5\,\text{¢}\) or \(10\,\text{¢}\) coin is inserted, the next part of the execution must proceed without a kick until either coffee or refund occurs.

Using the words employed in the slide, the specification is shown below. The cent symbol is written with \text{¢}, which renders reliably in Quarto and MathJax.

\[
\varphi = \operatorname{ALWAYS}\Bigl(
  (10\,\text{¢} \operatorname{OR} 5\,\text{¢})
  \rightarrow
  \operatorname{NEXT}\bigl(
    (\operatorname{NOT}\,\mathit{kick})
    \operatorname{UNTIL}
    (\mathit{coffee}\operatorname{OR}\mathit{refund})
  \bigr)
\Bigr).
\]

Each operator has a specific role:

ALWAYS applies the obligation at every position of an execution;
the implication activates the obligation when a coin event occurs;
NEXT starts checking after the coin transition;
UNTIL requires NOT kick at preceding positions and eventually requires coffee OR refund.

The verification question is whether all infinite executions of the model satisfy \(\varphi\). A standard automata-theoretic strategy searches for a counterexample rather than proving the universal statement directly. Negating the specification gives, in the notation of the deck,

\[
\neg\varphi = \operatorname{EVENTUALLY}\Bigl(
(10\,\text{¢} \operatorname{OR} 5\,\text{¢})
\operatorname{AND}
\operatorname{NEXT}\bigl(
   \operatorname{ALWAYS}(\operatorname{NOT}(\mathit{coffee}\operatorname{OR}\mathit{refund}))
   \operatorname{OR}
   (\operatorname{NOT}(\mathit{coffee}\operatorname{OR}\mathit{refund})
      \operatorname{UNTIL}\mathit{kick})
\bigr)
\Bigr).
\]

This formula describes a violating execution: eventually a coin is inserted, after which either coffee and refund never occur, or a kick occurs before either of them. The negated property is compiled into an automaton and combined with the vending-machine model through a product construction. A successful run in the product is a concrete counterexample. Thus, the model, the logical specification, negation, automata, and product construction form one reasoning chain.
The following diagram condenses the verification procedure developed across the progressive slides. Read it from left to right: the model supplies the possible executions, while the negated specification supplies the accepting condition for violations. Their product is then searched for an accepting execution.






flowchart LR
  M["Vending-machine model"] --> P["Product construction"]
  S["Required property φ"] --> N["Negate: ¬φ"]
  N --> A["Automaton for violating executions"]
  A --> P
  P --> C{"Accepting execution exists?"}
  C -->|Yes| X["Counterexample: the model violates φ"]
  C -->|No| V["All model executions satisfy φ"]


 Counterexample-oriented verification workflow for the vending-machine example. 









Important



For oral explanation, distinguish the property from its negation. The original formula expresses required behaviour. The negated formula characterises precisely the executions that violate it, enabling counterexample search.
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
text:
3.1 Vocabulary, syntax, and semantics
A logic functions first as a language. Any such language must specify:

a vocabulary, namely the symbols available for constructing formulas;
a syntax, namely the rules determining which combinations are well-formed;
a semantics, namely the interpretation that gives formulas meaning and determines truth.

These levels cannot replace one another. A string may use allowed symbols but violate the grammar. A well-formed formula may still be ambiguous until the kinds of objects and relations denoted by its symbols are fixed.
The question “Are you two married?” illustrates the role of vocabulary and semantics. Two distinct relations might be intended:

\(\mathit{Married}(x,y)\): \(x\) and \(y\) are married to one another;
\(\mathit{Married}(x)\): \(x\) is a married person.

These predicates have different arities and express different facts. If the binary relation holds, then both corresponding unary statements hold:
\[
\mathit{Married}(x,y)
\rightarrow
\bigl(\mathit{Married}(x)\land\mathit{Married}(y)\bigr).
\]
The reverse implication does not follow: two people can each be married without being married to each other. Formalisation forces the relevant distinction to be stated rather than left to conversational context.
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
text:
3.2 Validity and tautologies
Consider the argument:

If all humans are mortal and Socrates is human, then Socrates is mortal.

Abstracting “human” as \(A\), “mortal” as \(B\), and Socrates as \(y_0\), the deck gives the form
\[
\Bigl((\forall x\,(A(x)\rightarrow B(x)))\land A(y_0)\Bigr)
\rightarrow B(y_0).
\]
The formula is valid: it is true in every structure and under every interpretation of \(A\), \(B\), and \(y_0\). The slides call such a formula a tautology. Validity depends on logical form, not on whether the chosen predicates describe the real world. Replacing humans, mortality, and Socrates by beetles, having six legs, and John Lennon preserves the same valid form, even though a premise may be false in the intended real-world interpretation.
A related example is “If Alice sleeps, then someone sleeps.” If \(a\) denotes Alice and \(S(x)\) means that \(x\) sleeps, a suitable translation is
\[
S(a)\rightarrow \exists x\,S(x).
\]
The implication is valid provided that the constant \(a\) denotes an element of the domain, as is standard in first-order structures.
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
text:
3.3 Unsatisfiability and contradictions
The barber statement is:

There is a barber who shaves all and only those men who do not shave themselves.

Writing \(R(x,y)\) for “\(x\) shaves \(y\)”, its logical core is
\[
\exists x\,\forall y\,
\bigl(R(x,y)\leftrightarrow \neg R(y,y)\bigr).
\]
Assume that an element \(b\) witnesses the existential quantifier. Substituting \(y=b\) yields
\[
R(b,b)\leftrightarrow \neg R(b,b),
\]
which cannot be true. Therefore no interpretation satisfies the formula. It is unsatisfiable, meaning false in every structure or interpretation, and the slides call it a contradiction.
This is structurally related to the statement that there exists a set containing exactly the sets that do not contain themselves. The contradiction arises from applying the defining condition to the purported object itself.
The exercise “Everyone sleeps, but Alice is awake” can be translated as
\[
(\forall x\,S(x))\land \neg S(a).
\]
The universal conjunct entails \(S(a)\), which directly conflicts with \(\neg S(a)\). The formula is therefore unsatisfiable.






Note



Validity and satisfiability are different notions. A valid formula is true in every structure. A satisfiable formula is true in at least one structure. An unsatisfiable formula is true in none.
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
text:
3.4 Typed variables and temporal relationships
The statement

Every incoming order is eventually processed

requires variables of different types. Let \(o\) range over orders and \(t,t'\) over times. Let \(A(o,t)\) mean that order \(o\) arrives at time \(t\), and \(B(o,t')\) mean that \(o\) is processed at time \(t'\). Then:
\[
\forall o\,\forall t\,
\Bigl(A(o,t)\rightarrow
\exists t'\,(t'>t\land B(o,t'))\Bigr).
\]
The typing matters because orders and time points range over different universes or subdomains. The inequality \(t'>t\) makes “eventually” explicit as a later time, while the same order variable \(o\) connects arrival and processing.
The exercise “If I study long enough from now on, I will pass the exam afterwards” similarly requires a temporal relation and a careful account of what interval counts as “long enough.” The lesson of the slide is not a unique translation but the need to choose an adequate vocabulary, variable types, and temporal ordering before the natural-language statement becomes a precise formula.
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
text:
3.5 First-order and second-order variables
The scheduling example states:

Exams can be scheduled in three slots so that no student has two exams at once.

The deck distinguishes:

first-order variables \(x,y,z,\ldots\) for individual exams;
first-order variables \(s,t,u,\ldots\) for individual students;
second-order variables \(A,B,C,\ldots\) for sets of exams, representing the three slots.

Let \(H(x,s)\) mean that student \(s\) has exam \(x\). A direct reconstruction of the slide’s formula is:
\[
\begin{aligned}
\exists A\,\exists B\,\exists C\;\Bigl(&
  \forall x\,(A(x)\lor B(x)\lor C(x)) \\
&\land \neg\exists x\,\bigl(
   (A(x)\land B(x))\lor
   (A(x)\land C(x))\lor
   (B(x)\land C(x))
  \bigr) \\
&\land \neg\exists x\,\exists y\,\exists s\;\bigl(
x\neq y\land H(x,s)\land H(y,s) \\
&\qquad\land ((A(x)\land A(y))\lor
               (B(x)\land B(y))\lor
               (C(x)\land C(y)))
  \bigr)
\Bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
The three conjuncts play separate roles:

every exam belongs to at least one slot;
no exam belongs to two different slots, so the three sets form a partition;
no student has two distinct exams in the same slot.

The outer existential quantification over \(A\), \(B\), and \(C\) expresses the existence of a valid schedule. Because these variables denote sets rather than individual objects, the formula uses second-order quantification.
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
text:
4.1 Reductions
A reduction from a problem \(P\) to a problem \(Q\) is an algorithmic method for solving instances of \(P\) using solutions to \(Q\). Informally, it establishes that \(P\) is no harder than \(Q\) under the chosen kind of reduction.
For a many-to-one reduction, an algorithm \(F\) transforms each input \(x\) so that
\[
P(x) \quad\text{if and only if}\quad Q(F(x)).
\]
Once \(F(x)\) is computed, one call to a solver for \(Q\) determines the answer for \(P(x)\). The direction matters: a reduction from \(P\) to \(Q\) transfers an algorithmic upper bound from \(Q\) to \(P\), while hardness is usually transferred in the opposite interpretive direction.
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
text:
4.2 Time and space complexity
Let \(f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\). An algorithm is time-bounded or space-bounded by \(f\) if, on an input of size \(n\), it uses at most \(f(n)\) units of the corresponding resource.
Asymptotic analysis ignores constant-scale differences. The deck phrases an \(O(f)\) bound by requiring constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that resource use is at most
\[
c\,f(n)+d.
\]
The progression of classes shown is
\[
\mathbf{P}\subseteq\mathbf{NP}\subseteq\mathbf{PSPACE}
\subseteq\mathbf{EXP}\subseteq\cdots
\]
Here \(\mathbf{P}\) contains decision problems solvable in deterministic polynomial time, \(\mathbf{NP}\) those solvable in nondeterministic polynomial time, \(\mathbf{PSPACE}\) those solvable using polynomial space, and \(\mathbf{EXP}\) those solvable in deterministic exponential time. The displayed inclusions do not assert that every adjacent inclusion is strict.
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
text:
4.3 Expressiveness and related trade-offs
When comparing logical formalisms, several questions must remain distinct:

Expressiveness: Which properties can the logic express? Is one logic more expressive than another?
Decidability: Are its central reasoning problems algorithmically solvable?
Succinctness: How large must a formula be to express a property? Two logics may express the same properties while one gives much shorter formulas.
Efficiency: What computational resources do the best known decision procedures require?
Normal forms: Can formulas be transformed into a simpler standard syntax without changing meaning?
Algebraic representations: Is there an equivalent lower-level or algebraic formalism?

Greater expressiveness is not automatically better. It may cause undecidability or higher complexity. A less expressive fragment can be valuable precisely because it admits more efficient analysis. Likewise, equal expressiveness does not imply equal succinctness or equal verification cost.
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
text:
5.1 Model checking
The model-checking problem receives a structure \(S\) and a formula \(\varphi\) and asks whether
\[
S\models\varphi.
\]
The output is yes or no according to whether \(\varphi\) holds in \(S\). In some settings the structure is fixed and omitted from the input, particularly when reasoning over a standard infinite structure.
In computer-science applications, a structure often represents a set of computations or behaviours. Model checking can then be viewed as an implication or containment question: are all behaviours admitted by the system contained in the behaviours satisfying the property?
This definition explains the vending-machine example. The transition system is \(S\), the temporal requirement is \(\varphi\), and a counterexample is an execution in \(S\) that is not among the executions satisfying \(\varphi\).
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
text:
5.2 Validity and satisfiability
The validity problem asks whether a formula holds in every structure:
\[
\models\varphi.
\]
The satisfiability problem asks whether there exists at least one structure in which it holds:
\[
\exists S\;(S\models\varphi).
\]
Validity and unsatisfiability are inter-reducible through negation:
\[
\varphi\text{ is valid}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\neg\varphi\text{ is unsatisfiable}.
\]
Equivalently, \(\varphi\) fails to be valid exactly when \(\neg\varphi\) is satisfiable. This identity is the logical basis of counterexample-oriented verification: instead of directly proving that every interpretation or execution satisfies a formula, search for one satisfying its negation.
The three questions introduced so far can be compared directly:









Decision problem
Input
Question
Positive answer means




Model checking
Structure \(S\) and formula \(\varphi\)
Does \(S\models\varphi\)?
The property holds in the given structure.


Validity
Formula \(\varphi\)
Does \(\varphi\) hold in every structure?
\(\models\varphi\).


Satisfiability
Formula \(\varphi\)
Does \(\varphi\) hold in at least one structure?
There exists an \(S\) such that \(S\models\varphi\).
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
text:
5.3 Logical equivalence
Two formulas \(\varphi_1\) and \(\varphi_2\) are logically equivalent if they have the same truth value in every structure:
\[
\forall S\;\bigl(S\models\varphi_1
\Longleftrightarrow S\models\varphi_2\bigr).
\]
Equivalence can be reduced to validity. In classical logic,
\[
\varphi_1\equiv\varphi_2
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\models(\varphi_1\leftrightarrow\varphi_2).
\]
Thus, a solver for validity can test whether a proposed rewriting, normal form, or translation preserves meaning.
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic
text:
5.4 Definability between logics
Given a formula \(\varphi_1\) in a logic \(L_1\), the definability problem asks whether there exists a formula \(\varphi_2\) in another logic \(L_2\) such that
\[
\varphi_1\equiv\varphi_2.
\]
Often \(L_2\) is a fragment of \(L_1\) with better algorithmic complexity. A positive answer means that the property expressed by \(\varphi_1\) does not require the full expressive power of \(L_1\) and can be transferred to the more tractable formalism. This connects definability directly with the earlier trade-off among expressiveness, succinctness, and efficiency.
crumbs: Introduction to Formal Verification and Logic

title: Preliminaries on Automata Theory: Finite Words and Finite-State Automata
text:
The lecture begins with automata over finite words. Finite-state automata and regular expressions are introduced as two ways of representing the same kind of objects. Before defining automata, it establishes the basic vocabulary for symbols, words, concatenation, alphabets and languages.


A symbol is an elementary character from which words are formed. Symbols are commonly denoted by letters such as (a), (b), and (c).
A word is a finite sequence of symbols. For example,
[ w = abcaa ]
is a word consisting of five symbols. The length of a word (w), written (|w|), is the number of symbols in that sequence. Thus, (|abcaa|=5).
The empty word, denoted by (), is the unique word containing no symbols. Its length is zero:
[ ||=0. ]
The empty word is still a word. It plays the role of an identity for concatenation.



The basic operation on words is concatenation. Given two words (w) and (v), their concatenation, written (wv) (or simply (wv)), is the word obtained by writing the symbols of (v) immediately after the symbols of (w), without inserting a separator.
For example, let
[ w=abba, v=ccc. ]
Then
[ wv=abbaccc. ]
Concatenation is not commutative in general: the order of the two words matters. In this example,
[ wv=abbaccc cccabba=vw. ]
The empty word is the identity element:
[ w=w=w. ]
The dot is often omitted when the meaning is clear. The lecture uses it explicitly when introducing concatenation and then relies on the shorter notation where convenient.



Let (A) and (B) be two sets of words. Their concatenation is the set containing every word obtained by concatenating one element of (A) with one element of (B):
[ AB ={uw uA wB}. ]
This definition lifts word concatenation to sets: every possible choice of a first word from (A) and a second word from (B) contributes a concatenated word to the result.
The empty word and the empty set give the following identities:
[ A{}=A, {}A=A, A=. ]
The first two identities follow because concatenating any word with () leaves it unchanged. The last identity follows because there is no element to choose from the empty set.



For every integer (m), the power (A^m) denotes the concatenation of (m) copies of (A):
[ A^m=_{m}. ]
The zero-th power is defined separately as
[ A^0={}, ]
and the powers can be defined recursively by
[ A{m+1}=AmA. ]
The Kleene closure of a set of words (A), denoted by (A^*), is the union of all its finite powers, including the zero-th power:
[ A^*=_{m} A^m ={}AA^2A^3. ]
Consequently, (A^*) contains the empty word as well as every word that can be formed by concatenating finitely many elements of (A).
For the example (A={a}), the closure is
[ A^*={,a,aa,aaa,}. ]
The positive closure excludes the empty word:
[ A+=A*{} =_{m>0}A^m. ]
The distinction is therefore whether zero repetitions are allowed: (A^*) includes zero repetitions, while (A^+) contains only positive numbers of repetitions.

title: Preliminaries on Automata Theory: Finite Words and Finite-State Automata
section: 2.1 Alphabets and words over an alphabet
text:
2.1 Alphabets and words over an alphabet
An alphabet is a finite set of symbols. For example, consider
[ A={a,b,c}. ]
A word over the alphabet (A) is any finite sequence whose symbols all belong to (A). Equivalently, it is an element of (A^*).
For example, the word
[ w=abbca ]
has length five and satisfies
[ wA^5A^*. ]
Here, (A^5) is the set of all words of length five over the alphabet (A), whereas (A^*) contains words of every finite length, including zero.
crumbs: Preliminaries on Automata Theory: Finite Words and Finite-State Automata

title: Preliminaries on Automata Theory: Finite Words and Finite-State Automata
text:
2.2 Languages
A language over the alphabet (A) is any subset of (A^*):
[ LA^*. ]
Thus, a language is a set of words over a fixed alphabet. It may contain words of different lengths. The automata introduced next provide a finite-state mechanism for deciding which words belong to a language.
crumbs: Preliminaries on Automata Theory: Finite Words and Finite-State Automata

title: Preliminaries on Automata Theory: Finite Words and Finite-State Automata
text:
3.1 Formal definition of a DFA
A DFA (A) is a tuple
[ A=(Q,A,,q_0,F), ]
where:

(Q) is a finite set of states, often written (Q={q_0,q_1,,q_n});
(A) is a finite input alphabet;
() is the transition function, [ :QAQ; ]
(q_0Q) is the initial state;
(FQ) is the set of final, or accepting, states.

The transition function takes a state-symbol pair and returns exactly one state. This is the formal meaning of deterministic: there is one prescribed next state for every current state and input symbol.
In the graphical notation for automata, states are drawn as nodes, transitions as directed labelled edges, and the initial state is identified by an incoming arrow from nowhere. Accepting states are represented by double circles. The following is the transition-graph example introduced with the definition.



Example of a finite-state automaton in graphical notation.
crumbs: Preliminaries on Automata Theory: Finite Words and Finite-State Automata

title: Preliminaries on Automata Theory: Finite Words and Finite-State Automata
section: 3.2 Extending the transition function to words
text:
3.2 Extending the transition function to words
The function () is initially defined for one input symbol. To describe the effect of reading a complete word, it is extended to
[ :QA^*Q. ]
The extension is defined recursively. Reading the empty word leaves the automaton in the state where it started:
[ (q,)=q. ]
If a word is written as (wa), where (wA^*) and (aA), first read (w), then process the final symbol (a):
[ (q,wa) =((q,w),a). ]
The recursive definition follows the order in which the symbols are read. It first determines the state reached after the prefix (w), and then applies the ordinary one-symbol transition for (a).
For a single symbol, the extended and original functions agree:
[ (q,a)=(q,a). ]
For simplicity, the notation ((q,w)) is also often used for the extended function, with the hat omitted when the meaning is clear.
crumbs: Preliminaries on Automata Theory: Finite Words and Finite-State Automata

title: Preliminaries on Automata Theory: Finite Words and Finite-State Automata
section: 3.3 Acceptance of words and the language of a DFA
text:
3.3 Acceptance of words and the language of a DFA
A word (wA^*) is accepted by a DFA (A) if and only if the state reached after reading the entire word is final:
[ (q_0,w)F. ]
The initial state matters because the computation always begins at (q_0). The final-state condition is checked only after all symbols of the word have been consumed.
The language accepted by (A), denoted by (L(A)), consists of all and only the words over its alphabet that it accepts:
[ L(A) ={wA^*(q_0,w)F}. ]

3.3.1 Example: processing the word cbaba
The following automaton reproduces the example in the lecture. Its initial state is (q_0), its accepting state is (q_1), and its third state is (q_2).



A DFA whose accepting state is q1, with transitions q0 to q1, q1 to q2, and q2 back to q1.


For the input word (w=cbaba), the computation proceeds as follows:



Input read so far
Current state




()
(q_0)


(c)
(q_1)


(cb)
(q_2)


(cba)
(q_1)


(cbab)
(q_2)


(cbaba)

The word is accepted because the computation finishes in (q_1), which is an accepting state. In the notation of the extended transition function,
[ (q_0,cbaba)=q_1F. ]
This illustrates that acceptance depends on the state reached after the whole word, not on whether an accepting state was visited at some intermediate point.

title: Preliminaries on Automata Theory: Finite Words and Finite-State Automata
text:
3.4 Completing an incomplete automaton
The formal definition of a DFA uses a transition function
[ :QAQ. ]
This function is defined for every pair consisting of a state and an alphabet symbol. A diagram may nevertheless omit some transitions. Such a drawing is an incomplete representation of the transition function.
The lecture’s completion method is to add a sink state. Every transition that was missing is directed to this new state, and the sink state loops to itself on every input symbol. The sink is not accepting. Therefore, once a computation enters it, it cannot later reach an accepting state.
This completion does not change the language recognized by the automaton: a word that previously encountered a missing transition is rejected, and after completion it reaches the non-accepting sink instead.

title: Preliminaries on Automata Theory: Finite Words and Finite-State Automata
section: 3.5 The membership problem and regular languages
text:
3.5 The membership problem and regular languages
Given an automaton (A) and a word (w), the membership problem asks whether
[ wL(A)? ]
For a language (LA^*), the lecture uses the following definition:
[ L AL=L(A). ]
In other words, a language is regular when some deterministic finite-state automaton accepts exactly its words.

title: Preliminaries on Automata Theory: Finite Words and Finite-State Automata
text:
4.1 Formal definition of an NFA
An NFA (A) is a tuple
[ A=(Q,A,,q_0,F), ]
with:

(Q) a finite set of states;
(A) a finite alphabet;
() a transition function of type [ :QA^Q; ]
(q_0Q) the initial state;
(FQ) the set of final states.

The notation (2^Q) denotes the power set of (Q), namely the set of all subsets of (Q). Consequently, for a state (q) and symbol (a), the value ((q,a)) is a set of possible destination states.
Equivalently, the transitions can be represented as a relation
[ QAQ. ]
A triple ((q,a,q’)) means that the automaton may move from (q) to (q’) while reading symbol (a). Unlike a function into a single state, this relation can associate the same state-symbol pair with several destinations.

4.2 Reading the same symbol along multiple possible transitions
The following schematic diagram shows the non-deterministic choice represented in the lecture: from state (q), reading (a) may leave the machine in (q), or move it to (q’), or move it to (q’’).



NFA transition example: from q, input a can lead to q, q-prime, or q-double-prime.


Thus, after reading one symbol, an NFA may have several possible current states. The transition function records all of them together as a subset of (Q).

section: 4.3 Extending the NFA transition function to words
text:
4.3 Extending the NFA transition function to words
For an NFA, the extended transition function returns a set of states:
[ :QA^*^Q. ]
The base case is
[ (q,)={q}. ]
For a word (wa), the automaton considers every state reachable after reading (w), takes its possible transitions on (a), and unions all the resulting sets:
[ (q,wa) =_{r(q,w)}(r,a). ]
The union is essential. It collects every state that can be reached by extending any possible computation on the prefix (w) with the final symbol (a).
The lecture also gives the corresponding extension to a set of starting states. For (PQ) and (wA^*),
[ :2^QA^*^Q, (P,w)=_{qP}(q,w). ]
This expression combines the states reachable after reading (w) from each possible starting state in (P).

4.4 Acceptance of words by an NFA
A word (wA^*) is accepted by an NFA (A) if and only if at least one state reachable after reading the complete word is final:
[ (q_0,w)F. ]
The intersection condition expresses the existential nature of NFA acceptance. It is sufficient that one possible computation ends in a final state; other possible computations may end in non-final states.
As for a DFA, the language (L(A)) consists of all and only the words over (A) accepted by the automaton. The definition of the language is therefore the same in purpose, although the acceptance test differs:

title: The Gap Theorem and Relationships Between Time and Space Complexity
text:
The deterministic time hierarchy theorem shows that suitable, sufficiently separated time bounds give different complexity classes. A natural question is whether this separation can always be obtained when one replaces a time bound by a much larger one. The Gap Theorem gives a surprising answer: for some computable functions, increasing the time bound from \(f(n)\) to \(2^{f(n)}\) does not enlarge the class at all.
This is also a way to see why the condition that a time bound be proper matters in the hierarchy theorem. Mere computability is not enough.


Gap Theorem

There exists a computable, increasing function \(f:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}\) such that
\[
\operatorname{TIME}(f(n))=\operatorname{TIME}(2^{f(n)}).
\]
The function obtained by the construction below is not proper in the sense required by the deterministic time hierarchy theorem.



Fix an effective enumeration of all Turing machines:
\[
M_0,M_1,M_2,\ldots
\]
An enumeration is an algorithm that outputs the encodings of the machines one after another. It includes machines that do not halt on every input: deciding in advance which machines always halt is not possible. Let \(\Sigma_j\) be the input alphabet of \(M_j\).
The proof constructs a function \(f\) by looking, at each input length \(i\), at the first \(i+1\) machines and all their inputs of exactly that length.



For natural numbers \(i\) and \(k\), define the predicate \(P(i,k)\) by
\[
\begin{aligned}
P(i,k)\ \Longleftrightarrow\ &\forall j\leq i\;\forall x\in\Sigma_j^i,\\
&\bigl(M_j(x)\text{ halts in fewer than }k\text{ steps}\bigr)\\
&\qquad\lor\bigl(M_j(x)\text{ does not halt within }2^k\text{ steps}\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
The second alternative includes both possibilities in which the computation halts only after more than \(2^k\) steps and in which it never halts. Equivalently, no computation considered by the predicate is allowed to halt at a time between \(k\) and \(2^k\), inclusive.
Why is \(P(i,k)\) decidable? There are finitely many machines \(M_0,\ldots,M_i\) and finitely many inputs of length \(i\) for each machine. For each machine-input pair, simulate the machine for at most \(2^k\) steps:

if it halts before step \(k\), that pair satisfies the predicate;
if it halts at a step between \(k\) and \(2^k\), the predicate is false;
if it has not halted after \(2^k\) steps, that pair satisfies the second alternative.

All these simulations have a finite bound. Therefore the truth of \(P(i,k)\) can be decided, even though some of the simulated machines may run forever.
For example, consider \(P(10,3)\). We inspect \(M_0,\ldots,M_{10}\) on every input of length \(10\), and compare each halting time with \(3\) and \(2^3=8\). If one of these computations halts in \(5\) steps, then \(P(10,3)\) is false. A computation that has not halted within \(8\) steps does not falsify the predicate.



For a fixed \(i\), the number of inputs of length \(i\) over the alphabet of \(M_j\) is \(|\Sigma_j|^i\). Thus the total number of machine-input pairs under consideration is
\[
N(i)=\sum_{j=0}^{i}|\Sigma_j|^i.
\]
This counts one pair for each choice of a machine \(M_j\), with \(j\leq i\), and an input \(x\in\Sigma_j^i\). Each such pair has at most one halting time: if its computation halts, it does so at one particular step; otherwise it has no halting time.



Assume that \(f(i-1)\) has already been defined. Set the first endpoint to
\[
k_1=2^{f(i-1)},
\]
and define the subsequent endpoints recursively by
\[
k_{r+1}=2^{k_r}+1.
\]
These endpoints determine intervals of integer step counts
\[
[k_1,k_2),\ [k_2,k_3),\ldots.
\]
Consider the first \(N(i)+1\) such intervals. There are \(N(i)\) machine-input pairs but \(N(i)+1\) intervals. Since each pair can have only one halting time, it can place a halting time in at most one interval. Consequently, at least one of the \(N(i)+1\) intervals contains no halting time of any of the machines \(M_0,\ldots,M_i\) on any input of length \(i\).
Suppose that the empty interval is \([k_r,k_{r+1})\). By construction,
\[
k_{r+1}=2^{k_r}+1.
\]
Therefore none of the considered computations halts at any integer step from \(k_r\) through \(2^{k_r}\). Every computation either halts before \(k_r\) or has not halted within \(2^{k_r}\) steps. Hence
\[
P(i,k_r)\text{ is true}.
\]
We can now define \(f(i)\) as the left endpoint of the first interval in this sequence that contains no halting time, or equivalently as the first \(k_r\) for which \(P(i,k_r)\) is true:
\[
f(i)=k_r\quad\text{for the least }r\text{ such that }P(i,k_r)\text{ holds}.
\]
Choose a fixed positive starting value for \(f(0)\). The use of \(2^{f(i-1)}\) as the first endpoint makes the resulting function increasing.


To compute \(f(i)\):

Compute \(f(0),f(1),\ldots,f(i-1)\) recursively, so that the first endpoint \(k_1\) is known.
Compute the finite number \(N(i)\).
Generate the endpoints \(k_1,k_2,\ldots\) in order.
Test \(P(i,k_r)\) for each candidate, stopping at the first true value.

Every predicate test is decidable. The pigeonhole argument proves that a successful candidate occurs among the first \(N(i)+1\) intervals. Thus the search terminates, and \(f\) is computable. The search may be extremely expensive; computability alone does not make the function proper.




We prove both inclusions.


This direction is immediate. Since \(f(n)\leq 2^{f(n)}\) for positive \(f(n)\), a machine that runs in time \(O(f(n))\) also runs in time \(O(2^{f(n)})\). Therefore
\[
\operatorname{TIME}(f(n))\subseteq\operatorname{TIME}(2^{f(n)}).
\]



Let \(L\in\operatorname{TIME}(2^{f(n)})\). There is a deterministic Turing machine \(M_s\) that decides \(L\) and halts on every input \(x\) of length \(n\) within at most \(2^{f(n)}\) steps.
Now take any \(n\geq s\). The predicate \(P(n,f(n))\) is true by the definition of \(f(n)\). Since \(s\leq n\), it applies to the machine \(M_s\) and every input \(x\) of length \(n\). Thus, for each such input, one of the following must hold:

\(M_s(x)\) halts in fewer than \(f(n)\) steps;
\(M_s(x)\) does not halt within \(2^{f(n)}\) steps.

The second possibility is excluded because \(M_s\) is a decider that halts within at most \(2^{f(n)}\) steps. Hence, for every input of length \(n\geq s\), the machine actually halts in fewer than \(f(n)\) steps.
There are only finitely many strings whose lengths are smaller than \(s\). The decision for these short inputs can be built into a modified machine using a finite lookup table (equivalently, a finite-state procedure for this finite set). This changes only finitely many input lengths and does not change the asymptotic time class. The proper-bound assumptions used for the time classes absorb this finite initial range.
We have therefore obtained a machine deciding \(L\) in time \(O(f(n))\), so
\[
\operatorname{TIME}(2^{f(n)})\subseteq\operatorname{TIME}(f(n)).
\]
Combining the two inclusions proves the Gap Theorem.




The construction gives a computable function for which the two time classes coincide. If this function also satisfied the properness conditions required by the deterministic time hierarchy theorem, that theorem would force the corresponding time classes to be strictly different. This would contradict the equality just proved.
Thus the construction establishes both points emphasized in the lecture:

there are computable functions that are not proper;
for one such function, even the exponential increase from \(f(n)\) to \(2^{f(n)}\) leaves the deterministic time class unchanged.

The gap is not a claim that all time bounds behave this way. It shows why the hierarchy theorem needs its properness hypothesis.

title: The Gap Theorem and Relationships Between Time and Space Complexity
text:
2.1 The immediate inclusions
The first three statements follow directly from the definitions.

A deterministic machine is a special case of a nondeterministic machine: it simply has one possible next move at each step. Allowing nondeterministic choices cannot reduce the set of languages that can be decided within the same space bound. Hence \[
\operatorname{SPACE}(f(n))\subseteq\operatorname{NSPACE}(f(n)).
\]
The same reasoning applies to time. A deterministic computation is one possible form of a nondeterministic computation, so \[
\operatorname{TIME}(f(n))\subseteq\operatorname{NTIME}(f(n)).
\]
In \(f(n)\) computation steps, a Turing machine cannot visit more than \(O(f(n))\) tape cells: in one step, a head can move by at most one cell. Therefore a time bound also gives a space bound: \[
\operatorname{TIME}(f(n))\subseteq\operatorname{SPACE}(f(n)).
\]
crumbs: The Gap Theorem and Relationships Between Time and Space Complexity

title: The Gap Theorem and Relationships Between Time and Space Complexity
section: 2.2 From nondeterministic time to deterministic space
text:
2.2 From nondeterministic time to deterministic space
We prove inclusion 5:
\[
\operatorname{NTIME}(f(n))\subseteq\operatorname{SPACE}(f(n)).
\]
Let \(L\in\operatorname{NTIME}(f(n))\). By definition, there is a nondeterministic Turing machine \(N\) that decides \(L\) and whose computation branches halt within at most \(f(n)\) steps on inputs of length \(n\).
A computation of \(N\) can be represented as a tree. Each node is a configuration, and its children are the configurations reachable by one of the possible nondeterministic moves. A deterministic machine can decide whether an accepting branch exists by exploring this tree depth first and backtracking when a branch does not accept.
The deterministic simulation stores:

the current simulated configuration of \(N\);
an additional record of the nondeterministic choices made along the current branch, so that it can return to a previous choice and try the next one.

The number of choices on a branch is at most \(f(n)\). Since the branching degree of the fixed machine is bounded by a constant, each choice requires only a constant number of bits, and the additional choice record uses \(O(f(n))\) space. The simulated machine itself also uses at most \(O(f(n))\) space, because a computation of at most \(f(n)\) steps cannot visit more than that many tape cells.
When a branch fails, the deterministic simulation changes the last available choice and replays the corresponding branch from its beginning. It reuses the same simulated working space; it does not keep a separate copy of the work tape for every branch. The total space is therefore still \(O(f(n))\).






flowchart TD
    S["Initial configuration"] --> A["Choice 1"]
    S --> B["Choice 2"]
    A --> A1["Choice 1.1"]
    A --> A2["Choice 1.2"]
    B --> B1["Choice 2.1"]
    B --> B2["Choice 2.2"]
    A1 --> Y["Accept"]
    A2 --> R["Reject"]
    B1 --> R
    B2 --> Y


 The nondeterministic computation branches; a deterministic depth-first simulation explores one branch at a time and backtracks to try alternatives. 



The simulation may take much more time than the original nondeterministic computation, because it can inspect many branches. The point of this argument is that it uses only \(O(f(n))\) space. Consequently,
\[
L\in\operatorname{SPACE}(f(n)),
\]
which proves inclusion 5.
crumbs: The Gap Theorem and Relationships Between Time and Space Complexity

title: The Gap Theorem and Relationships Between Time and Space Complexity
section: 2.3 From nondeterministic space to deterministic time: reachability
text:
2.3 From nondeterministic space to deterministic time: reachability
The sixth inclusion is proved by turning the computation into a finite directed graph and deciding a reachability problem on that graph. This is the reachability method emphasized in the lecture.
Let \(N\) be a nondeterministic Turing machine with input and output tapes and \(k-2\) working tapes, using at most \(f(n)\) space on inputs of length \(n\). Assume that \(N\) decides the language \(L\).

2.3.1 Configurations of the machine
Fix an input \(x\) of length \(n\). A configuration records the information needed to determine the next move:

the current state \(q\);
the position \(j\) of the head on the read-only input tape, where \(1\leq j\leq n+1\);
the contents of the working tapes and the position of each working-tape head.

For a working tape, its content can be represented by two strings: \(u_r\) to the left of the head and \(v_r\) at and to the right of the head. The configuration can therefore be written in the form
\[
C=(q,j,u_2,v_2,\ldots,u_{k-1},v_{k-1}).
\]
The input string itself is fixed, so it need not be copied into every configuration. The output tape is write-only: its contents cannot be read to influence future transitions. Since the machine is deciding a language, the output is not relevant to whether an accepting computation exists, and that tape can be omitted from the configuration description. The accepting and rejecting states are included as two distinguished states, denoted YES and NO.


2.3.2 Counting the configurations
Let \(\mathcal{K}\) be the set of ordinary states of \(N\), and let \(\Sigma\) be its tape alphabet. The number of choices for the state, including the two distinguished halting states, is \(|\mathcal{K}|+2\). The input head has \(n+1\) possible positions.
Each of the \(k-2\) working tapes is represented by two strings, each of length at most \(f(n)\). The number of strings of length at most \(f(n)\) over \(\Sigma\) is
\[
\sum_{\ell=0}^{f(n)}|\Sigma|^\ell.
\]
It follows that the number \(V\) of possible configurations is bounded by
\[
V\leq (|\mathcal{K}|+2)(n+1)
\left(\sum_{\ell=0}^{f(n)}|\Sigma|^\ell\right)^{2(k-2)}.
\]
For a fixed machine, its state set, tape alphabet and number of tapes are constants. Their contribution can therefore be absorbed into a constant base \(c>1\). The factor \(n+1\) contributes the \(\log n\) term in the exponent. Thus
\[
V\leq c^{f(n)+\log n}
\]
for a suitable machine-dependent constant \(c\).
The \(\log n\) term is important. In a space-bounded computation, \(f(n)\) may be smaller than \(\log n\) (for example, it may be constant or \(\log\log n\)). Even then, the input head can occupy any of the \(n+1\) positions, and these possibilities must be counted.


2.3.3 The configuration graph
Define a directed graph \(G_{N,x}\) as follows:

each node represents a possible configuration of \(N\) on input \(x\);
there is a directed edge from configuration \(C\) to configuration \(C'\) if one legal transition of \(N\) can take \(C\) to \(C'\).

The graph is finite because the space bound restricts the number of possible configurations. Its edges represent the possible nondeterministic moves. All accepting configurations can be identified with a single YES node, and all rejecting configurations with a single NO node. The initial configuration reaches YES if and only if at least one computation branch of \(N\) accepts \(x\).






flowchart LR
    I["Initial configuration"] --> C1["Configuration 1"]
    I --> C2["Configuration 2"]
    C1 --> C3["Configuration 3"]
    C2 --> C3
    C2 --> R["NO"]
    C3 --> A["YES"]


 The computation is represented as a directed graph; membership is equivalent to reachability of the accepting node from the initial configuration. 



A deterministic algorithm can construct or explore this finite graph and solve the corresponding reachability problem. The graph has at most \(V\) nodes, and each configuration has only a machine-dependent finite number of possible next moves. A standard graph search therefore takes time polynomial in the size of the graph. Since
\[
V\leq c^{f(n)+\log n},
\]
any fixed polynomial in \(V\) can be absorbed by increasing the constant base. The resulting deterministic running time is bounded by
\[
c'^{\,f(n)+\log n}
\]
for another constant \(c'>1\) depending on the machine. Hence
\[
\operatorname{NSPACE}(f(n))
\subseteq
\operatorname{TIME}\!\left(c^{f(n)+\log n}\right).
\]
This proves inclusion 6.


2.3.4 Why the graph viewpoint is useful
The graph construction illustrates a general way to reason about computations. A system is given an operational semantics that describes its possible steps; these steps define a directed graph whose nodes are system configurations. A property of the graph can then express a property of the system. Here, the property is reachability: does the initial configuration have a path to an accepting configuration?
The same viewpoint applies whether the computation comes from a program or from a protocol in which components exchange messages. The graph may be very large, but for a fixed input and a fixed space bound it is finite. An infinite state graph in another setting does not, by itself, imply that every property of interest is undecidable; the relevant question is whether the property can be decided for the graph at hand.

title: The Gap Theorem and Relationships Between Time and Space Complexity
text:
2.4 The remaining containment
The fourth inclusion follows immediately from the first and the sixth. By inclusion 1,
\[
\operatorname{SPACE}(f(n))\subseteq\operatorname{NSPACE}(f(n)),
\]
and by inclusion 6,
\[
\operatorname{NSPACE}(f(n))
\subseteq
\operatorname{TIME}\!\left(c^{f(n)+\log n}\right).
\]
Combining them gives
\[
\operatorname{SPACE}(f(n))
\subseteq
\operatorname{TIME}\!\left(c^{f(n)+\log n}\right),
\]
which is inclusion 4. Thus the two nontrivial arguments in this part of the lecture are the depth-first simulation for inclusion 5 and the configuration-graph reachability argument for inclusion 6; the other containments follow directly from the definitions or from these results.

title: Shannon Codes, Huffman Codes, and Asymptotic Optimality
text:
Let
\[
\mathcal A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}
\]
be a source alphabet with probability mass function
\[
p_i=P(X=a_i),
\qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{k}p_i=1,
\]
and let
\[
\mathcal B=\{b_1,\ldots,b_D\}
\]
be an output alphabet of size \(D\).
A code
\[
\varphi:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B^*
\]
assigns a codeword to each source symbol. If
\[
l_i=|\varphi(a_i)|
\]
is the length of the codeword assigned to \(a_i\), the expected codeword length is
\[
EL(\varphi)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{k}p_i l_i.
\]
This is the average number of output symbols used to encode one source symbol. A codeword with length \(l_i\) contributes proportionally to how often the corresponding source symbol occurs.
For a binary output alphabet, the unit is bits per source symbol. For a \(D\)-ary output alphabet, the unit is \(D\)-ary digits per source symbol.


For a source message
\[
m=m_1m_2\cdots m_n\in\mathcal A^*,
\]
the extended code concatenates the individual codewords:
\[
\varphi(m)
=
\varphi(m_1)\varphi(m_2)\cdots\varphi(m_n).
\]
Consequently, encoded lengths add:
\[
|\varphi(m)|
=
|\varphi(m_1)|+
|\varphi(m_2)|+
\cdots+
|\varphi(m_n)|.
\]
The lecture assumes a stationary memoryless source. Stationarity means that the probability distribution does not change from one source position to another. The absence of memory means that successive source symbols are independent. Therefore,
\[
p(m)
=
p(m_1)p(m_2)\cdots p(m_n).
\]

title: Shannon Codes, Huffman Codes, and Asymptotic Optimality
section: 2.1 Proof from Kraft-McMillan and relative entropy
text:
2.1 Proof from Kraft-McMillan and relative entropy
Let
\[
K=\sum_{i=1}^{k}D^{-l_i}.
\]
Because \(\varphi\) is uniquely decodable, the inverse Kraft-McMillan theorem gives
\[
K\leq1.
\]
Normalise the Kraft terms to obtain a probability distribution
\[
q_i=\frac{D^{-l_i}}{K}.
\]
Indeed,
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{k}q_i
=
\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{k}D^{-l_i}
=1.
\]
From the definition of \(q_i\),
\[
D^{-l_i}=Kq_i.
\]
Taking logarithms in base \(D\) gives
\[
l_i
=-\log_D(Kq_i)
=-\log_DK-\log_Dq_i.
\]
Substitute this expression into the expected length:
\[
\begin{aligned}
EL(\varphi)
&=\sum_{i=1}^{k}p_i l_i\\
&=-\log_DK-\sum_{i=1}^{k}p_i\log_Dq_i.
\end{aligned}
\]
The second term is the cross-entropy between \(p\) and \(q\). Using
\[
-\sum_ip_i\log_Dq_i
=
H_D(p)+D_{\mathrm{KL},D}(p\Vert q),
\]
we obtain
\[
EL(\varphi)
=
H_D(p)
+D_{\mathrm{KL},D}(p\Vert q)
-\log_DK.
\]
Both additional terms are non-negative:

relative entropy satisfies \(D_{\mathrm{KL},D}(p\Vert q)\geq0\);
since \(K\leq1\), we have \(-\log_DK\geq0\).

Therefore,
\[
EL(\varphi)\geq H_D(p).
\]
This proof also explains why the lower bound is natural. Any difference between the true distribution \(p\) and the distribution represented by the code lengths creates a KL-divergence penalty, while any unused Kraft capacity creates the additional penalty \(-\log_DK\).
