title: Shannon Codes, Huffman Codes, and Asymptotic Optimality
text:
4.1 Binary example
Let
\[
\mathcal A=\{a,b\},
\qquad
p(a)=\frac14,
\qquad
p(b)=\frac34.
\]
The binary entropy satisfies
\[
H_2(p)<1.
\]
However, a binary uniquely decodable symbol code must assign at least one bit to each of the two symbols. The code
\[
\varphi(a)=0,
\qquad
\varphi(b)=1
\]
has
\[
EL(\varphi)=1.
\]
No binary symbol code can achieve a smaller average length, so this code is optimal even though
\[
H_2(p)<EL(\varphi).
\]
This example separates two concepts:

optimality means no admissible code has a smaller expected length;
perfect entropy matching means the expected length equals entropy.

The first does not imply the second.

title: Shannon Codes, Huffman Codes, and Asymptotic Optimality
section: 5.1 Why the Shannon lengths define a prefix code
text:
5.1 Why the Shannon lengths define a prefix code
Since
\[
l_i\geq-\log_Dp_i,
\]
and the function \(D^{-x}\) is decreasing, we obtain
\[
D^{-l_i}
\leq
D^{\log_Dp_i}
=
p_i.
\]
Summing over all source symbols gives
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{k}D^{-l_i}
\leq
\sum_{i=1}^{k}p_i
=1.
\]
The lengths therefore satisfy the Kraft-McMillan inequality. By the direct Kraft-McMillan theorem, there exists a \(D\)-ary prefix code whose codeword lengths are exactly \(l_1,\ldots,l_k\).
This argument establishes the existence of a prefix code with the Shannon lengths. A separate constructive procedure may then assign actual codewords of those lengths.
crumbs: Shannon Codes, Huffman Codes, and Asymptotic Optimality

title: Shannon Codes, Huffman Codes, and Asymptotic Optimality
text:
5.2 Expected-length guarantee
Because
\[
l_i
=
\left\lceil-\log_Dp_i\right\rceil
<
-\log_Dp_i+1,
\]
we have
\[
\begin{aligned}
EL(\varphi_S)
&=\sum_{i=1}^{k}p_i l_i\\
&<\sum_{i=1}^{k}p_i
  \left(-\log_Dp_i+1\right)\\
&=-\sum_{i=1}^{k}p_i\log_Dp_i
  +\sum_{i=1}^{k}p_i\\
&=H_D(p)+1.
\end{aligned}
\]
Combining this upper bound with Shannon’s lower bound for uniquely decodable codes gives
\[
\boxed{
H_D(p)
\leq
EL(\varphi_S)
<
H_D(p)+1
}.
\]
Therefore, a Shannon code uses, on average, less than one additional output symbol per source symbol relative to the entropy lower bound.

title: Shannon Codes, Huffman Codes, and Asymptotic Optimality
text:
5.3 Example with two source symbols
Let
\[
\mathcal A=\{a,b\},
\qquad
p(a)=\frac{31}{32},
\qquad
p(b)=\frac{1}{32},
\]
and let the output alphabet be binary:
\[
\mathcal B=\{0,1\}.
\]
The Shannon lengths are
\[
\begin{aligned}
l_a
&=\left\lceil-\log_2\frac{31}{32}\right\rceil
=1,\\
l_b
&=\left\lceil-\log_2\frac{1}{32}\right\rceil
=5.
\end{aligned}
\]
Their Kraft sum is
\[
2^{-1}+2^{-5}
=
\frac12+\frac1{32}
=
\frac{17}{32}
<1.
\]
Hence a binary prefix code with lengths \(1\) and \(5\) exists. One possible assignment is
\[
\varphi(a)=0,
\qquad
\varphi(b)=10000.
\]
The corresponding prefix tree is:






flowchart LR
    R((root))
    A["a: 0"]
    N1(("1"))
    N10(("10"))
    N100(("100"))
    N1000(("1000"))
    B["b: 10000"]

    R -->|0| A
    R -->|1| N1
    N1 -->|0| N10
    N10 -->|0| N100
    N100 -->|0| N1000
    N1000 -->|0| B

    classDef codeword fill:#dff3e4,stroke:#27864a,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef internal fill:#eef3f8,stroke:#5b6b7a;
    class A,B codeword;
    class R,N1,N10,N100,N1000 internal;


 Binary prefix tree for the Shannon lengths 1 and 5. 



The path labelled (0) immediately reaches the codeword for (a). The path labelled (10000) reaches the codeword for (b). Neither codeword is a prefix of the other, so the code is prefix-free.
The expected length is
\[
\begin{aligned}
EL(\varphi_S)
&=\frac{31}{32}\cdot1
+\frac1{32}\cdot5\\
&=\frac{36}{32}\\
&=1.125\text{ bits per source symbol}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The highly probable symbol receives the shortest possible non-empty binary codeword, while the rare symbol receives a much longer codeword.

p & 40/100 & 18/100 & 15/100 & 13/100 & 10/100 & 4/100

title: Shannon Codes, Huffman Codes, and Asymptotic Optimality
text:
8.1 Product source
Let
\[
X_1,\ldots,X_m
\]
be independent and identically distributed source variables with pmf \(p\). The block
\[
X^m=(X_1,\ldots,X_m)
\]
has product distribution
\[
p^m(x_1,\ldots,x_m)
=
\prod_{j=1}^{m}p(x_j).
\]
Independence makes entropy additive:
\[
\begin{aligned}
H_D(p^m)
&=H_D(X_1,\ldots,X_m)\\
&=\sum_{j=1}^{m}H_D(X_j)\\
&=mH_D(p).
\end{aligned}
\]
Apply the Shannon construction to the block alphabet \(\mathcal A^m\). Let
\[
\varphi_S^{(m)}:\mathcal A^m\to\mathcal B^*
\]
be the resulting block code. The ordinary Shannon bound, now applied to one whole block, is
\[
H_D(p^m)
\leq
EL(\varphi_S^{(m)})
<
H_D(p^m)+1.
\]
Since \(H_D(p^m)=mH_D(p)\),
\[
mH_D(p)
\leq
EL(\varphi_S^{(m)})
<
mH_D(p)+1.
\]
The quantity \(EL(\varphi_S^{(m)})\) is the expected length of one encoded block containing \(m\) original source symbols. To obtain the expected output length per original source symbol, divide by \(m\):
\[
\boxed{
H_D(p)
\leq
\frac{EL(\varphi_S^{(m)})}{m}
<
H_D(p)+\frac1m
}.
\]
crumbs: Shannon Codes, Huffman Codes, and Asymptotic Optimality

title: Shannon Codes, Huffman Codes, and Asymptotic Optimality
text:
8.2 Why block coding approaches entropy
The rounding overhead remains less than one output symbol per block, not per original source symbol. Since a block contains \(m\) source symbols, the overhead per source symbol is less than
\[
\frac1m.
\]
As the block size grows,
\[
\frac1m\longrightarrow0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\frac{EL(\varphi_S^{(m)})}{m}
\longrightarrow
H_D(p).
\]
Shannon block coding is consequently asymptotically optimal. For every \(\varepsilon>0\), a sufficiently large block size \(m\) can be chosen so that
\[
H_D(p)
\leq
\frac{EL(\varphi_S^{(m)})}{m}
<
H_D(p)+\varepsilon.
\]
The result does not claim that a finite block necessarily reaches entropy exactly. It states that the average rate per source symbol can be made arbitrarily close to entropy by increasing the block length.
crumbs: Shannon Codes, Huffman Codes, and Asymptotic Optimality

title: Properties of Entropy and Conditional Entropy
text:
Let \(X\) be a discrete random variable with finite alphabet \(\mathcal{X}\) and probability mass function \(p\). Its entropy is
\[
H(X)=H(p)=-\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}p(x)\log_2p(x).
\]
The lecture studies two fundamental properties of this quantity.


Entropy is always non-negative:
\[
H(p)\geq0.
\]
For every value \(x\) with \(p(x)>0\), we have \(p(x)\leq1\), hence
\[
\log_2p(x)\leq0.
\]
Therefore,
\[
-p(x)\log_2p(x)\geq0,
\]
and the sum of these terms cannot be negative.
Moreover,
\[
H(p)=0
\]
if and only if there exists a value \(x_0\in\mathcal{X}\) such that
\[
p(x_0)=1.
\]
Indeed, a term \(-p(x)\log_2p(x)\) is zero only when \(p(x)=0\) or \(p(x)=1\). For the whole sum to be zero, one value must therefore have probability \(1\) and all the others probability \(0\).
This matches the interpretation of entropy as uncertainty: if \(X\) is known in advance with certainty, observing it provides no new information.



If the alphabet has size
\[
|\mathcal{X}|=k,
\]
then
\[
H(p)\leq\log_2k.
\]
Equality holds if and only if \(X\) is uniformly distributed:
\[
p(x)=\frac1k
\qquad
\text{for every }x\in\mathcal{X}.
\]
For the uniform distribution \(u=(1/k,\ldots,1/k)\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(u)
&=-\sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac1k\log_2\frac1k\\
&=-k\frac1k\log_2\frac1k\\
&=\log_2k.
\end{aligned}
\]
The uniform distribution is the most uncertain distribution on a fixed alphabet because it gives no preference to any possible value. Any imbalance makes some outcomes more predictable and decreases entropy.

title: Properties of Entropy and Conditional Entropy
text:
2.1 Concave functions
A function \(f\) is concave when, for \(a,b\) in its domain and \(\lambda\in[0,1]\),
\[
f\bigl(\lambda a+(1-\lambda)b\bigr)
\geq
\lambda f(a)+(1-\lambda)f(b).
\]
Geometrically, the graph of a concave function lies above the chord joining any two points of the graph.
For a twice differentiable function, the condition
\[
f''(x)\leq0
\]
implies concavity. The logarithm is strictly concave because
\[
\frac{d^2}{dx^2}\log_2x
=-\frac{1}{x^2\ln2}<0
\qquad (x>0).
\]

title: Properties of Entropy and Conditional Entropy
text:
2.2 Jensen’s inequality
For a concave function \(f\), values \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\), and non-negative weights \(\lambda_i\) satisfying \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\), Jensen’s inequality states that
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i f(x_i)
\leq
f\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\lambda_i x_i\right).
\]
In words:

The weighted average of the function values is no greater than the function evaluated at the weighted average.

The direction is reversed for convex functions.
crumbs: Properties of Entropy and Conditional Entropy

title: Properties of Entropy and Conditional Entropy
text:
2.3 Application to entropy
Let the positive probabilities of \(p\) be \(p_1,\ldots,p_m\), where \(m\leq k\). Write entropy as
\[
H(p)=\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_i\log_2\frac1{p_i}.
\]
Apply Jensen’s inequality to the concave function \(\log_2\), using weights \(p_i\) and values \(1/p_i\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(p)
&=\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_i\log_2\frac1{p_i}\\
&\leq
\log_2\left(\sum_{i=1}^{m}p_i\frac1{p_i}\right)\\
&=\log_2m\\
&\leq\log_2k.
\end{aligned}
\]
Because the logarithm is strictly concave, equality in Jensen’s inequality requires all values \(1/p_i\) to be equal. Thus all positive probabilities must be equal. Equality with \(\log_2k\) additionally requires \(m=k\), so
\[
p_i=\frac1k
\]
for every value in the alphabet.
This proves both the upper bound and its equality condition.

title: Properties of Entropy and Conditional Entropy
section: 4.1 Joint and marginal probability mass functions
text:
4.1 Joint and marginal probability mass functions
The joint probability mass function is
\[
p_{X,Y}(x,y)=P(X=x,Y=y).
\]
For a particular pair \((x,y)\), this is the probability that both events occur simultaneously: the species is \(x\) and the sensor output is \(y\).
The marginal probability mass function of \(X\) is
\[
p_X(x)=P(X=x)=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}p_{X,Y}(x,y).
\]
The variable \(Y\) is summed out because only the probability of \(X=x\) is required. Similarly, the marginal pmf of \(Y\) is
\[
p_Y(y)=P(Y=y)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}p_{X,Y}(x,y).
\]
Thus:

\(p_{X,Y}(x,y)\) refers to one cell of the joint table;
\(p_X(x)\) refers to the total probability of column \(x\);
\(p_Y(y)\) refers to the total probability of row \(y\).

For the running example, the joint distribution is



\(p_{X,Y}(x,y)\)
\(X=c\)
\(X=d\)
\(X=f\)
\(X=w\)
\(p_Y(y)\)




\(Y=0\)
\(3/8\)
\(1/8\)
\(0\)
\(0\)
\(1/2\)


\(Y=1\)
\(1/8\)
\(1/8\)
\(1/8\)
\(1/8\)
\(1/2\)


\(p_X(x)\)
\(1/2\)
\(1/4\)
\(1/8\)
\(1/8\)
\(1\)



For example,
\[
p_{X,Y}(c,0)=P(X=c,Y=0)=\frac38.
\]
The cat marginal is obtained by adding the two cells in the cat column:
\[
p_X(c)
=p_{X,Y}(c,0)+p_{X,Y}(c,1)
=\frac38+\frac18
=\frac12.
\]
The no-alert marginal is obtained by adding the first row:
\[
p_Y(0)
=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}p_{X,Y}(x,0)
=\frac38+\frac18+0+0
=\frac12.
\]
Therefore, \(p_X\) and \(p_Y\) are not new unrelated distributions. They are derived from the joint distribution by summing over the variable that is not of interest.

title: Properties of Entropy and Conditional Entropy
text:
4.2 Deriving the joint-entropy formula
For one outcome \(x\) of \(X\), the self-information is
\[
I_X(x)=-\log_2p_X(x).
\]
The pair \((X,Y)\) is itself a discrete random variable whose possible outcomes are all pairs
\[
(x,y)\in\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}.
\]
The probability of the pair \((x,y)\) is
\[
p_{X,Y}(x,y)=P(X=x,Y=y).
\]
Therefore, the self-information obtained when the observed pair is \((x,y)\) is
\[
I_{X,Y}(x,y)=-\log_2p_{X,Y}(x,y).
\]
Entropy is the expected self-information. Taking the expectation over every possible pair gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(X,Y)
&=\mathbb{E}[I_{X,Y}(X,Y)]\\
&=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}
  p_{X,Y}(x,y)I_{X,Y}(x,y)\\
&=-\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}
  p_{X,Y}(x,y)\log_2p_{X,Y}(x,y).
\end{aligned}
\]
The compact notation
\[
H(X,Y)=-\sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\log_2p(x,y)
\]
means exactly the same thing. In that abbreviated expression, \(p(x,y)\) stands for the joint pmf \(p_{X,Y}(x,y)\), and the sum runs over all pairs \((x,y)\).
The formula is therefore not a separate rule to memorise. It is the ordinary entropy formula applied to the single random object \((X,Y)\).
For the running example, the table contains one non-zero cell of probability \(3/8\) and five cells of probability \(1/8\). Cells with probability zero contribute zero by the convention \(0\log 0=0\). Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(X,Y)
&=-\frac38\log_2\frac38
  -5\cdot\frac18\log_2\frac18\\
&=\frac38\log_2\frac83+\frac{15}{8}\\
&\approx2.406\text{ bits}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Joint entropy measures the average information needed to identify both the species and the sensor output.

title: Properties of Entropy and Conditional Entropy
text:
5.1 Deriving the average conditional-entropy formula
Before observing \(X\), the value \(x\) that will occur is not known. Each possible value \(x\) occurs with probability \(p_X(x)\). Therefore, the overall remaining uncertainty about \(Y\) after \(X\) is revealed is the weighted average of the separate conditional entropies:
\[
H(Y\mid X)
=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}
p_X(x)H(Y\mid X=x).
\]
The weight \(p_X(x)\) is necessary because some values of \(X\) occur more frequently than others. Without these weights, rare and common cases would incorrectly contribute equally to the average.
Substituting the definition of \(H(Y\mid X=x)\) gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(Y\mid X)
&=\sum_x p_X(x)
  \left[-\sum_y p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)
  \log_2p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)\right]\\
&=-\sum_x\sum_y
  p_X(x)p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)
  \log_2p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x).
\end{aligned}
\]
Using the product rule
\[
p_X(x)p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x)=p_{X,Y}(x,y),
\]
we obtain the equivalent formula
\[
H(Y\mid X)
=-\sum_{x\in\mathcal{X}}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}
p_{X,Y}(x,y)
\log_2p_{Y\mid X}(y\mid x).
\]
In compact notation,
\[
H(Y\mid X)
=-\sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\log_2p(y\mid x).
\]
The two formulas express the same idea:

\(\sum_x p_X(x)H(Y\mid X=x)\) emphasises the weighted average over the possible known values of \(X\);
\(-\sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\log_2p(y\mid x)\) expands that average over all joint outcomes.

title: Properties of Entropy and Conditional Entropy
section: 5.2 Uncertainty of the alert given the species
text:
5.2 Uncertainty of the alert given the species
The conditional alert probabilities can be derived directly from the joint probability table shown above.
For each species (x), the probability of receiving an alert after learning that the observed species is (x) is
\[
P(Y=1\mid X=x)
=
\frac{P(X=x,Y=1)}{P(X=x)}
=
\frac{p_{X,Y}(x,1)}{p_X(x)}.
\]
The numerator is the joint probability found in the (Y=1) row and in the column corresponding to species (x). The denominator is the marginal probability of that species, shown at the bottom of the same column.
For a cat,
\[
P(Y=1\mid X=c)
=
\frac{p_{X,Y}(c,1)}{p_X(c)}
=
\frac{1/8}{1/2}
=
\frac14.
\]
For a dog,
\[
P(Y=1\mid X=d)
=
\frac{p_{X,Y}(d,1)}{p_X(d)}
=
\frac{1/8}{1/4}
=
\frac12.
\]
For a fox,
\[
P(Y=1\mid X=f)
=
\frac{p_{X,Y}(f,1)}{p_X(f)}
=
\frac{1/8}{1/8}
=
1.
\]
Similarly, for a wolf,
\[
P(Y=1\mid X=w)
=
\frac{p_{X,Y}(w,1)}{p_X(w)}
=
\frac{1/8}{1/8}
=
1.
\]
Therefore, the complete conditional distributions of (Y), written in the order ((Y=0,Y=1)), are
\[
p_{Y\mid X}(\cdot\mid c)
=
\left(\frac34,\frac14\right),
\]
\[
p_{Y\mid X}(\cdot\mid d)
=
\left(\frac12,\frac12\right),
\]
and
\[
p_{Y\mid X}(\cdot\mid f)
=
p_{Y\mid X}(\cdot\mid w)
=
(0,1).
\]
Using the binary entropy function
\[
h(t)
=
-t\log_2t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t),
\]
we obtain
\[
H(Y\mid X=c)
=
h\left(\frac14\right)
\approx 0.811,
\]
\[
H(Y\mid X=d)
=
h\left(\frac12\right)
=
1,
\]
and
\[
H(Y\mid X=f)
=
H(Y\mid X=w)
=
h(1)
=
0.
\]
The conditional entropy (H(YX)) is the weighted average of these four values. Each conditional entropy must be weighted by the marginal probability of the corresponding species:
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(Y\mid X)
&=
p_X(c)H(Y\mid X=c)
+p_X(d)H(Y\mid X=d)\\
&\quad
+p_X(f)H(Y\mid X=f)
+p_X(w)H(Y\mid X=w)\\
&=
\frac12h\left(\frac14\right)
+\frac14h\left(\frac12\right)
+\frac18\cdot0
+\frac18\cdot0\\
&\approx0.656\text{ bits}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Knowing that the animal is a fox or a wolf completely determines the sensor output, because the sensor always produces an alert in those cases. For cats and dogs, both alert values remain possible, so the conditional entropy is positive. The conditional alert probabilities are
\[
P(Y=1\mid X=c)=\frac14,
\qquad
P(Y=1\mid X=d)=\frac12,
\]
and
\[
P(Y=1\mid X=f)=P(Y=1\mid X=w)=1.
\]
Using the binary entropy function
\[
h(t)=-t\log_2t-(1-t)\log_2(1-t),
\]
we obtain
\[
H(Y\mid X=c)=h\left(\frac14\right)\approx0.811,
\]
\[
H(Y\mid X=d)=h\left(\frac12\right)=1,
\]
and
\[
H(Y\mid X=f)=H(Y\mid X=w)=h(1)=0.
\]
The average conditional entropy is therefore
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(Y\mid X)
&=p_X(c)H(Y\mid X=c)
+p_X(d)H(Y\mid X=d)\\
&\quad +p_X(f)H(Y\mid X=f)
+p_X(w)H(Y\mid X=w)\\
&=\frac12h\left(\frac14\right)
+\frac14h\left(\frac12\right)
+\frac18\cdot0
+\frac18\cdot0\\
&\approx0.656\text{ bits}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Knowing the species does not always determine the alert. The alert remains uncertain for cats and dogs, but it is certain for foxes and wolves.

title: Properties of Entropy and Conditional Entropy
section: 5.3 Uncertainty of the species given the alert
text:
5.3 Uncertainty of the species given the alert
The conditional distributions of \(X\) are
\[
p_{X\mid Y}(\cdot\mid0)
=\left(\frac34,\frac14,0,0\right)
\]
and
\[
p_{X\mid Y}(\cdot\mid1)
=\left(\frac14,\frac14,\frac14,\frac14\right).
\]
Here \(p_{X\mid Y}(\cdot\mid0)\) means the entire conditional distribution of \(X\) after observing \(Y=0\); the dot is a placeholder for all possible values of \(X\).
Thus
\[
H(X\mid Y=0)=h\left(\frac14\right)\approx0.811\text{ bits},
\]
while
\[
H(X\mid Y=1)=\log_2 4=2\text{ bits}.
\]
Since
\[
p_Y(0)=p_Y(1)=\frac12,
\]
the average is
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(X\mid Y)
&=\sum_{y\in\{0,1\}}p_Y(y)H(X\mid Y=y)\\
&=\frac12H(X\mid Y=0)+\frac12H(X\mid Y=1)\\
&=\frac12\cdot0.811+\frac12\cdot2\\
&\approx1.406\text{ bits}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The two conditional entropies are not equal:
\[
H(Y\mid X)\approx0.656
\neq
H(X\mid Y)\approx1.406.
\]
They answer different questions. \(H(Y\mid X)\) asks how uncertain the alert remains after the species is known. \(H(X\mid Y)\) asks how uncertain the species remains after the alert is known.

title: Mutual Information, Relative Entropy, and Source Coding
text:
Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be discrete random variables. The chain rule for entropy gives
\[
H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y\mid X)
\]
and, reversing the order,
\[
H(X,Y)=H(Y)+H(X\mid Y).
\]
The notation has the following meaning:

\(H(X)\) is the uncertainty of \(X\) before \(Y\) is known;
\(H(X\mid Y)\) is the uncertainty that remains about \(X\) after \(Y\) is known;
\(H(X,Y)\) is the uncertainty of the pair \((X,Y)\).

If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent, knowing one variable does not change the distribution of the other. Therefore,
\[
H(Y\mid X)=H(Y)
\]
and
\[
H(X,Y)=H(X)+H(Y).
\]
Without independence, the sum \(H(X)+H(Y)\) counts some shared information twice. This motivates a quantity that measures how much information is shared by the two variables.


The mutual information between \(X\) and \(Y\) is
\[
I(X;Y)=H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y).
\]
Using the chain rule,
\[
H(X,Y)=H(Y)+H(X\mid Y),
\]
so
\[
\begin{aligned}
I(X;Y)
&=H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y)\\
&=H(X)+H(Y)-H(Y)-H(X\mid Y)\\
&=H(X)-H(X\mid Y).
\end{aligned}
\]
Similarly,
\[
I(X;Y)=H(Y)-H(Y\mid X).
\]
Therefore,
\[
I(X;Y)
=H(X)-H(X\mid Y)
=H(Y)-H(Y\mid X).
\]
This gives the main interpretation:

Mutual information is the average reduction in uncertainty about one variable obtained by observing the other.




The lecture represents entropy with overlapping regions:

the entire \(X\) region has size \(H(X)\);
the entire \(Y\) region has size \(H(Y)\);
the overlap is \(I(X;Y)\);
the part of \(X\) outside the overlap is \(H(X\mid Y)\);
the part of \(Y\) outside the overlap is \(H(Y\mid X)\);
the union of both regions is \(H(X,Y)\).

The diagram is an intuition aid. The equalities above, rather than geometric area, are the formal definitions.



Mutual information satisfies:
\[
I(X;Y)\geq0,
\]
\[
I(X;Y)=I(Y;X),
\]
and
\[
I(X;Y)=0
\]
if and only if \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.
Symmetry follows immediately from
\[
I(X;Y)=H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y).
\]
The non-negativity and independence condition will follow from the representation of mutual information as a relative entropy.

title: Mutual Information, Relative Entropy, and Source Coding
section: 2.1 Why does KL divergence measure extra information?
text:
2.1 Why does KL divergence measure extra information?
If the true distribution is \(p\), the ideal information assigned to outcome \(x\) is
\[
-\log_2p(x).
\]
If the incorrect model \(q\) is used, the assigned information is
\[
-\log_2q(x).
\]
The additional information assigned to outcome \(x\) is
\[
-\log_2q(x)-\bigl(-\log_2p(x)\bigr)
=
\log_2\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}.
\]
Averaging this difference under the true distribution \(p\) gives
\[
\sum_xp(x)\log_2\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}
=
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q).
\]
Thus KL divergence is the average extra information required when outcomes generated according to \(p\) are described using \(q\) instead of the correct distribution \(p\).
crumbs: Mutual Information, Relative Entropy, and Source Coding

title: Mutual Information, Relative Entropy, and Source Coding
section: 2.2 Example: a wrong model for two coins
text:
2.2 Example: a wrong model for two coins
Consider two coin tosses. Under the true distribution \(p\), the first coin is fair and the second coin always produces tails. Hence



Outcome
\(p\)




\(HH\)
\(0\)


\(HT\)
\(1/2\)


\(TH\)
\(0\)


\(TT\)
\(1/2\)



The true entropy is
\[
H(p)=1\text{ bit},
\]
because only two equiprobable outcomes can occur.
Suppose that the mistaken model \(q\) assigns probability \(1/4\) to all four outcomes:



Outcome
\(q\)




\(HH\)
\(1/4\)


\(HT\)
\(1/4\)


\(TH\)
\(1/4\)


\(TT\)
\(1/4\)



This model has entropy
\[
H(q)=2\text{ bits}.
\]
The divergence from the true distribution to the mistaken model is
\[
\begin{aligned}
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)
&=\frac12\log_2\frac{1/2}{1/4}
+\frac12\log_2\frac{1/2}{1/4}\\
&=\frac12\cdot1+\frac12\cdot1\\
&=1\text{ bit}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The terms corresponding to \(HH\) and \(TH\) contribute zero because \(p\) assigns probability zero to those outcomes.
The one-bit divergence means that using the uniform model \(q\) costs, on average, one additional bit per observed pair compared with using the true distribution \(p\).

title: Mutual Information, Relative Entropy, and Source Coding
text:
2.3 Basic properties of KL divergence
Relative entropy satisfies:
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)\geq0,
\]
with equality if and only if
\[
p=q
\]
on their support.
It is generally not symmetric:
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)
\neq
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\Vert p).
\]
Therefore, KL divergence is not a distance metric.
It may also be infinite. If there exists an outcome \(x\) such that
\[
p(x)>0
\qquad\text{but}\qquad
q(x)=0,
\]
then
\[
-\log_2q(x)=+\infty
\]
and consequently
\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)=+\infty.
\]
The model declares an outcome impossible even though that outcome can occur under the true distribution.

title: Mutual Information, Relative Entropy, and Source Coding
text:
3.1 Derivation of the entropy form
Starting from the KL expression,
\[
\begin{aligned}
I(X;Y)
&=\sum_{x,y}p(x,y)
  \log_2\frac{p(x,y)}{p_X(x)p_Y(y)}\\
&=\sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\log_2p(x,y)\\
&\quad-
  \sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\log_2p_X(x)\\
&\quad-
  \sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\log_2p_Y(y).
\end{aligned}
\]
The first term is
\[
-H(X,Y).
\]
For the second term, summing the joint distribution over \(y\) gives the marginal \(p_X(x)\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
-\sum_{x,y}p(x,y)\log_2p_X(x)
&=-\sum_x
  \left(\sum_yp(x,y)\right)
  \log_2p_X(x)\\
&=-\sum_xp_X(x)\log_2p_X(x)\\
&=H(X).
\end{aligned}
\]
Similarly, the third contribution becomes \(H(Y)\). Hence
\[
I(X;Y)
=-H(X,Y)+H(X)+H(Y).
\]
This recovers the earlier definition:
\[
I(X;Y)=H(X)+H(Y)-H(X,Y).
\]
Because KL divergence is non-negative,
\[
I(X;Y)\geq0.
\]
Moreover,
\[
I(X;Y)=0
\]
exactly when
\[
p_{X,Y}(x,y)=p_X(x)p_Y(y)
\]
for every relevant pair, which is precisely the condition that \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent.

title: Mutual Information, Relative Entropy, and Source Coding
text:
4.1 Alarm feature
Let \(Y\) denote the alarm feature. From the preceding lecture,
\[
H(X\mid Y)=1.406\text{ bits}.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\begin{aligned}
I(X;Y)
&=H(X)-H(X\mid Y)\\
&=1.75-1.406\\
&=0.344\text{ bits}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus observing the alarm reduces uncertainty about the species by \(0.344\) bits on average.
The weighted impurity calculation is
\[
H(X\mid Y)
=
\frac12(0.811)+\frac12(2)
=1.406\text{ bits},
\]
because:

for \(Y=0\), the conditional label distribution is \((3/4,1/4,0,0)\) and has entropy approximately \(0.811\);
for \(Y=1\), the conditional label distribution is uniform \((1/4,1/4,1/4,1/4)\) and has entropy \(2\).

title: Mutual Information, Relative Entropy, and Source Coding
text:
4.2 Size feature
Let \(W\) denote a binary size feature. The notes divide the data into two branches.
For \(W=0\):

the branch has probability \(5/8\);
the conditional label distribution is \((4/5,0,1/5,0)\);
its entropy is approximately \(0.722\) bits.

For \(W=1\):

the branch has probability \(3/8\);
the conditional label distribution is \((0,2/3,0,1/3)\);
its entropy is approximately \(0.918\) bits.

The weighted impurity after splitting on size is
\[
\begin{aligned}
H(X\mid W)
&=\frac58(0.722)+\frac38(0.918)\\
&\approx0.796\text{ bits}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore, the information gain is
\[
\begin{aligned}
I(X;W)
&=H(X)-H(X\mid W)\\
&=1.75-0.796\\
&\approx0.954\text{ bits}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Since
\[
I(X;W)>I(X;Y),
\]
the size feature reduces the label uncertainty more than the alarm feature. Equivalently, the size split leaves a lower weighted impurity:
\[
0.796<1.406.
\]
For an entropy-based classifier or decision tree, size is therefore the better of the two candidate features in this example.

title: Random-Access Machines and Nondeterministic Complexity
text:
The lecture first returns briefly to random-access machines (RAMs), a register-based computational model similar to the unlimited register machine introduced earlier in the course. A RAM has an unbounded sequence of registers
\[
R_0,R_1,R_2,\ldots,
\]
each capable of storing a non-negative integer. Its instruction set is richer than that of a basic register machine and includes both direct and indirect access.


A direct instruction identifies the register explicitly. For example,
\[
\operatorname{ADD}(i)
\]
has the effect
\[
R_0 \mathrel{:=} R_0+R_i.
\]
An indirect instruction instead treats the content of a register as an address. An instruction of the form
\[
\operatorname{ADD}(*i)
\]
has the effect
\[
R_0 \mathrel{:=} R_0+R_{R_i}.
\]
The difference is important: \(i\) is the address used by the direct instruction, whereas the indirect instruction first reads the value stored in \(R_i\) and then uses that value as the address of a second register.

  
    R₀100
    R₁5
    R₂0
    ⋯⋯
    R₅30
  
  For the indirect instruction ADD(*1), register R₁ contains the address 5, so the value in R₅ is added to R₀.

In the example,
\[
R_0=100,
\qquad
R_1=5,
\qquad
R_5=30.
\]
Executing \(\operatorname{ADD}(*1)\) therefore produces
\[
R_0=100+30=130.
\]



The input size \(n\) is the number of bits needed to encode the input. However, under the uniform-cost criterion, every RAM instruction costs one unit, independently of the sizes of the integers manipulated by that instruction.
This convention is deliberately strong. A single RAM instruction may operate on an integer occupying many bits, while a Turing machine must process the representation bit by bit. The simulation results below show that, despite this difference, the two models remain polynomially related for the instruction set considered in the lecture.


Turing-machine simulation by a RAM

A Turing machine performing at most \(f(n)\) steps can be simulated by a RAM performing
\[
O(f(n))
\]
steps.

The simulation uses RAM registers as cells of the simulated tape. Since RAM access is direct, the current head position identifies the register containing the currently scanned symbol.


RAM simulation by a multitape Turing machine

Under the uniform-cost criterion used in the lecture, a RAM performing at most \(f(n)\) steps can be simulated by a seven-tape Turing machine performing
\[
O\!\left((f(n))^3\right)
\]
steps.




Two size observations control the simulation.

Size of each value. An addition can increase the bit length of its result by at most one relative to the longer operand. Starting from an \(n\)-bit input, after at most \(f(n)\) instructions, every value that occurs has length at most \[
n+f(n).
\]
Number of touched registers. One instruction can introduce at most a constant number of previously untouched registers. Hence at most \(O(f(n))\) registers are relevant after \(f(n)\) instructions.

The simulated memory can therefore be stored as a sequence of address-value pairs:
\[
\langle i_1,R_{i_1}\rangle,
\langle i_2,R_{i_2}\rangle,
\ldots,
\langle i_m,R_{i_m}\rangle,
\]
where \(m=O(f(n))\). Since each address and value has \(O(n+f(n))\) bits and the standing complexity setting assumes \(f(n)\ge n\), the memory representation has length
\[
O\!\left((f(n))^2\right).
\]
A simulated RAM instruction may require a constant number of scans across this memory tape. Thus one RAM step costs \(O((f(n))^2)\) Turing-machine steps, and simulating all \(f(n)\) RAM steps costs
\[
f(n)\cdot O\!\left((f(n))^2\right)
=
O\!\left((f(n))^3\right).
\]



Quantity after at most \(f(n)\) RAM steps
Bound




Bit length of one stored value
\(O(n+f(n))=O(f(n))\)


Number of touched registers
\(O(f(n))\)


Length of the encoded memory
\(O((f(n))^2)\)


Cost of simulating one RAM instruction
\(O((f(n))^2)\)


Total simulation time
\(O((f(n))^3)\)



The two simulations show that RAMs and Turing machines are polynomially related. They therefore satisfy the extended Church–Turing thesis in the sense used in the course, even though their elementary cost criteria differ.

title: Random-Access Machines and Nondeterministic Complexity
section: 2.1 From one computation path to a branching computation
text:
2.1 From one computation path to a branching computation
For a deterministic machine and a fixed input, every non-halting configuration has one successor. Its computation is therefore a single path, possibly ending in a halting configuration or entering a loop.
For a nondeterministic machine, one configuration may have several successors. The resulting computation is naturally a directed graph. Two distinct branches may even reach the same configuration, so the graph is not necessarily a tree. Nevertheless, it is normally unfolded into a computation tree by duplicating a configuration whenever different branches reach it.






flowchart TD
  C0["Initial configuration"] --> C1["Configuration 1"]
  C0 --> C2["Configuration 2"]
  C1 --> C3A["Configuration 3"]
  C2 --> C3B["Configuration 3"]
  C1 --> N1["no"]
  C3A --> Y1["yes"]
  C3B --> N2["no"]
  classDef config fill:#0d6efd,color:#ffffff,stroke:#084298
  classDef accept fill:#198754,color:#ffffff,stroke:#0f5132
  classDef reject fill:#6c757d,color:#ffffff,stroke:#495057
  class C0,C1,C2,C3A,C3B config
  class Y1 accept
  class N1,N2 reject


 A nondeterministic computation branches into several possible successor configurations; converging configurations can be duplicated in the tree representation. 



In this lecture, only nondeterministic machines that halt on every branch are considered. Consequently, the unfolded computation tree is finite and has no infinite branch.

title: Random-Access Machines and Nondeterministic Complexity
text:
2.2 Nondeterminism is not ordinary parallelism
A computation tree may suggest that every branch is executed by a different processor. This analogy is misleading for two reasons.

If the maximum branching factor is \(d\) and the tree height is \(h\), the last level may contain as many as \(d^h\) branches. A physical parallel machine has a finite number of processors, whereas the required number here grows exponentially with the computation depth.
Different nondeterministic branches evolve independently. They do not communicate or share intermediate results.

Nondeterminism is therefore a mathematical acceptance mechanism, not a conventional parallel architecture.

title: Random-Access Machines and Nondeterministic Complexity
section: 4.1 Time as the height of the computation tree
text:
4.1 Time as the height of the computation tree
A nondeterministic computation contains many branches, so several measures might appear plausible: the number of nodes, the length of an accepting branch, or the time needed to explore the complete tree. The convention adopted in complexity theory is different.


Nondeterministic time on an input

The time complexity of a nondeterministic machine \(N\) on input \(x\) is the length of the longest computation branch of \(N\) on \(x\). Equivalently, it is the height of the computation tree.

This definition considers the longest branch even if an accepting branch is much shorter. A language is decided by \(N\) in time \(f(n)\) if \(N\) decides the language and every computation tree on an input \(x\) has height at most \(f(|x|)\).

title: Random-Access Machines and Nondeterministic Complexity
section: 4.2 Space as the maximum over all branches
text:
4.2 Space as the maximum over all branches
Space is defined by the same worst-branch principle. For an I/O nondeterministic Turing machine, only working-tape occupancy is counted, exactly as in the deterministic I/O model.


Nondeterministic space on an input

The space complexity of \(N\) on input \(x\) is the maximum number of working-tape cells occupied by any configuration occurring on any computation branch of \(N\) on \(x\).

The read-only input tape and write-only output tape are excluded from the measure.

title: Reachability, Proper Complexity Bounds, and Complements
text:
The lecture begins by collecting the consequences of the deterministic and nondeterministic simulations introduced previously. For a suitable time bound \(f(n)\), deterministic computation is a special case of nondeterministic computation, and a computation using at most \(f(n)\) steps cannot visit more than \(O(f(n))\) tape cells. Therefore,
\[
\operatorname{TIME}(f(n))
\subseteq
\operatorname{NTIME}(f(n))
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{TIME}(f(n))
\subseteq
\operatorname{SPACE}(f(n)).
\]
The same deterministic-as-nondeterministic observation yields
\[
\operatorname{SPACE}(f(n))
\subseteq
\operatorname{NSPACE}(f(n)).
\]
The previous lecture established that a nondeterministic machine running in time \(f(n)\) can be simulated deterministically in time exponential in \(f(n)\). When the bound is polynomial, this gives the class-level containment
\[
\mathrm{P}
\subseteq
\mathrm{NP}
\subseteq
\mathrm{EXP}.
\]
Combining the time-to-space observation with the definitions of the aggregate classes also gives
\[
\mathrm{P}
\subseteq
\mathrm{PSPACE}
\subseteq
\mathrm{NPSPACE}.
\]






flowchart LR
  P["P"] --> NP["NP"]
  NP --> EXP["EXP"]
  P --> PSP["PSPACE"]
  PSP --> NPSP["NPSPACE"]
  classDef det fill:#0d6efd,color:#ffffff,stroke:#084298
  classDef nondet fill:#6f42c1,color:#ffffff,stroke:#432874
  class P,PSP,EXP det
  class NP,NPSP nondet


 The introductory deterministic and nondeterministic classes are related by simulation and by the fact that time bounds space. 



The lecture uses these containments as a bridge from general definitions to the concrete reachability problem.
crumbs: Reachability, Proper Complexity Bounds, and Complements

title: Reachability, Proper Complexity Bounds, and Complements
text:
2.1 A nondeterministic logarithmic-space algorithm
A nondeterministic machine can decide reachability without storing the complete set of visited vertices. The machine keeps only:

the current vertex \(w\);
a nondeterministically generated candidate successor \(w'\);
a counter recording how many edges have been traversed.

The procedure is:

store \(u\) as the current vertex;
if the current vertex is \(v\), accept;
nondeterministically generate a vertex \(w'\);
scan the read-only graph encoding and verify that \((w,w')\in E\);
if the edge does not exist, reject that branch;
otherwise replace \(w\) by \(w'\), increment the counter, and repeat;
reject the branch once the counter exceeds \(|V|-1\).







flowchart TD
  S["Current vertex u"] --> T{"Current vertex is v?"}
  T -->|"yes"| A["Accept"]
  T -->|"no"| G["Guess a vertex u prime"]
  G --> E{"Edge exists?"}
  E -->|"no"| R["Reject branch"]
  E -->|"yes"| C["Increment counter"]
  C --> B{"Counter below vertex bound?"}
  B -->|"yes"| U["Set current vertex to u prime"]
  U --> T
  B -->|"no"| R
  classDef data fill:#0d6efd,color:#ffffff,stroke:#084298
  classDef process fill:#6f42c1,color:#ffffff,stroke:#432874
  classDef accept fill:#198754,color:#ffffff,stroke:#0f5132
  classDef reject fill:#6c757d,color:#ffffff,stroke:#495057
  class S,G,C,U,T,E,B process
  class A accept
  class R reject


 The nondeterministic reachability algorithm guesses one adjacent vertex at a time and uses a counter to guarantee termination. 



The counter is essential. Without it, a branch could repeatedly traverse a cycle and never halt. If a path from \(u\) to \(v\) exists, a simple path exists as well, and a simple path contains at most \(|V|-1\) edges. Hence stopping after this many traversals does not remove every accepting branch.
A vertex name requires
\[
O(\log |V|)
\]
bits, because vertices can be numbered from \(1\) to \(|V|\). The counter up to \(|V|-1\) has the same asymptotic size. Only a constant number of such quantities is stored.


Reachability in nondeterministic logarithmic space

Directed reachability can be decided using nondeterministic logarithmic working space:
\[
\mathrm{REACHABILITY}\in\mathrm{NSPACE}(\log n)=\mathrm{NL},
\]
where \(n\) is the length of the graph encoding.

The lecture leaves the best deterministic-space algorithm as a problem to reason about separately.
crumbs: Reachability, Proper Complexity Bounds, and Complements

title: Reachability, Proper Complexity Bounds, and Complements
text:
6.1 Unary padding idea
Run the machine \(M_f\) for the proper bound and obtain \(f(n)\) unary marks. Then simulate the language decider \(M\), erasing one mark for each simulated step. If \(M\) terminates early, erase the remaining marks before halting. This second phase therefore always lasts exactly \(f(n)\) steps, independently of the input contents.






flowchart LR
  X["Input of length n"] --> F["Compute unary f(n)"]
  F --> S["Simulate the decider"]
  S --> E["Erase one mark per step"]
  E --> P["Erase remaining marks"]
  P --> H["Halt with the decider answer"]
  classDef data fill:#0d6efd,color:#ffffff,stroke:#084298
  classDef process fill:#6f42c1,color:#ffffff,stroke:#432874
  class X data
  class F,S,E,P,H process


 Unary output from the proper-function machine is used as a clock that pads every computation to the same length-dependent duration. 



The lecture explicitly notes a technical caveat: the padding argument directly makes the running time precise, but the simultaneous space-precision requirement needs an additional adjustment. This missing space detail is not developed further in the lesson.

title: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality
text:
Let
\[
\mathcal A=\{a_1,\ldots,a_k\}
\]
be the source alphabet and
\[
\mathcal B=\{b_1,\ldots,b_D\}
\]
be an output alphabet of size \(D\). A code assigns every source symbol a finite output string:
\[
\varphi:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B^*.
\]
The code extends to complete source messages through concatenation. If
\[
m=a_{i_1}a_{i_2}\cdots a_{i_n},
\]
then
\[
\varphi(m)
=
\varphi(a_{i_1})\varphi(a_{i_2})\cdots\varphi(a_{i_n}).
\]
A code is uniquely decodable when two different source messages can never produce the same encoded string. Equivalently, the extended mapping
\[
\varphi:\mathcal A^*\to\mathcal B^*
\]
must be injective.
Unique decodability guarantees that the complete encoded message has one source interpretation. It does not necessarily guarantee that each source symbol can be decoded immediately while the encoded sequence is still arriving.


The decoding delay is the amount of future encoded data that must be read before the decoder can determine the current source symbol.
A uniquely decodable code may require the decoder to postpone a decision. The decoder may have read a valid codeword but still be unable to know whether that codeword should be accepted immediately or whether the received symbols are the beginning of a longer codeword.
This motivates a stronger class of codes for which a source symbol can be recognised as soon as its codeword ends.
crumbs: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality

title: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality
text:

A uniquely decodable code may require the decoder to postpone a decision. The decoder may have read a valid codeword but still be unable to know whether that codeword should be accepted immediately or whether the received symbols are the beginning of a longer codeword.

title: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality
section: 2.1 Why a prefix code can be decoded immediately
text:
2.1 Why a prefix code can be decoded immediately
Suppose the encoded string is read from left to right. As soon as the symbols read so far form a complete codeword, the decoder may output the corresponding source symbol.
There is no need to inspect future symbols, because the prefix property guarantees that the current codeword cannot be the beginning of any other codeword. The decoder can therefore remove the recognised codeword and repeat the same procedure on the remaining suffix.
Prefix codes are consequently also called instantaneous codes. Their decoding delay is zero.
crumbs: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality

title: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality
section: 2.2 Every prefix code is uniquely decodable
text:
2.2 Every prefix code is uniquely decodable
The instantaneous procedure also proves the following proposition.

If \(\varphi\) is a prefix code, then \(\varphi\) is uniquely decodable.

To see why, assume that an encoded string is produced by the code. Its first codeword is determined uniquely: two different codewords cannot both match the beginning of the string, because then the shorter one would be a prefix of the longer one. After removing the first codeword, the same argument determines the second codeword, and the process continues until the entire encoded string has been consumed.
Hence the encoded sequence has one unique segmentation into codewords and therefore one unique source message.
The converse is false: a uniquely decodable code need not be a prefix code. Prefix codes form a particularly convenient subclass of uniquely decodable codes because they permit instantaneous decoding.
crumbs: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality

title: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality
text:
2.3 Tree representation
A \(D\)-ary rooted tree gives a useful representation of a code over an alphabet with \(D\) output symbols:

the root represents the empty string;
each edge is labelled by one output symbol;
a node at depth \(h\) represents a string of length \(h\);
the path from the root to a node spells the represented string.

A set of codewords is prefix-free exactly when no selected codeword node is an ancestor of another selected codeword node. Codewords may therefore be placed at leaves of the pruned code tree.
This tree interpretation explains instantaneous decoding. Reading one output symbol corresponds to following one edge. Reaching a codeword leaf identifies the current source symbol; no codeword continues below that leaf.

2.3.1 Example of a binary prefix tree
Consider the binary prefix code
\[
\varphi(a)=0,
\qquad
\varphi(b)=10,
\qquad
\varphi(c)=11.
\]
The corresponding tree is:






flowchart TD
    R((root))
    A["a: 0"]
    N1(("1"))
    B["b: 10"]
    C["c: 11"]

    R -->|0| A
    R -->|1| N1
    N1 -->|0| B
    N1 -->|1| C

    classDef codeword fill:#dff3e4,stroke:#27864a,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef internal fill:#eef3f8,stroke:#5b6b7a;
    class A,B,C codeword;
    class R,N1 internal;


 Binary prefix tree for the code a -> 0, b -> 10, c -> 11. 



The tree should be read from the root downward:

following edge \(0\) reaches the leaf for \(a\);
following edges \(1,0\) reaches the leaf for \(b\);
following edges \(1,1\) reaches the leaf for \(c\).

No codeword leaf has descendants. In particular, \(0\) is not the beginning of either \(10\) or \(11\), and neither \(10\) nor \(11\) is the beginning of another codeword. Consequently, as soon as the decoder reaches one of the green leaves, one source symbol has been identified.
For example, the encoded string
\[
01011
\]
is decoded by traversing the tree repeatedly:
\[
0\mid10\mid11
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
abc.
\]
crumbs: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality

title: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality
text:
3.1 Block-to-block codes
A block-to-block code maps source blocks of one fixed length to output blocks of another fixed length. All input blocks have the same number of source symbols and all output codewords have the same number of output symbols.
Because the output block length is known, codeword boundaries occur at fixed positions.
crumbs: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality

title: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality
text:
3.2 Block-to-variable-length codes
A block-to-variable-length code maps fixed-length source blocks to output codewords of different lengths.
Shannon-Fano and Huffman codes are examples of this category. Variable codeword lengths make it possible to assign shorter codewords to more probable source blocks and longer codewords to less probable blocks.
crumbs: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality

title: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality
text:
3.3 Variable-to-variable-length codes
A variable-to-variable-length code maps variable-length source phrases to variable-length output strings. Lempel-Ziv methods belong to this category.
The categories describe the form of the input and output blocks. Properties such as prefix-freeness and unique decodability are separate requirements.
crumbs: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality

title: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality
section: 6.1 Why very short lengths can be impossible
text:
6.1 Why very short lengths can be impossible
Consider a binary output alphabet and three source symbols. If all three codeword lengths were equal to one, then
\[
2^{-1}+2^{-1}+2^{-1}
=
\frac32
>
1.
\]
Such a code cannot exist: a binary tree has only the two length-one strings \(0\) and \(1\), but three source symbols would require three distinct length-one codewords.






flowchart TD
    R((root))
    Z["available word: 0"]
    O["available word: 1"]

    R -->|0| Z
    R -->|1| O

    classDef available fill:#fff2cc,stroke:#b58b00,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef internal fill:#eef3f8,stroke:#5b6b7a;
    class Z,O available;
    class R internal;


 At depth 1, a binary tree has only two available leaves. 



The value
\[
3\cdot2^{-1}=\frac32
\]
means that the requested codewords would consume one and a half times the available depth-one capacity.
The lecture gives two proofs of the inverse theorem. The first proves the inequality for the special case of a prefix code by using its tree representation. The second proves the full statement for every uniquely decodable code by a counting argument.
crumbs: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality

title: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality
text:
7.1 A concrete tree satisfying equality
Consider the binary lengths
\[
l_1=1,
\qquad
l_2=2,
\qquad
l_3=l_4=3.
\]
Their Kraft sum is
\[
2^{-1}+2^{-2}+2^{-3}+2^{-3}
=
\frac12+\frac14+\frac18+\frac18
=1.
\]
One prefix code with these lengths is
\[
\varphi(a)=0,
\qquad
\varphi(b)=10,
\qquad
\varphi(c)=110,
\qquad
\varphi(d)=111.
\]






flowchart TD
    R((root))
    A["a: 0 (length 1)"]
    N1(("1"))
    B["b: 10 (length 2)"]
    N11(("11"))
    C["c: 110 (length 3)"]
    D["d: 111 (length 3)"]

    R -->|0| A
    R -->|1| N1
    N1 -->|0| B
    N1 -->|1| N11
    N11 -->|0| C
    N11 -->|1| D

    classDef codeword fill:#dff3e4,stroke:#27864a,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef internal fill:#eef3f8,stroke:#5b6b7a;
    class A,B,C,D codeword;
    class R,N1,N11 internal;


 A complete binary prefix tree with lengths 1, 2, 3, and 3. 



At the common depth \(L=3\):

codeword \(0\) commits \(2^{3-1}=4\) leaves;
codeword \(10\) commits \(2^{3-2}=2\) leaves;
codewords \(110\) and \(111\) commit one leaf each.

Thus
\[
4+2+1+1=8=2^3,
\]
and, after normalisation by \(2^3\),
\[
\frac48+\frac28+\frac18+\frac18=1.
\]
The equality means that this prefix tree is complete: all available depth-three capacity is committed.
crumbs: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality

title: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality
text:
8.1 Why \(N(m,h)\leq D^h\)
There are exactly \(D^h\) different strings of length \(h\) over the output alphabet \(\mathcal B\).
Because the code is uniquely decodable, different source strings must produce different encoded strings. Therefore, the number of \(m\)-symbol source strings encoded with length \(h\) cannot exceed the number of available output strings of length \(h\):
\[
N(m,h)\leq D^h.
\]
This is exactly where unique decodability is used. Without it, two or more source strings could share the same encoded string, and the bound would not follow.
crumbs: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality

title: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality
text:
8.2 Expanding the Kraft sum
Let
\[
S=\sum_{i=1}^{k}D^{-l_i}.
\]
Consider its \(m\)-th power:
\[
S^m
=
\left(
\sum_{i=1}^{k}D^{-l_i}
\right)^m.
\]
Expanding this product means choosing one source symbol from each of the \(m\) factors. A source string
\[
a_{i_1}a_{i_2}\cdots a_{i_m}
\]
contributes
\[
D^{-(l_{i_1}+l_{i_2}+\cdots+l_{i_m})}.
\]
The exponent is the negative of the total length of the encoded source string. Grouping source strings according to their encoded length \(h\) gives
\[
S^m
=
\sum_hN(m,h)D^{-h}.
\]
Since each of the \(m\) source symbols has codeword length at most \(l_{\max}\), the total encoded length satisfies
\[
h\leq ml_{\max}.
\]
Using \(N(m,h)\leq D^h\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
S^m
&=\sum_hN(m,h)D^{-h}\\
&\leq\sum_{h=1}^{ml_{\max}}D^hD^{-h}\\
&=\sum_{h=1}^{ml_{\max}}1\\
&=ml_{\max}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The right-hand side grows only linearly with \(m\).
If \(S>1\), then \(S^m\) grows exponentially with \(m\). For sufficiently large \(m\), an exponentially growing quantity cannot remain bounded by the linear quantity \(ml_{\max}\). Therefore \(S>1\) is impossible, and
\[
S\leq1.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{
\sum_{i=1}^{k}D^{-l_i}\leq1
}.
\]
This completes the second proof and establishes the inverse theorem for every uniquely decodable code.
crumbs: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality

title: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality
section: 9.1 Tree interpretation of the direct theorem
text:
9.1 Tree interpretation of the direct theorem
Order the desired lengths so that
\[
l_1\leq l_2\leq\cdots\leq l_k.
\]
In the full \(D\)-ary tree, a codeword of length \(l_i\) must be placed at depth \(l_i\). Once a node is selected as a codeword, none of its descendants may be selected, otherwise the chosen word would be a prefix of another codeword.
At a common depth \(L\geq\max_i l_i\), selecting a codeword of length \(l_i\) commits
\[
D^{L-l_i}
\]
of the \(D^L\) depth-\(L\) leaves. Its normalised tree cost is therefore
\[
\frac{D^{L-l_i}}{D^L}=D^{-l_i}.
\]
The hypothesis
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{k}D^{-l_i}\leq1
\]
states that the total requested cost does not exceed the capacity of the tree.
A constructive procedure chooses codeword nodes from the shortest requested depth to the longest, always avoiding subtrees already committed by earlier codewords. The inequality guarantees that enough uncommitted capacity remains to place all requested codewords. The selected nodes form a prefix-free set, so the resulting code is a prefix code with exactly the prescribed lengths.
crumbs: Prefix Codes and the Kraft-McMillan Inequality

title: LZ77 Compression and Kolmogorov Complexity
text:
The lecture first completes the discussion of lossless source coding from the preceding lecture and then moves from probability-based compression to algorithmic descriptions of individual objects.


Shannon-Fano codes are not necessarily optimal, although the construction can improve on a direct Shannon code for a given source. Huffman coding instead builds the code tree from the leaves to the root, which is the opposite direction from the top-down Shannon-Fano construction.
The central operation is:

Repeatedly merge the two currently least probable symbols or compound nodes into a phantom node whose probability is their sum.

For the six-symbol example
\[
\mathcal A=\{a,b,c,d,e,f\},
\]
with probabilities
\[
\left(
\frac{40}{100},
\frac{15}{100},
\frac{18}{100},
\frac{13}{100},
\frac{10}{100},
\frac{4}{100}
\right),
\]
the successive combinations are
\[
\frac4{100}+\frac{10}{100}=\frac{14}{100},
\]
\[
\frac{13}{100}+\frac{14}{100}=\frac{27}{100},
\]
\[
\frac{15}{100}+\frac{18}{100}=\frac{33}{100},
\]
\[
\frac{27}{100}+\frac{33}{100}=\frac{60}{100},
\]
and finally
\[
\frac{40}{100}+\frac{60}{100}=1.
\]
The resulting code has expected length
\[
EL(\varphi_H)=2.34
\]
bits per source symbol. Huffman codes are optimal among binary prefix codes for the given symbol probabilities.



A direct Shannon code may be inefficient for very low-probability symbols because each ideal length must be rounded to an integer. The lecture therefore revisits the idea of encoding blocks of \(n\) independent source symbols.
Let
\[
\varphi_S^{(n)}:\mathcal A^n\to\mathcal B^*
\]
be a Shannon code for the product distribution \(p^n\). Shannon’s bound applied to one block gives
\[
EL(\varphi_S^{(n)})<H_D(p^n)+1.
\]
For independent and identically distributed source symbols,
\[
H_D(p^n)=nH_D(p).
\]
Consequently,
\[
EL(\varphi_S^{(n)})<nH_D(p)+1.
\]
After division by the block length,
\[
H_D(p)
\leq
\frac{EL(\varphi_S^{(n)})}{n}
<
H_D(p)+\frac1n.
\]
The lecture calls
\[
\boxed{
\frac{EL(\varphi^{(n)})}{n}
}
\]
the compression rate of a code operating on blocks of \(n\) source symbols. It is the expected number of output symbols assigned per original source symbol.
As \(n\) grows,
\[
\frac1n\longrightarrow0,
\]
so Shannon block codes, and similarly block versions of Shannon-Fano coding, are asymptotically optimal.

title: LZ77 Compression and Kolmogorov Complexity
text:
2.1 Sliding-window structure
View the input message as a stream of bytes. At a given moment:

one part of the stream has already been encoded;
the next part remains unencoded;
the search buffer contains a fixed number of recently encoded bytes;
the look-ahead buffer contains the first fixed number of unencoded bytes.

In the example from the lecture, both buffers contain five bytes.






flowchart LR
    P["Previously encoded stream"] --> S["Search buffer: last 5 encoded bytes"]
    S --> J["Current boundary"]
    J --> L["Look-ahead buffer: first 5 unencoded bytes"]
    L --> U["Remaining unencoded stream"]


 Sliding-window organisation used by the basic LZ77 example. 



The encoder searches for the longest prefix of the look-ahead buffer that already occurs as a substring in the search buffer.

title: LZ77 Compression and Kolmogorov Complexity
text:
2.2 LZ77 output triple
The lecture represents a match by a triple
\[
(o,l,s),
\]
where:

\(o\) is the backward offset, namely the distance from the beginning of the selected occurrence in the search buffer to the current position;
\(l\) is the length of the matching prefix;
\(s\) is the first symbol in the look-ahead buffer after the matched prefix, that is, the first mismatch.

If no non-empty prefix can be matched, the encoder outputs
\[
(0,0,s),
\]
where \(s\) is the next literal symbol.
For example, the tuple
\[
(3,2,a)
\]
means:

move three positions backwards in the already encoded text;
copy two symbols from that position;
append the literal symbol \(a\).

The tuple therefore describes a matched phrase followed by the symbol that first prevents the match from being extended.

title: LZ77 Compression and Kolmogorov Complexity
text:
2.3 Initial phantom symbols
At the beginning of the stream, the search buffer would otherwise be empty. The worked example fills the initial search buffer with phantom symbols, written as #, so that the window always has the same size.
The first literal output recorded in the notes is of the form
\[
(0,0,b),
\]
because no previous occurrence of \(b\) is available in the initial phantom buffer. As real symbols are produced, the window advances and those symbols enter the search buffer. Later tuples can then refer to repeated substrings.
The handwritten example subsequently includes references such as
\[
(2,1,b),
\qquad
(3,2,a),
\qquad
(5,4,b),
\qquad
(3,3,a),
\]
illustrating matches of increasing length in the changing search buffer.

The exact full input string and some intermediate window contents in the handwritten example are not fully legible in the supplied PDF. The tuples above are preserved because they are readable, but the chapter does not invent a complete byte sequence that cannot be recovered reliably from the notes.

title: LZ77 Compression and Kolmogorov Complexity
LZ77 Compression and Kolmogorov Complexity
text:
2.5 Computational and coding observations
With the fixed-size buffers used in the lecture, the working memory is constant with respect to the total input length. Processing proceeds sequentially through the input. The precise running time of match search depends on how the search buffer is implemented; under the fixed small-window model used in the notes, the overall scan is treated as linear in the message length.
LZ77 is not optimal for every input, but performs well in many practical cases because it exploits repeated local patterns.
The comparison made in the lecture is:

Huffman coding requires symbol probabilities, or equivalent frequency information, to construct its code;
LZ77 does not require an a-priori global probability distribution;
LZ77 adapts to local repetition because its effective dictionary changes with the search buffer.

title: LZ77 Compression and Kolmogorov Complexity
text:
4.1 Machines that produce a string
For Kolmogorov complexity, the lecture considers a Turing machine executed on an empty tape. A machine produces a string \(x\) when it eventually halts with \(x\) on its output portion of the tape.
There are infinitely many machines capable of producing the same string. The objective is to identify the shortest description among them.
The notes denote the size of a machine by
\[
|M|,
\]
where the size is the length of an encoding of the machine’s finite description, including its states, alphabet, and transition function.

title: Introduction to Automated Reasoning and Constraint Programming
text:
The course studies Automated Reasoning as a central area of Artificial Intelligence. The opening question is therefore not only what automated reasoning is, but also where it belongs within the broader history and aims of AI.


In 1950, Alan Turing opened Computing Machinery and Intelligence with the question:

Can machines think?

Rather than answering the philosophical question directly, Turing proposed the imitation game. In the original game, an interrogator communicates with two hidden participants and tries to determine their identities from their answers. Turing’s operational reformulation replaces one participant with a machine: if the interrogator cannot reliably distinguish the machine from the human participant through the conversation, the machine succeeds in the game.
The important methodological move is that intelligence is evaluated through observable behaviour rather than through an inaccessible internal property called “thinking”.



The name Artificial Intelligence was introduced by John McCarthy in connection with the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence. The proposal gathered researchers interested in describing intelligence precisely enough that aspects of it could be simulated by machines. Participants and contributors associated with this early period included Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, whose early program addressed problem solving.






Figure 1: Alan Turing in 1951. Public-domain photograph by Elliott & Fry, obtained from Wikimedia Commons.



Two formulations presented in the lecture describe different emphases:

Strong AI: “the science and engineering of making intelligent machines”;
Weak AI: the science of making machines perform tasks that would require intelligence if performed by humans.

The first formulation focuses on constructing intelligent machines. The second focuses on reproducing intelligent behaviour, without requiring a claim about whether the machine possesses intelligence in the same sense as a person.






Figure 2: John McCarthy at Stanford in 2006. Photograph by null0, CC BY-SA 2.0, obtained from Wikimedia Commons.






The lecture connects this history to the 2025 AAAI Presidential Panel report. Automated reasoning is identified as a major challenge because AI systems require forms of reasoning whose conclusions can be checked and justified.






ImportantAI is not only machine learning



Machine learning is one major part of contemporary AI, but it does not exhaust the field. Knowledge representation, logical inference, constraint solving, planning, search, and automated reasoning address questions that cannot be reduced to statistical prediction alone.

title: Introduction to Automated Reasoning and Constraint Programming
text:
5.1 Why use a declarative model?
Constraint Programming separates two concerns:

problem modelling, which states what constitutes a solution;
solution search, which determines how to find one.

This separation makes models comparatively readable and easy to modify. The modeller may express heterogeneous constraints directly, while solver techniques handle propagation and search. Search is also amenable to parallelisation, and heuristics can be added to guide the exploration.
The annotation summarises the intended workflow as:

The programmer states the constraints; the system finds a solution.

This does not mean that modelling choices are irrelevant. A clear model, a suitable representation, and effective search heuristics can determine whether a solver handles an instance efficiently.






flowchart LR
    P["Problem"] --> M["Variables, domains, constraints"]
    M --> S["Solver"]
    S --> I["Propagation and inference"]
    I --> H["Search and heuristics"]
    H --> R["Solution or proof of infeasibility"]

    classDef model fill:#fff2cc,stroke:#b38600,stroke-width:2px;
    classDef solve fill:#e2f0d9,stroke:#548235,stroke-width:2px;
    class M model;
    class S,I,H solve;


 Separation between declarative modelling and solver-controlled search.

text:
6.1 Horizontal attacks
For every pair of columns \(i<j\),
\[
X_i\neq X_j.
\]
If \(X_i=X_j\), the two queens occupy the same row and therefore attack horizontally.
crumbs: Introduction to Automated Reasoning and Constraint Programming

title: Introduction to Automated Reasoning and Constraint Programming
text:
6.2 Diagonal attacks
For every pair \(i<j\),
\[
|X_j-X_i|\neq j-i.
\]
The horizontal distance between the queens is \(j-i\). They share a diagonal exactly when the absolute row difference equals that column difference.
crumbs: Introduction to Automated Reasoning and Constraint Programming

title: Introduction to Automated Reasoning and Constraint Programming
text:
6.3 Wrong and correct assignments
The assignment
\[
X_1=X_2=X_3=X_4=1
\]
is invalid because all queens occupy the same row.
A valid assignment shown in the lecture is
\[
(X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4)=(2,4,1,3).
\]
The row values are all different, and for every pair \(i<j\) the row difference is different from the column difference. Hence no two queens attack horizontally or diagonally.








Figure 4: The invalid assignment \((1,1,1,1)\) and the valid assignment \((2,4,1,3)\) under the column-variable representation.

title: Introduction to Automated Reasoning and Constraint Programming
text:
10.1 Generate and test
The most direct method enumerates complete assignments and tests each one afterward.
For 4-Queens, every variable has four possible values, so the number of complete assignments is
\[
4^4=256.
\]
The progressive slides show assignments such as
\[
(1,1,1,1),
(1,1,1,2),
(1,1,1,3),
(1,1,1,4),
(1,1,2,1),\ldots
\]
being generated and rejected. The repeated animation frames represent successive visits to the same search tree, not distinct algorithms.
Generate and test corresponds to a guess-and-verify view: generate a potential solution, then verify whether all constraints hold. The weakness is that a violation discovered from the first two variables does not prevent the method from generating values for the remaining variables.
For anything beyond very small instances, complete enumeration is generally unusable.

title: Introduction to Automated Reasoning and Constraint Programming
section: 13.1 Solving a CSP with a COP solver
text:
13.1 Solving a CSP with a COP solver
Assume a COP solver is available. Given a CSP
\[
P=\langle X_1\in D_1,\ldots,X_n\in D_n;C\rangle,
\]
define a constant objective, for example
\[
f(X_1,\ldots,X_n)=0.
\]
Every feasible assignment has the same objective value. Therefore, any solution returned by the COP solver is also a solution of the original CSP.
crumbs: Introduction to Automated Reasoning and Constraint Programming

title: Introduction to Automated Reasoning and Constraint Programming
section: 13.2 Solving a discrete COP with a CSP solver
text:
13.2 Solving a discrete COP with a CSP solver
Now assume a CSP solver can answer threshold questions of the form
\[
P_k=
\langle
X_1\in D_1,\ldots,X_n\in D_n;
C,
f(X_1,\ldots,X_n)\leq k
\rangle.
\]
If the objective takes natural-number values and an upper bound \(M\) is known, binary search over \(k\) can locate the optimum using at most logarithmically many threshold calls.
The lecture’s example assumes the unknown minimum is \(15\) and begins with \(M=205\). Thresholds such as
\[
205,102,51,25,12
\]
are tested. The first negative answer at \(12\) confines the optimum to the interval \([13,25]\). Further midpoint tests narrow the interval until the value \(15\) is identified.
For real-valued objectives, the same idea applies only up to a chosen numerical precision.

    COP["Discrete COP"] -->|"add f(x) <= k"| CSPsolver["CSP solver"]
    CSPsolver -->|"binary search on k"| OPT["Optimal objective value"]


 Relationship between feasibility and optimisation used in the final slides.

title: Bounds, Hyper-Arc, and Path Consistency
text:
The lecture continues the study of constraint propagation by comparing several levels of local consistency. Let

\(n\) be the number of variables;
\(c\) be the number of constraints;
\(d\) be the maximum domain size.

The previous lecture established the following coarse worst-case bounds:
\[
\text{Node consistency: }O(cd),
\]
\[
\text{Arc consistency: }O(cnd^3).
\]
For node consistency, at most \(c\) unary constraints are examined, and checking one unary constraint may require inspecting at most \(d\) domain values. Hence the total work is bounded by a constant multiple of \(cd\).
For arc consistency, revising one binary constraint may require comparing up to \(d^2\) pairs of values. Since at most \(nd\) values can be removed overall, revisions may be reactivated up to that order of magnitude, leading to the conservative bound
\[
O(nd\cdot cd^2)=O(cnd^3).
\]
The notation \(O(\cdot)\) expresses asymptotic worst-case growth. It suppresses constant factors and lower-order terms and describes how the computational cost scales as the numbers of constraints, variables, and domain values increase.
All the propagation rules considered here are domain reduction rules: domains can shrink but never grow. The process is therefore monotone and eventually reaches a unique fixpoint, independent of the order in which valid reduction rules are applied.

title: Bounds, Hyper-Arc, and Path Consistency
section: 2.1 Bounds consistent but not arc consistent
text:
2.1 Bounds consistent but not arc consistent
Consider
\[
\langle 2X=Y;
X\in\{0,1,2\},
Y\in\{0,4\}\rangle.
\]
The domain bounds are supported:

\(X=0\) is supported by \(Y=0\);
\(X=2\) is supported by \(Y=4\);
\(Y=0\) is supported by \(X=0\);
\(Y=4\) is supported by \(X=2\).

The CSP is therefore bounds consistent. However, the internal value
\[
X=1
\]
would require
\[
Y=2,
\]
and \(2\notin D_Y\). Thus \(X=1\) has no actual support, so the CSP is not arc consistent. Applying arc-consistency filtering removes it:
\[
\langle 2X=Y;
X\in\{0,2\},
Y\in\{0,4\}\rangle.
\]








Consistency notion
Scope of the check
Main filtering effect




Node consistency
One variable and unary constraints
Removes values violating unary constraints


Arc consistency
One binary constraint
Every domain value must have support in the other domain


Bounds consistency
Bounds of numerical domains
Checks only current minima and maxima


Path consistency
Three variables
Every allowed pair must extend through a third variable


\(k\)-consistency
\(k\) variables
Every consistent assignment to \(k-1\) variables extends to the \(k\)th


Strong \(k\)-consistency
All levels up to \(k\)
The CSP is \(j\)-consistent for every \(j\leq k\)

title: Bounds, Hyper-Arc, and Path Consistency
text:
3.1 Example: propagating \(X<Y\)
Start with
\[
\langle X<Y;
X\in5..20,
Y\in1..10\rangle.
\]
The upper bound \(X=20\) has no support because no value in \(Y\) is greater than \(20\). For \(X<Y\) to hold, the largest supported value of \(X\) is
\[
\max(D_Y)-1=9.
\]
Hence BC1 yields
\[
\langle X<Y;
X\in5..9,
Y\in1..10\rangle.
\]
Now the lower bound \(Y=1\) has no support in \(X\in5..9\). The smallest supported value of \(Y\) is
\[
\min(D_X)+1=6.
\]
BC2 therefore yields
\[
\langle X<Y;
X\in5..9,
Y\in6..10\rangle.
\]
For constraints such as \(<\), \(=\), and \(\neq\), bounds can often be revised using a constant number of arithmetic operations rather than scanning every pair of values.

title: Bounds, Hyper-Arc, and Path Consistency
section: 5.1 Directional propagators for a binary constraint
text:
5.1 Directional propagators for a binary constraint
A binary constraint \(c(X,Y)\) can be viewed as two directional revision operators:
\[
c(X,Y)_1:
D_X
\leftarrow
\{a\in D_X:\exists b\in D_Y,
(a,b)\in c\},
\]
and
\[
c(X,Y)_2:
D_Y
\leftarrow
\{b\in D_Y:\exists a\in D_X,
(a,b)\in c\}.
\]
The first revises \(D_X\) using \(D_Y\); the second revises \(D_Y\) using \(D_X\).
If \(D_X\) changes, the revision that may newly become useful is \(c(X,Y)_2\), because supports in \(D_X\) for values of \(Y\) may have disappeared. Conversely, if \(D_Y\) changes, enqueue \(c(X,Y)_1\).
This directional view permits finer scheduling than treating each binary constraint as one indivisible operation. Further optimisations may use the constraint graph, variable ordering, or propagator-specific information.

title: Bounds, Hyper-Arc, and Path Consistency
text:
6.1 Example: \(2X+3Y<Z\)
Consider
\[
\langle 2X+3Y<Z;
X\in1..10,
Y\in1..10,
Z\in1..10\rangle.
\]
The smallest possible left-hand side is obtained with \(X=1\) and \(Y=1\):
\[
2\cdot1+3\cdot1=5.
\]
Therefore, \(Z=1,2,3,4,5\) cannot be supported because the strict inequality requires \(Z>5\). Hence
\[
D_Z=6..10.
\]
For \(Y=3\), even the smallest value \(X=1\) gives
\[
2\cdot1+3\cdot3=11,
\]
which cannot be strictly smaller than any \(Z\in1..10\). Thus \(Y=3\) and every larger value are unsupported, leaving
\[
D_Y=1..2.
\]
Similarly, \(X=4\) is unsupported even with the smallest \(Y=1\):
\[
2\cdot4+3\cdot1=11.
\]
Therefore,
\[
D_X=1..3.
\]
The hyper-arc-consistent CSP is
\[
\langle 2X+3Y<Z;
X\in1..3,
Y\in1..2,
Z\in6..10\rangle.
\]

title: Bounds, Hyper-Arc, and Path Consistency
text:
8.1 Normalised and standard CSPs
A CSP is normalised when, for each unordered pair of variables \(X,Y\), there is at most one binary constraint on that pair. Denote it by
\[
C(X,Y)
\]
when it exists.
If more than one binary constraint concerns the same pair, replace them by their intersection because constraints are sets of admitted tuples. For example, constraints \(C_1(X,Z)\) and \(C_2(X,Z)\) can be combined as
\[
C(X,Z)=C_1(X,Z)\cap C_2(X,Z).
\]
A CSP is standard when every unordered pair of variables has exactly one binary constraint. When no explicit constraint exists between \(X\) and \(Y\), add the universal relation
\[
D_X\times D_Y,
\]
which admits every pair and therefore does not exclude any assignment.
Every CSP can be rewritten into an equivalent standard CSP. During this rewriting, intersections may expose inconsistency and propagate domain reductions.

Syntax of Logic Programming and Definite-Clause Programs
text:
Logic programming starts from a small formal vocabulary: terms represent objects, atoms express elementary properties or relations, and rules describe how atoms depend on other atoms. The lecture develops these layers in this order and then uses them to build executable database-style programs.


Let:

\(\mathcal{C}\) be a set of constant symbols, such as \(a\), \(b\), \(c\), socrate, and uomo;
\(\mathcal{V}\) be a set of variable symbols, such as \(X\), \(Y\), \(Z\), \(X1\), and \(X2\);
\(\mathcal{F}\) be a set of function symbols, such as \(f\), \(g\), \(h\), sqrt, piu, and per.

Every function symbol \(f\in\mathcal{F}\) has an arity \(\operatorname{ar}(f)>0\), namely its number of arguments. For example,
\[
\operatorname{ar}(\mathrm{sqrt})=1,
\qquad
\operatorname{ar}(\mathrm{piu})=2.
\]
For uniformity, constants and variables are regarded as symbols of arity zero:
\[
\operatorname{ar}(c)=0 \quad\text{for }c\in\mathcal{C},
\qquad
\operatorname{ar}(X)=0 \quad\text{for }X\in\mathcal{V}.
\]
Terms are defined recursively:

if \(c\in\mathcal{C}\), then \(c\) is a term;
if \(X\in\mathcal{V}\), then \(X\) is a term;
if \(f\in\mathcal{F}\), \(\operatorname{ar}(f)=n\), and \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\) are terms, then \(f(t_1,\ldots,t_n)\) is a term.

A term containing no variables is a ground term.

Here \(\operatorname{ar}(s)=\operatorname{ar}(\mathrm{sqrt})=1\) and \(\operatorname{ar}(\mathrm{piu})=2\).
The handwritten annotation on the slide reads the nested term as a tree: the outer function is the root, and each argument becomes a child. For the non-ground term \(\mathrm{sqrt}(\mathrm{piu}(s(s(Y)),s(0)))\), the structure is:






flowchart TD
  A["sqrt"] --> B["piu"]
  B --> C["s"]
  B --> D["s"]
  C --> E["s"]
  E --> F["Y"]
  D --> G["0"]


 The syntax tree of the annotated term; the leaf Y explains why the term is not ground. 



The outermost symbol determines the main constructor. The occurrence of \(Y\) at a leaf is enough to make the complete term non-ground.



Let \(\mathcal{P}\) be a set of predicate symbols, such as \(p\), \(q\), \(r\), genitore, allievo, coetaneo, eq, leq, and integer. Each \(p\in\mathcal{P}\) has an arity \(\operatorname{ar}(p)\ge 0\).
If \(p\in\mathcal{P}\) has arity \(n\) and \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\) are terms, then
\[
p(t_1,\ldots,t_n)
\]
is an atomic formula, or simply an atom. Examples include
\[
\mathrm{integer}(s(s(s(0)))),
\qquad
\mathrm{leq}(0,s(s(0))),
\qquad
\mathrm{father}(\mathrm{abramo},\mathrm{isacco}),
\qquad
p(X,Y,a).
\]
A literal is either an atom \(A\) or its negated form not A.
The course also uses predicates of arity zero. Thus \(p\), \(q\), and \(r\) may themselves be atoms. This special case permits propositional logic to be represented inside the same syntax, whereas atoms with arguments support first-order structure.








Syntactic object
Built from
Role




Term
Constants, variables and function symbols
Denotes an object


Atom
Predicate symbol applied to terms
Expresses an elementary relation or property


Literal
An atom or not followed by an atom
Positive or negative condition






An ASP rule has the form
\[
H \leftarrow B_1,\ldots,B_m,
\operatorname{not} B_{m+1},\ldots,
\operatorname{not} B_n,
\tag{1}
\]
where \(H,B_1,\ldots,B_n\) are atoms and \(n,m\ge 0\). In concrete program syntax, the arrow \(\leftarrow\) is written :-, while the comma represents conjunction.

\(H\) is the head of the rule.
Everything to the right of \(\leftarrow\) is the body.
If \(m=n\), no occurrence of not is present and the rule is a definite rule, also called a definite clause.
If \(m=n=0\), the body is empty and the rule is a fact.

Operationally, the rule says that \(H\) may be concluded when all positive body atoms hold and the negative body conditions are satisfied.


The implication represented by (1) can be written as
\[
(B_1\land\cdots\land B_m\land
\neg B_{m+1}\land\cdots\land\neg B_n)
\to H.
\]
Eliminating the implication gives the disjunction
\[
H\lor\neg B_1\lor\cdots\lor\neg B_m
\lor B_{m+1}\lor\cdots\lor B_n.
\]
This is a disjunction of literals, also called a clause. The handwritten example on the slide performs exactly this transformation for
\[
A\leftarrow B,C,\operatorname{not}D,
\]
obtaining
\[
A\lor\neg B\lor\neg C\lor D.
\]
When the rule is definite, there is exactly one positive literal in the corresponding clause: the head \(H\).




A denial has no head:
\[
\leftarrow B_1,\ldots,B_m,
\operatorname{not} B_{m+1},\ldots,
\operatorname{not} B_n.
\tag{2}
\]
Logically, it is equivalent to
\[
\neg B_1\lor\cdots\lor\neg B_m
\lor B_{m+1}\lor\cdots\lor B_n.
\]
A denial therefore excludes situations in which its entire body is satisfied. If \(m=n\), there are no positive literals in the corresponding clause.
A Horn clause is a clause containing at most one positive literal. Consequently:

a definite clause has exactly one positive literal;
a definite denial has no positive literals;
both satisfy the Horn restriction.
