title: Syntax of Logic Programming and Definite-Clause Programs
text:
3.1 Extensional information: facts
The first program records parent relationships:
parent(elizabeth, charles).
parent(philip, charles).
parent(diana, william).
parent(diana, harry).
parent(charles, william).
parent(charles, harry).
Here parent is a predicate and each name is a constant symbol. Every statement has an empty body, so every statement is a fact. As stressed in the annotation, facts have no body and therefore no written implication. They populate the database extensionally, by listing the relationships that hold.
crumbs: Syntax of Logic Programming and Definite-Clause Programs

title: Syntax of Logic Programming and Definite-Clause Programs
text:
3.2 Intensional information: the grandparent predicate
A new relation can be defined from the stored parent facts:
grandparent(X, Y) :- parent(X, Z), parent(Z, Y).
This definite clause says that \(X\) is a grandparent of \(Y\) whenever an intermediate individual \(Z\) connects two parent relationships.
The slide presents two readings of the variable \(Z\).
View 1. For given \(X\) and \(Y\), if there exists a \(Z\) satisfying both parent relationships, then grandparent(X,Y) holds:
\[
(\forall X)(\forall Y)
\left(
(\exists Z)(\mathrm{parent}(X,Z)\land\mathrm{parent}(Z,Y))
\to \mathrm{grandparent}(X,Y)
\right).
\]
View 2. Universally quantify all three variables:
\[
(\forall X)(\forall Y)(\forall Z)
\left(
\mathrm{parent}(X,Z)\land\mathrm{parent}(Z,Y)
\to \mathrm{grandparent}(X,Y)
\right).
\]
The two formulas are equivalent because grandparent(X,Y) does not contain \(Z\). If a suitable \(Z\) exists, View 2 gives the conclusion for that witness. Conversely, if View 1 holds and the conjunction is true for an arbitrary \(Z\), then the existential premise of View 1 is true, so the same conclusion follows.
Using the facts in the database, a solver should derive:
grandparent(elizabeth, william).
grandparent(elizabeth, harry).
grandparent(philip, william).
grandparent(philip, harry).
For example, grandparent(elizabeth, william) follows by choosing charles for \(Z\) and combining parent(elizabeth,charles) with parent(charles,william).
crumbs: Syntax of Logic Programming and Definite-Clause Programs

title: Syntax of Logic Programming and Definite-Clause Programs
text:
3.3 Recursion: the ancestor predicate
The database is enlarged with:
parent(william, george).
parent(william, charlotte).
parent(kate, george).
parent(kate, charlotte).
The ancestor relation is then defined by two clauses:
ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Y).
ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Z), ancestor(Z, Y).
The first clause is the base case: every parent is an ancestor. The second clause is recursive: if \(X\) is a parent of \(Z\) and \(Z\) is an ancestor of \(Y\), then \(X\) is an ancestor of \(Y\).
A derivation of ancestor(elizabeth,george) unfolds as follows:

use parent(elizabeth,charles);
reduce the remaining question to ancestor(charles,george);
use parent(charles,william);
reduce again to ancestor(william,george);
close the derivation using the base fact parent(william,george).

This is the lecture’s first use of recursion. Recursion is fundamental in both functional and logic declarative programming because it defines relations over paths or structures of unbounded depth using a finite program.
crumbs: Syntax of Logic Programming and Definite-Clause Programs

title: Syntax of Logic Programming and Definite-Clause Programs
section: 3.4 Detecting and repairing an overgeneral definition
text:
3.4 Detecting and repairing an overgeneral definition
The lecture next proposes:
married(X, Y) :- parent(X, Z), parent(Y, Z).
sibling(X, Y) :- parent(Z, X), parent(Z, Y).
Both definitions accidentally allow \(X=Y\). Anyone who appears as a parent satisfies the first rule with oneself, and anyone with a recorded parent satisfies the second rule with oneself. The intended relations require distinct arguments, so the patch is:
married(X, Y) :- parent(X, Z), parent(Y, Z), X \= Y.
sibling(X, Y) :- parent(Z, X), parent(Z, Y), X \= Y.
The condition X \= Y prevents the two variables from denoting the same term. The lesson is methodological: a syntactically valid rule can still define a relation broader than intended, so boundary cases must be tested explicitly.
crumbs: Syntax of Logic Programming and Definite-Clause Programs

title: Syntax of Logic Programming and Definite-Clause Programs
text:
3.5 Adding classifications and derived predicates
The database receives further facts:
female(elizabeth).
female(diana).
female(kate).
female(charlotte).
male(philip).
male(charles).
male(william).
male(harry).
male(george).
These facts support additional intensional definitions:
isfather(X) :- parent(X, Y), male(X).
ismother(X) :- parent(X, Y), female(X).
brother(X, Y) :- sibling(X, Y), male(X).
has_a_sister(X) :- sibling(X, Y), female(Y).
Notice how the position of a variable determines the meaning. In brother(X,Y), the condition male(X) classifies \(X\). In has_a_sister(X), the condition female(Y) classifies the sibling whose existence establishes the property of \(X\).
crumbs: Syntax of Logic Programming and Definite-Clause Programs

title: Syntax of Logic Programming and Definite-Clause Programs
text:
4.1 Natural numbers as terms
Natural numbers can be represented using the constant \(0\) and the unary successor function \(s\):
nat(0).
nat(s(X)) :- nat(X).
The first clause establishes \(0\) as a natural number. The recursive clause says that whenever \(X\) is natural, so is \(s(X)\). The expected consequences are
nat(0), nat(s(0)), nat(s(s(0))), ...
Thus a finite program describes an infinite set of answers. The lecture abbreviates the term with \(n\) nested occurrences of \(s\) by \(\overline{n}\):
\[
\overline{n}
=
\underbrace{s(s(\cdots s}_{n\text{ occurrences}}(0)\cdots)).
\]
This is a representation of natural numbers by syntax: for example, \(\overline{2}=s(s(0))\).
crumbs: Syntax of Logic Programming and Definite-Clause Programs

title: Syntax of Logic Programming and Definite-Clause Programs
text:
4.2 Addition as a relation
Addition is defined by recursion on the second argument:
sum(X, 0, X) :- nat(X).
sum(X, s(Y), s(Z)) :- sum(X, Y, Z).
The first rule states that adding zero leaves a natural number unchanged. The second states that, if \(X+Y=Z\), then \(X+s(Y)=s(Z)\). Therefore the program supports answers such as
\[
\mathrm{sum}(\overline{5},0,\overline{5})
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\mathrm{sum}(\overline{2},\overline{4},\overline{6}).
\]
Again, the intended relation contains infinitely many answers.
crumbs: Syntax of Logic Programming and Definite-Clause Programs

title: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming
text:
Stable-model semantics is introduced to give logic programs a meaning that supports non-monotonic, commonsense-style reasoning. A central difficulty is negation: adding information can invalidate a conclusion that was previously justified. In particular, the absence of a proof for an atom may be used as a reason to conclude its negation.
This differs from monotonic reasoning, where adding premises cannot invalidate an earlier conclusion. The lecture highlights the following ideas:

Negated literals cause a loss of monotonicity.
Commonsense reasoning is generally non-monotone.
The meaning of a rule is not exhausted by reading it as a material logical implication.
Informally, when there are no reasons or proofs for believing an atom, one may adopt the opposite conclusion.
Stable-model semantics formalises this intuition through a guess-and-verify view of candidate models.

The completion of a program is useful for identifying logical consequences and atoms that cannot belong to minimal models. The lecture states that stable models of a program are among the minimal models of its completion. The completion is therefore an important logical characterisation, but it does not by itself remove every non-minimal model.


Consider the program:
p :- p.
q :- p, not s.
q :- not p, not s.
s :- not q.
For an atom that occurs in rule heads, its completion expresses that the atom is true exactly when at least one of the bodies of the rules defining it is true. Applying this idea to the program gives:
[
\[\begin{aligned}
p &\leftrightarrow p,\\
q &\leftrightarrow (p \land \neg s) \lor (\neg p \land \neg s),\\
s &\leftrightarrow \neg q.
\end{aligned}\]
]
The first equivalence, (p p), imposes no restriction on the truth value of (p). The completion therefore permits models in which (p) is true even though the rule p :- p. does not provide an independent reason for introducing it.
The slide identifies two minimal models of the completion, ({q}) and ({s}), and also points out that ({p,q}) is a model. The latter is not minimal because it has the proper subset ({q}), which is already a model. The example illustrates why minimality matters: satisfying the completion is not enough to guarantee that an atom is justified in the intended stable-model sense.







Set of atoms
Role in the example




({q})
A minimal model of the completion identified in the lecture.


({s})
The other minimal model identified in the lecture.


({p,q})
A model of the completion, but not a minimal one because ({q}{p,q}).



The key point is not simply whether a set of atoms satisfies the completion. It is also whether the set is minimal with respect to set inclusion and whether its atoms have the support required by stable-model semantics.



Theorem. Given a program (P), its stable models are among the minimal models of the completion of (P).
In symbols, if ((P)) denotes the completion of (P), then every stable model of (P) is a minimal model of ((P)). The statement is a necessary relationship; it should not be read as saying that every model of the completion is stable.



A SAT solver can be used to find classical models of the formulas in the completion. The lecture considers a typical equivalence of the form
[ H ((_1_m) (r_1r_n)), ]
where the (_i) and (r_j) are literals. To obtain a conjunctive normal form (CNF), the two directions of the equivalence are treated separately.
Let
[ L=_{i=1}^{m}i, R={j=1}^{n}r_j. ]
The direction (H(LR)), equivalently ((LR)H), becomes
[ (H_1_m) (Hr_1r_n). ]
The other direction, (H(LR)), becomes a conjunction containing one clause for each pair ((_i,r_j)):

[ _{i=1}{m}_{j=1}{n} (H_ir_j). ]

Combining the two directions gives the following CNF representation:

[
\[\begin{aligned}
&\left(H\lor\bigvee_{i=1}^{m}\neg\ell_i\right)
\land
\left(H\lor\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}\neg r_j\right)\\
&\qquad\land
\bigwedge_{i=1}^{m}\bigwedge_{j=1}^{n}
\left(\neg H\lor\ell_i\lor r_j\right).
\end{aligned}\]
]

A SAT solver can find models of these CNF formulas. However, as the lecture emphasises, it can also return non-minimal models. The completion example above explains the distinction: a SAT solver may return a model such as ({p,q}), even though a smaller model ({q}) exists. Satisfiability of the completion and stable-model minimality are therefore different requirements.



Consider:
p :- not p, d.
d.
The set ({p,d}) is a logical model when the rules are read as implications: the fact makes (d) true, while the body of the first rule is false when (p) is true. Nevertheless, the program has no stable models.
Its completion is
[
\[\begin{aligned}
p &\leftrightarrow (\neg p\land d),\\
d &\leftrightarrow \top.
\end{aligned}\]
]
The fact forces (d) to be true. The first equivalence then reduces to (pp), which cannot be satisfied by either truth value of (p). Thus the completion has no classical model, and the program has no stable model.

The slide identifies two minimal models of the completion, ({q}) and ({s}), and also points out that ({p,q}) is a model. The latter is not minimal because it has the proper subset ({q}), which is already a model. The example illustrates why minimality matters: satisfying the completion is not enough to guarantee that an atom is justified in the intended stable-model sense.







Set of atoms
Role in the example




({q})
A minimal model of the completion identified in the lecture.


({s})
The other minimal model identified in the lecture.


({p,q})
A model of the completion, but not a minimal one because ({q}{p,q}).



The key point is not simply whether a set of atoms satisfies the completion. It is also whether the set is minimal with respect to set inclusion and whether its atoms have the support required by stable-model semantics.

title: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming
text:
Theorem. Given a program (P), its stable models are among the minimal models of the completion of (P).
In symbols, if ((P)) denotes the completion of (P), then every stable model of (P) is a minimal model of ((P)). The statement is a necessary relationship; it should not be read as saying that every model of the completion is stable.
crumbs: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming

title: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming
text:
A SAT solver can be used to find classical models of the formulas in the completion. The lecture considers a typical equivalence of the form
[ H ((_1_m) (r_1r_n)), ]
where the (_i) and (r_j) are literals. To obtain a conjunctive normal form (CNF), the two directions of the equivalence are treated separately.
Let
[ L=_{i=1}^{m}i, R={j=1}^{n}r_j. ]
The direction (H(LR)), equivalently ((LR)H), becomes
[ (H_1_m) (Hr_1r_n). ]
The other direction, (H(LR)), becomes a conjunction containing one clause for each pair ((_i,r_j)):

[ _{i=1}{m}_{j=1}{n} (H_ir_j). ]

Combining the two directions gives the following CNF representation:

[
\[\begin{aligned}
&\left(H\lor\bigvee_{i=1}^{m}\neg\ell_i\right)
\land
\left(H\lor\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}\neg r_j\right)\\
&\qquad\land
\bigwedge_{i=1}^{m}\bigwedge_{j=1}^{n}
\left(\neg H\lor\ell_i\lor r_j\right).
\end{aligned}\]
]

A SAT solver can find models of these CNF formulas. However, as the lecture emphasises, it can also return non-minimal models. The completion example above explains the distinction: a SAT solver may return a model such as ({p,q}), even though a smaller model ({q}) exists. Satisfiability of the completion and stable-model minimality are therefore different requirements.
crumbs: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming

title: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming
text:
Consider:
p :- not p, d.
d.
The set ({p,d}) is a logical model when the rules are read as implications: the fact makes (d) true, while the body of the first rule is false when (p) is true. Nevertheless, the program has no stable models.
Its completion is
[
\[\begin{aligned}
p &\leftrightarrow (\neg p\land d),\\
d &\leftrightarrow \top.
\end{aligned}\]
]
The fact forces (d) to be true. The first equivalence then reduces to (pp), which cannot be satisfied by either truth value of (p). Thus the completion has no classical model, and the program has no stable model.

title: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming
section: 2.1 Replacing an unsupported self-negating rule with a denial
text:
2.1 Replacing an unsupported self-negating rule with a denial
If p does not occur as the head of any other rule in the program, the rule
p :- not p, d.
has, from the answer-set point of view, the effect that d must be false. This can be expressed directly by a denial, also called a constraint:
:- d.
A denial has no head. It rules out any candidate answer set in which its body is true. Thus :- d. rejects every candidate containing d.
The lecture revisits this transformation with:
a.
p :- not p, a.
The fact makes a true, while the second rule does not provide support for p; the program has no stable models. The corresponding denial formulation is:
a.
:- a.
This is also inconsistent because the fact requires a, while the denial forbids it.
A related question is obtained by replacing the fact with a choice:
{a}.
:- a.
The choice rule permits a to be selected or omitted, and the denial rejects every candidate that selects it. Consequently, the only permitted answer set is the empty set.
crumbs: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming

title: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming
text:
3.1 Representing truth-tellers and liars
Consider four students: Albert, Bob, Charlie and Dexter. The atom a represents that Albert tells the truth, while na represents that Albert is a liar. Exactly one of these two atoms is intended to be true. The same convention is used for Bob (b, nb), Charlie (c, nc) and Dexter (d, nd).



Student
Tells the truth
Is a liar




Albert
a
na


Bob
b
nb


Charlie
c
nc


Dexter
d
nd



There are two alternatives for each of four students, so there are (2^4=16) possible worlds. The following pair of rules for Albert expresses the choice between the two alternatives:
a  :- not na.
na :- not a.
The complete program is:
a  :- not na.    na :- not a.
b  :- not nb.    nb :- not b.
c  :- not nc.    nc :- not c.
d  :- not nd.    nd :- not d.
Its answer sets contain exactly one atom from each pair:
[ {a,na},{b,nb}, {c,nc},{d,nd}. ]
There are therefore sixteen answer sets, one for each possible assignment of truth-teller/liar status to the four students.
crumbs: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming

title: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming
text:
3.2 Adding relationships between the choices
The lecture then asks what happens if the following rules are added:
a :- b.
c :- nb.
The rules express two implications: if Bob tells the truth, Albert must tell the truth; if Bob is a liar, Charlie must tell the truth. They restrict which of the original sixteen combinations can remain answer sets. The slide poses this as a question and does not provide a solver enumeration, so no additional count of answer sets is assumed here.
crumbs: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming

title: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming
text:
3.3 Choice rules as syntactic sugar
The pair
a  :- not na.
na :- not a.
can be written using the choice-rule notation:
{a}.
This is the compact form presented in the lecture. It allows the atom a to be selected or not selected. The same shorthand can be used for the other individual choices in the truth-teller example.

title: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming
section: 3.4 Denials revisited with a choice rule
text:
3.4 Denials revisited with a choice rule
The previous discussion of denials can be combined with a choice rule:
{a}.
:- a.
The choice rule generates the two possibilities concerning a; the denial removes the possibility in which a is present. The remaining answer set contains no a.

title: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming
text:
4.1 Membership in NP
A candidate stable model (S) needs to contain only atoms that occur in the ground program. Therefore, its size is bounded by the size of the program:
[ |S||P|. ]
The lecture’s verification procedure is:

Guess a candidate set of atoms (S).
Compute the reduct (P^S) associated with the candidate.
Compute the fixpoint model (M_{P^S}).
Check whether (S=M_{P^S}).

The computation of the reduct, the fixpoint computation and the final equality check are polynomial in (|P|). A candidate can therefore be guessed and verified in nondeterministic polynomial time, establishing membership in NP.
crumbs: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming

title: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming
text:
4.2 NP-hardness by reduction from 3SAT
For hardness, the lecture considers the following 3CNF instance:
[ =(ABC) (ABC). ]
Let the two clauses be denoted by (c_1) and (c_2). The program uses pairs of atoms to choose a truth value for each Boolean variable:
a  :- not na.    na :- not a.
b  :- not nb.    nb :- not b.
c  :- not nc.    nc :- not c.
Here a, b and c represent the positive assignments, while na, nb and nc represent the corresponding negative assignments. Each answer set chooses exactly one atom from each pair.
The clause atoms are derived from the literals that make the corresponding clause true:
c1 :- a.
c1 :- nb.
c1 :- c.

c2 :- na.
c2 :- b.
c2 :- nc.
Thus c1 is supported when at least one of (A), (B) or (C) is true. Similarly, c2 is supported when at least one of (A), (B) or (C) is true.
Finally, the program requires both clauses to be satisfied:
satisfied :- c1, c2.
:- not satisfied.
The first rule derives satisfied when both clause atoms hold. The denial rejects any answer set in which satisfied is absent. Consequently, the constructed program has a stable model if and only if the 3SAT instance is satisfiable.
The construction can be computed in LOGSPACE, as stated in the lecture. This establishes NP-hardness. Together with membership in NP, it gives the NP-completeness result.
crumbs: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming

title: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming
text:
5.1 The size of a grounding
Let (H_P) be the Herbrand universe of a program (P). If (H_P) is infinite, then the grounding can be infinite as well. The lecture therefore considers the case in which (H_P) is finite and
[ |H_P|=c. ]
Suppose that (P) contains rules (r_1,,r_n), where (n|P|). Let (_i) be the number of distinct variables occurring in rule (r_i). Each variable can be instantiated with one of the (c) elements of the Herbrand universe. The number of possible ground instances contributed by rule (r_i) is therefore bounded by (c^{_i}), and the total number of ground rule instances is bounded by
[ _{i=1}^{n} c^{_i}. ]
Let
[ k=_i{_i} ]
and let (h) be the size of the largest rule. The lecture gives the following upper bound on the size of the ground program:
[ |(P)|n h c^k. ]
The bound makes the source of the growth explicit: the number of possible substitutions grows exponentially in the number (k) of distinct variables in a rule, when the domain size (c) is treated as a parameter greater than one.
The slide also notes that (c) can be specified implicitly. For example, a range such as p(1..1000) represents many values without listing every value separately in the source. As a result, grounding may require exponential time with respect to the size of the compact input program. The lecture remarks that this is not necessarily bad news: intervals can also be used to encode problems outside NP.
crumbs: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming

title: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming
text:
5.2 Example: exponentially many ground instances
Consider the program:
bit(0).
bit(1).

exp(X1, X2, ..., Xn) :-
    bit(X1), bit(X2), ..., bit(Xn).
Each variable (X_i) can be instantiated with either 0 or 1. There are two possibilities for each of the (n) variables, so the rule has
[ 2^n ]
possible ground instances. This example shows how a short non-ground rule can produce a very large ground program.
crumbs: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming

title: Stable Models and Answer Set Programming
section: 6.1 Domain predicates and strong range restriction
text:
6.1 Domain predicates and strong range restriction
The grounder must be able to determine a finite scope for the variables. The general rule introduced in the lecture is:

Every variable occurring in a rule must occur as an argument of a domain predicate that occurs positively in the body of that rule.

A program satisfying this condition is called strongly range restricted in the lecture. The positive occurrence matters: a variable that appears only inside a default-negated literal is not bounded by that literal.
Consider the examples:
p(X).

q(X,Y) :- r(X), not s(Y).
The fact p(X). has a variable in its head but no positive body predicate to restrict its values. In the second rule, X occurs in the positive body literal r(X) and can be bounded there if r is a domain predicate. However, Y occurs only in the default-negated literal not s(Y), so it has no positive domain-predicate occurrence. The fact p(X). has no positive body at all. The two examples therefore fail the strong range-restriction condition.
The lecture uses the following working definition of a domain predicate:

A predicate defined extensionally, by a set of ground facts, is a domain predicate.
A predicate defined by strongly range-restricted definite clauses is also a domain predicate.

The lecturer explicitly recommends stopping at this notion for the course discussion, noting that a wider notion can be found in the literature. The chapter retains this restricted definition rather than importing the broader one.

title: Constraint Propagation and Local Consistency
text:
A Constraint Satisfaction Problem (CSP) is a triple
\[
P=\langle V,D,C\rangle,
\]
where:

\(V=\{V_1,\ldots,V_n\}\) is a finite set of variables;
\(D=\{D_1,\ldots,D_n\}\) associates domain \(D_i\) with variable \(V_i\);
\(C\) is a set of constraints.

A constraint \(c\) involving variables
\[
V_{i_1},\ldots,V_{i_m}
\]
is a relation over their domains:
\[
c\subseteq D_{i_1}\times\cdots\times D_{i_m}.
\]
Thus, a constraint is the set of tuples admitted for the variables in its scope. It normally contains only some tuples of the Cartesian product, not every possible tuple.
An assignment is a mapping
\[
\sigma:V\to D_1\cup\cdots\cup D_n
\]
such that
\[
\sigma(V_i)\in D_i
\]
for every \(i\). The assignment is a solution when, for every constraint \(c\) on variables \(V_{i_1},\ldots,V_{i_m}\),
\[
\bigl(\sigma(V_{i_1}),\ldots,\sigma(V_{i_m})\bigr)\in c.
\]
This definition is independent of the concrete syntax used to write constraints. When the context is clear, one can write a familiar expression such as
\[
X\neq Y
\]
instead of explicitly listing the corresponding relation.
A Constraint Optimization Problem additionally contains an objective function to minimise or maximise. The feasible assignments are still the solutions of the underlying CSP; optimisation selects the best feasible solution according to the objective.


The set of solutions of a CSP \(P\) is denoted by
\[
\operatorname{Sol}(P).
\]
The problem is consistent or satisfiable if
\[
\operatorname{Sol}(P)\neq\varnothing.
\]
It is inconsistent or unsatisfiable if
\[
\operatorname{Sol}(P)=\varnothing.
\]
The same notation may be applied to a single constraint or a subset of constraints. For a constraint \(c\), or a set of constraints \(C\), the notation
\[
FV(C)
\]
denotes the variables occurring in \(C\).

title: Constraint Propagation and Local Consistency
text:
The set of solutions of a CSP \(P\) is denoted by
\[
\operatorname{Sol}(P).
\]
The problem is consistent or satisfiable if
\[
\operatorname{Sol}(P)\neq\varnothing.
\]
It is inconsistent or unsatisfiable if
\[
\operatorname{Sol}(P)=\varnothing.
\]
The same notation may be applied to a single constraint or a subset of constraints. For a constraint \(c\), or a set of constraints \(C\), the notation
\[
FV(C)
\]
denotes the variables occurring in \(C\).

title: Constraint Propagation and Local Consistency
text:
2.1 Horizontal constraints as relations
For two columns \(i\) and \(j\), the condition
\[
X_i\neq X_j
\]
stands for the binary relation
\[
\begin{aligned}
\{&(1,2),(1,3),(1,4),
(2,1),(2,3),(2,4),\\
&(3,1),(3,2),(3,4),
(4,1),(4,2),(4,3)\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every tuple with distinct row values is admitted. The four tuples
\[
(1,1),(2,2),(3,3),(4,4)
\]
are excluded because they place two queens on the same row.

title: Constraint Propagation and Local Consistency
text:
2.2 Diagonal constraints as relations
For \(i<j\), the diagonal condition is
\[
|X_j-X_i|\neq j-i.
\]
For example, if \(i=2\) and \(j=4\), the horizontal distance is \(2\). Therefore, row pairs at distance \(2\) are not admitted. In particular,
\[
(2,4)
\]
is excluded because
\[
|4-2|=4-2=2.
\]
The tuple \((2,2)\) is also not admitted in the full queens model because it violates the horizontal constraint.

title: Constraint Propagation and Local Consistency
text:
4.1 Proof rules
A propagator is based on repeated applications of proof rules of the form
\[
\frac{\phi}{\psi},
\]
where \(\phi\) and \(\psi\) are CSPs. The lower CSP may contain new variables that do not occur in the upper CSP.
A rule is equivalence preserving when
\[
\operatorname{Sol}(\phi)
=
\operatorname{Sol}(\psi)\big|_{FV(\phi)}.
\]
The restriction is essential because \(\psi\) may introduce auxiliary variables. The transformed CSP can therefore have assignments over a larger variable set, while its projections onto the original variables must coincide with the original solutions.






flowchart LR
    A["Solutions of phi"] --> O["Assignments on original variables"]
    B["Solutions of psi"] --> R["Restrict to FV(phi)"]
    R --> O


 Meaning of an equivalence-preserving propagation rule.

title: Constraint Propagation and Local Consistency
text:
6.1 Example: propagating \(X<Y\)
Start with
\[
\langle X<Y;
X\in5..15,
Y\in0..10\rangle.
\]
For \(X\) to have a supporting value in \(Y\)’s domain, \(X\) cannot exceed \(9\). For \(Y\) to have a supporting value in \(X\)’s domain, \(Y\) must be at least \(6\). Propagation therefore yields
\[
\langle X<Y;
X\in5..9,
Y\in6..10\rangle.
\]
The relation represented by the remaining values is
\[
\begin{aligned}
\{&(5,6),(5,7),(5,8),(5,9),(5,10),\\
&(6,7),(6,8),(6,9),(6,10),\\
&(7,8),(7,9),(7,10),\\
&(8,9),(8,10),(9,10)\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every retained value participates in at least one admitted pair.

title: Constraint Propagation and Local Consistency
text:
8.1 Example over the real numbers
Consider
\[
X^2-2XY+Y^2<5,
\qquad
X>0,
\qquad
Y>0.
\]
Since
\[
X^2-2XY+Y^2=(X-Y)^2,
\]
we have
\[
(X-Y)^2<5.
\]
The lecture adds the weaker but simpler implied constraint
\[
X-Y<3.
\]
This does not add new semantic information, because it follows from the original inequality, but the simpler constraint can help later propagation.

title: Constraint Propagation and Local Consistency
text:
11.1 Examples
The CSP
\[
\langle X_1\geq0,
X_2\geq0;
X_1\in\mathbb N,
X_2\in\mathbb N\rangle
\]
is node consistent because the natural-number domains already satisfy the unary lower bounds.
The CSP
\[
\langle X_1\geq5,
X_2\geq1;
X_1\in\mathbb N,
X_2\in\mathbb N\rangle
\]
is not node consistent, although it is consistent: it admits solutions, but the domains have not yet been restricted to the unary constraints.
The CSP
\[
\langle X_1\neq X_2,
X_1=0,
X_2=0;
X_1\in0..0,
X_2\in0..0\rangle
\]
is node consistent because the unary equalities coincide with the singleton domains. Nevertheless, it is inconsistent because the binary disequality cannot be satisfied.






ImportantLocal consistency is not global consistency



Node consistency considers unary constraints only. A node-consistent CSP may still be unsatisfiable because a binary or higher-arity constraint produces a contradiction.

title: Constraint Propagation and Local Consistency
text:
11.2 Achieving node consistency
To achieve node consistency, each unary constraint must be incorporated into the domain of the variable on which it is defined.
Let (u) be a unary constraint on variable (X), and let (D_X) be the current domain of (X). The corresponding domain-reduction rule is
\[
\langle u; X\in D_X\rangle
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\langle u; X\in D_X\cap u\rangle.
\]
Here, the unary constraint (u) can be viewed as the set of values that it permits. Therefore,
\[
D_X\cap u
\]
contains exactly the values that:

already belong to the current domain (D_X); and
satisfy the unary constraint (u).

For example, consider
\[
X\in\{1,2,3,4,5\}
\]
and the unary constraint
\[
X\geq3.
\]
The constraint admits the values
\[
u=\{3,4,5,\ldots\}.
\]
After intersecting the domain with the constraint, we obtain
\[
D_X\cap u
=
\{1,2,3,4,5\}\cap\{3,4,5,\ldots\}
=
\{3,4,5\}.
\]
The values (1) and (2) are removed because they cannot satisfy the unary constraint.

11.2.1 Complexity of achieving node consistency
Let
\[
c=|C|
\]
be the total number of constraints in the CSP, and let
\[
d=\max_i |D_i|
\]
be the size of the largest variable domain.
The notation
\[
O(cd)
\]
is an asymptotic upper bound on the running time. It means that, in the worst case, the amount of work grows proportionally to the product of:

the number (c) of constraints that must be examined; and
the maximum number (d) of domain values that may need to be checked for each constraint.

For one unary constraint on a variable (X), the algorithm may need to inspect every value in (D_X) to determine whether that value satisfies the constraint. Since
\[
|D_X|\leq d,
\]
processing one unary constraint requires at most (d) value checks. Its worst-case cost is therefore
\[
O(d).
\]
If there are at most (c) constraints to examine, and each one may require up to (d) checks, the total number of checks is bounded by
\[
c\cdot d.
\]
Therefore, the overall worst-case running time is
\[
\boxed{O(cd)}.
\]
For example, if the CSP contains (c=10) unary constraints and every domain contains at most (d=20) values, a direct implementation performs at most approximately
\[
10\cdot20=200
\]
constraint-value checks, ignoring constant implementation costs.






NoteMeaning of big-O notation



The expression (O(cd)) does not mean that the algorithm always performs exactly (cd) operations. It describes how the worst-case running time grows as the input becomes larger.
Constant factors and lower-order terms are omitted. For example, running times such as
\[
2cd,\qquad 5cd+c,\qquad cd+3d
\]
are all represented asymptotically as
\[
O(cd),
\]
because the product (cd) determines the dominant growth when the numbers of constraints and domain values increase.




11.2.2 Why the process terminates
Node-consistency rules only remove values from domains:
\[
D'_X\subseteq D_X.
\]
They never reintroduce a value that has already been removed. Domain reduction is therefore monotone.
Since every domain is finite, only finitely many values can be removed. The process must eventually reach a state in which no unary constraint can remove any additional value. At that point, the CSP is node consistent.
Because each unary constraint acts only on the domain of its own variable, the order in which the node-consistency rules are applied does not affect the final reduced domains.

title: Constraint Propagation and Local Consistency
section: 12.1 Example: a consistent but non-arc-consistent CSP
text:
12.1 Example: a consistent but non-arc-consistent CSP
Consider
\[
\langle X<Y;
X\in5..10,
Y\in3..7\rangle.
\]
The CSP is consistent because, for example, \((5,6)\) is a solution. It is not arc consistent:

\(X=7,8,9,10\) have no larger supporting value in \(D_Y\);
\(Y=3,4,5\) have no smaller supporting value in \(D_X\).

Arc-consistency filtering reduces the domains to
\[
X\in5..6,
\qquad
Y\in6..7.
\]

title: Constraint Propagation and Local Consistency
section: 12.2 Arc consistency does not imply satisfiability
text:
12.2 Arc consistency does not imply satisfiability
Consider
\[
X\neq Y,
\qquad
Y\neq Z,
\qquad
X\neq Z
\]
with
\[
X,Y,Z\in\{0,1\}.
\]
Each binary disequality is arc consistent: every value has the opposite value as support in the neighbouring domain. However, three variables cannot be pairwise different using only two values. The complete CSP is therefore inconsistent.
This example shows that arc consistency is local to individual binary constraints. It does not detect every global contradiction.

title: Constraint Propagation and Local Consistency
text:
15.1 Branch \(X_1=1\): propagation detects failure
After choosing
\[
D(X_1)=\{1\},
\]
propagation first removes values attacked by the queen at column \(1\), row \(1\):
\[
D(X_2)=\{3,4\},
\qquad
D(X_3)=\{2,4\},
\qquad
D(X_4)=\{2,3\}.
\]
Further support checks force
\[
D(X_2)=\{4\}
\]
and then
\[
D(X_3)=\{2\}.
\]
At this point, the remaining constraints remove the last support for \(X_3\), yielding
\[
D(X_3)=\varnothing.
\]
The branch becomes \(\mathit{fail}\) before a complete assignment is generated.










Propagation stage
\(D(X_1)\)
\(D(X_2)\)

15.2 Branch \(X_1=2\): propagation reaches a solution
Now choose

\]
and finally

an impossible choice can be rejected without enumerating complete continuations;
a promising choice can cause a chain of deterministic reductions that constructs the solution.

title: Constraint Optimization, Large Neighbourhood Search, and Bioinformatics Models
text:
A Constraint Optimization Problem (COP) extends a Constraint Satisfaction Problem with an objective function. It is a tuple
\[
\langle V,D,C,f\rangle,
\]
where:

\(V=\{V_1,\ldots,V_n\}\) is the set of variables;
\(D=\{D_1,\ldots,D_n\}\) contains their domains;
\(C\) is the set of constraints;
\(f:D_1\times\cdots\times D_n\to A\) maps complete assignments to an ordered set \(A\).

A constraint on variables \(V_{i_1},\ldots,V_{i_m}\) is a relation
\[
c\subseteq D_{i_1}\times\cdots\times D_{i_m}.
\]
An assignment \(\omega\) is admissible when \(\omega(V_i)\in D_i\) for every variable and every constraint contains the tuple of assigned values. A COP asks for an admissible assignment minimising \(f\), or equivalently maximising an objective after an appropriate sign change.

section: 7.2 Warm starts and a hand-made LNS
text:
7.2 Warm starts and a hand-made LNS
MiniZinc can compose searches using seq_search and can use restart schedules. The manual’s warm-start annotation is presented as a component for constructing LNS manually:
warm_start(<vars>, <vals>)
<vars> is a one-dimensional array of integer variables and <vals> is an equally long array of suggested starting values. The values may describe a partial or even invalid starting point; support depends on the solver.
A restart improves robustness by leaving an unproductive region. A warm start provides information about the incumbent around which the new search should begin. These mechanisms are related but not identical: restarting controls when search starts again, while a warm start suggests values for the new run.
crumbs: Constraint Optimization, Large Neighbourhood Search, and Bioinformatics Models

title: Constraint Optimization, Large Neighbourhood Search, and Bioinformatics Models
text:
9.1 Binary SNP encoding
At each biallelic SNP site, one allele is encoded as \(0\) and the other as \(1\). Thus a haplotype is a word over \(\{0,1\}\).
A genotype position records:

0 when both haplotypes contain 0;
1 when both contain 1;
2 when the two haplotypes disagree.

Define the combination operator \(\oplus\) by
\[
0\oplus0=0,
\qquad
1\oplus1=1,
\qquad
0\oplus1=1\oplus0=2.
\]
Applied positionwise, two haplotypes generate one genotype. The lecture example is
\[
0010\oplus0101=0222.
\]
The inverse is not unique. The same genotype 0222 can also be explained by 0110 and 0001. Every 2 permits two orientations, so a genotype with many heterogeneous positions can admit exponentially many haplotype pairs.
crumbs: Constraint Optimization, Large Neighbourhood Search, and Bioinformatics Models

title: Constraint Optimization, Large Neighbourhood Search, and Bioinformatics Models
text:
9.2 Formal explanation relation
Let
\[
H\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,
\qquad
G\subseteq\{0,1,2\}^n.
\]
A pair \(\{h_1,h_2\}\) explains genotype \(g\) exactly when, for each position \(i\):
\[
g_i\ne2
\implies
h_{1,i}=h_{2,i}=g_i,
\]
and
\[
g_i=2
\implies
h_{1,i}\ne h_{2,i}.
\]
A haplotype set \(H\) explains genotype set \(G\) when every \(g\in G\) has at least one explaining pair in \(H\).
The pure-parsimony problem seeks the smallest explanatory set. The decision form asks whether an explanatory set of size \(k\) exists. The slide states that this decision problem is NP-complete.






flowchart TD
    H1["haplotype h1"] --> G["observed genotype g"]
    H2["haplotype h2"] --> G
    H3["alternative haplotype"] --> G
    H4["alternative haplotype"] --> G
    G --> P["choose a minimum explaining set"]


 Several haplotype pairs may explain one observed genotype; pure parsimony seeks a small shared haplotype set explaining all observations. 



Biological experiments make genotypes easier and cheaper to obtain than the two underlying haplotypes. Computation is therefore used to infer a parsimonious explanation of population data.
crumbs: Constraint Optimization, Large Neighbourhood Search, and Bioinformatics Models

title: Constraint Optimization, Large Neighbourhood Search, and Bioinformatics Models
text:
12.1 Chain-adjacency constraint
Consecutive amino acids remain adjacent on the lattice:
\[
\operatorname{next}(\varphi(i),\varphi(i+1))
\]
for every \(i<n\).
For coordinates \((X_1,Y_1)\) and \((X_2,Y_2)\),
\[
\operatorname{next}((X_1,Y_1),(X_2,Y_2))
\iff
|X_1-X_2|+|Y_1-Y_2|=1.
\]
This is Manhattan distance one.
crumbs: Constraint Optimization, Large Neighbourhood Search, and Bioinformatics Models

title: Constraint Optimization, Large Neighbourhood Search, and Bioinformatics Models
text:
12.2 Self-avoidance constraint
Two distinct amino acids cannot occupy the same lattice point:
\[
i\ne j\implies\varphi(i)\ne\varphi(j).
\]
crumbs: Constraint Optimization, Large Neighbourhood Search, and Bioinformatics Models

title: Constraint Optimization, Large Neighbourhood Search, and Bioinformatics Models
text:
12.3 Energy
Non-consecutive amino acids can become spatial neighbours after folding. The energy is
\[
E(S,\varphi)=
\sum_{1\le i\le n-2}
\sum_{i+2\le j\le n}
\operatorname{Pot}(s_i,s_j)
\,[\operatorname{next}(\varphi(i),\varphi(j))].
\]
The potential used in the slide is
\[
\operatorname{Pot}(p,p)
=
\operatorname{Pot}(h,p)
=
\operatorname{Pot}(p,h)=0,
\]
and
\[
\operatorname{Pot}(h,h)=-1.
\]
The restriction \(j\ge i+2\) excludes adjacent amino acids already joined along the chain. Each non-consecutive hydrophobic contact contributes \(-1\), so minimising energy maximises favourable hydrophobic contacts.






flowchart LR
    S["HP sequence"] --> P["Lattice positions"]
    P --> A["Consecutive positions adjacent"]
    P --> U["All positions distinct"]
    A --> C["Count non-consecutive H-H contacts"]
    U --> C
    C --> E["Minimise energy"]


 Logical structure of the HP lattice optimisation model. 



The slide cites the result that deciding whether an HP sequence on the two-dimensional square lattice has a folding with energy below a threshold is NP-complete. This explains why complete exploration is difficult and connects the application back to the lecture’s optimisation and neighbourhood-search techniques.

title: Bottom-Up Semantics and Fixpoint Computation
text:
For a definite-clause program \(P\), let \(B_P\) denote its Herbrand base and \(M_P\) its minimum Herbrand model. The preceding lecture established the central equivalence
\[
P \models A
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
A\in M_P
\]
for every ground atom \(A\in B_P\).
The test \(A\in M_P\) can be approached top-down by SLD resolution. A successful SLD derivation not only establishes that \(A\) is a logical consequence of \(P\), but also explains which program clauses justify the conclusion. This explanatory derivation is relevant to explainable artificial intelligence: the proof structure records why the answer follows.
The present lecture develops the complementary bottom-up method. Instead of starting from a query, bottom-up evaluation starts from known facts and repeatedly derives every immediate consequence until a fixpoint is reached.

title: Bottom-Up Semantics and Fixpoint Computation
text:
2.1 Finite grounding
Suppose
\[
H_P=\{a,b\}
\]
and the program contains the rule
q(X) :- r(X,Y), p(Y).
Every pair of substitutions for \(X\) and \(Y\) produces one ground instance:
q(a) :- r(a,a), p(a).
q(a) :- r(a,b), p(b).
q(b) :- r(b,a), p(a).
q(b) :- r(b,b), p(b).
The grounding contains four rules because each of the two variables has two possible ground values.

title: Bottom-Up Semantics and Fixpoint Computation
text:
2.2 Infinite grounding
If
\[
H_P=\{0,s(0),s(s(0)),\ldots\},
\]
then the rule
num(s(X)) :- num(X).
has infinitely many ground instances:
num(s(0))       :- num(0).
num(s(s(0)))    :- num(s(0)).
num(s(s(s(0)))) :- num(s(s(0))).
...
The syntactic program is finite, but its grounding can be infinite because function symbols generate infinitely many ground terms.

title: Bottom-Up Semantics and Fixpoint Computation
text:
3.1 A finite bottom-up computation
Consider
r(a).
r(b).
p(a).
q(X) :- r(X), p(X).
Starting from the empty interpretation:
\[
T_P(\varnothing)
=
\{r(a),r(b),p(a)\}.
\]
The ground instance
q(a) :- r(a), p(a).
now has its complete body in the interpretation, so the next application also derives \(q(a)\):
\[
T_P\bigl(\{r(a),r(b),p(a)\}\bigr)
=
\{q(a),r(a),r(b),p(a)\}.
\]
A further application produces no change:
\[
T_P\bigl(\{q(a),r(a),r(b),p(a)\}\bigr)
=
\{q(a),r(a),r(b),p(a)\}.
\]
The computation has reached a fixpoint.



Iteration
Interpretation




\(0\)
\(\varnothing\)


\(1\)
\(\{r(a),r(b),p(a)\}\)


\(2\)
\(\{q(a),r(a),r(b),p(a)\}\)


\(3\)
unchanged, hence a fixpoint

title: Bottom-Up Semantics and Fixpoint Computation
text:
4.1 A looping top-down derivation
Consider
p(a).
q(X) :- q(X).
A top-down attempt to prove q(a) may repeatedly select the recursive rule:
\[
\leftarrow q(a)
\Longrightarrow
\leftarrow q(a)
\Longrightarrow
\leftarrow q(a)
\Longrightarrow\cdots
\]
At each step a fresh variable is introduced and unified with \(a\), but the selected goal remains q(a). SLD resolution may therefore loop.
Bottom-up evaluation terminates immediately:
\[
T_P(\varnothing)=\{p(a)\},
\]
and
\[
T_P(\{p(a)\})=\{p(a)\}.
\]
The atom \(q(a)\) is never derived. The fixpoint is simply \(\{p(a)\}\).

title: Bottom-Up Semantics and Fixpoint Computation
text:
4.2 Finite query, infinite bottom-up construction
Now consider
nat(0).
nat(s(X)) :- nat(X).
A top-down derivation for the specific query
?- nat(s(s(s(0)))).
is finite. Each resolution step removes one outer occurrence of \(s\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
\leftarrow \operatorname{nat}(s(s(s(0))))
&\Longrightarrow \leftarrow \operatorname{nat}(s(s(0)))\\
&\Longrightarrow \leftarrow \operatorname{nat}(s(0))\\
&\Longrightarrow \leftarrow \operatorname{nat}(0)\\
&\Longrightarrow \square.
\end{aligned}
\]
The bottom-up construction instead enumerates the complete infinite model:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_P(\varnothing)
&=\{\operatorname{nat}(0)\},\\
T_P^2(\varnothing)
&=\{\operatorname{nat}(0),\operatorname{nat}(s(0))\},\\
T_P^3(\varnothing)
&=\{\operatorname{nat}(0),\operatorname{nat}(s(0)),
\operatorname{nat}(s(s(0)))\},\\
&\hspace{1em}\vdots
\end{aligned}
\]
No finite iteration contains every natural-number atom. The limit is
\[
\{\operatorname{nat}(0),\operatorname{nat}(s(0)),
\operatorname{nat}(s(s(0))),\ldots\}.
\]
Thus, in practice, naive bottom-up execution may continue forever even though the semantic limit is well defined.








Program and request
Top-down behaviour
Bottom-up behaviour




q(X) :- q(X) with query q(a)
May loop on the recursive goal
Immediately reaches \(\{p(a)\}\)


Naturals with one ground query
Finite derivation for a fixed numeral
Enumerates an infinite ascending chain

title: Bottom-Up Semantics and Fixpoint Computation
text:
5.1 Proof

5.1.1 If \(T_P(I)\subseteq I\), then \(I\) is a model
Suppose
\[
T_P(I)\subseteq I.
\]
Take any ground rule
\[
a\leftarrow b_1,\ldots,b_n
\]
in \(\operatorname{ground}(P)\). If the body is not contained in \(I\), the implication is satisfied because its antecedent is false. If
\[
\{b_1,\ldots,b_n\}\subseteq I,
\]
then \(a\in T_P(I)\). By the hypothesis \(T_P(I)\subseteq I\), it follows that \(a\in I\). Hence the rule is satisfied. Since this holds for every ground rule, \(I\) is a model of \(P\).


5.1.2 If \(I\) is a model, then \(T_P(I)\subseteq I\)
We prove the contrapositive. Suppose
\[
T_P(I)\setminus I\ne\varnothing.
\]
Choose \(a\in T_P(I)\setminus I\). By the definition of \(T_P\), some ground rule
\[
a\leftarrow b_1,\ldots,b_n
\]
has its body contained in \(I\), while its head \(a\) is absent from \(I\). That rule is false in \(I\), so \(I\) is not a model.

title: Bottom-Up Semantics and Fixpoint Computation
text:
6.1 Proof
Take any \(a\in T_P(I)\). Some ground rule
\[
a\leftarrow b_1,\ldots,b_n
\]
has
\[
\{b_1,\ldots,b_n\}\subseteq I.
\]
Since \(I\subseteq J\), the same body is contained in \(J\). Therefore \(a\in T_P(J)\).
Monotonicity ensures that iteration from the bottom produces an ascending chain:
\[
\varnothing
\subseteq
T_P(\varnothing)
\subseteq
T_P^2(\varnothing)
\subseteq
T_P^3(\varnothing)
\subseteq\cdots
\]






flowchart LR
  I0["Empty interpretation"] --> I1["T_P at stage 1"]
  I1 --> I2["T_P at stage 2"]
  I2 --> I3["T_P at stage 3"]
  I3 --> IL["Limit at omega"]
  classDef stage fill:#0d6efd,color:#ffffff,stroke:#084298
  class I0,I1,I2,I3,IL stage


 Repeated application of the monotone immediate-consequence operator builds an ascending chain from the empty interpretation. 



At any finite stage there are two possibilities:

if \(T_P^{n+1}(\varnothing)=T_P^n(\varnothing)\), a fixpoint has been reached;
if the inclusion is strict, the current interpretation is not yet a model because \(T_P(I)\nsubseteq I\).

title: Bottom-Up Semantics and Fixpoint Computation
text:
7.1 Proof

7.1.1 Left-to-right inclusion
Suppose
\[
a\in T_P\left(\bigcup_{i\ge0}I_i\right).
\]
Then there is a ground rule
\[
a\leftarrow b_1,\ldots,b_n
\]
whose body atoms all belong to the union. For each \(b_j\), choose an index \(k_j\) such that \(b_j\in I_{k_j}\). Because the body is finite, the maximum
\[
k=\max\{k_1,\ldots,k_n\}
\]
exists. Since the chain is ascending, every body atom belongs to \(I_k\). Hence
\[
a\in T_P(I_k)
\subseteq
\bigcup_{i\ge0}T_P(I_i).
\]
The finiteness of rule bodies is crucial here: finitely many witnessing stages can be replaced by one largest stage.


7.1.2 Right-to-left inclusion
Suppose
\[
a\in\bigcup_{i\ge0}T_P(I_i).
\]
Then \(a\in T_P(I_k)\) for some \(k\). A ground rule derives \(a\) from body atoms contained in \(I_k\). Since
\[
I_k\subseteq\bigcup_{i\ge0}I_i,
\]
the same rule derives \(a\) from the union. Thus
\[
a\in T_P\left(\bigcup_{i\ge0}I_i\right).
\]

title: Bottom-Up Semantics and Fixpoint Computation
text:
8.1 Proof
Define the upward iterates of \(T_P\) by
\[
T_P\uparrow 0=\varnothing,
\]
\[
T_P\uparrow(n+1)=T_P(T_P\uparrow n),
\]
and
\[
T_P\uparrow\omega
=
\bigcup_{n\ge0}T_P\uparrow n.
\]
Upward continuity shows that the limit is a fixpoint:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_P(T_P\uparrow\omega)
&=T_P\left(\bigcup_{n\ge0}T_P\uparrow n\right)\\
&=\bigcup_{n\ge0}T_P(T_P\uparrow n)\\
&=\bigcup_{n\ge0}T_P\uparrow(n+1)\\
&=T_P\uparrow\omega.
\end{aligned}
\]
Moreover, every model \(I\) contains every stage of this construction. The proof is by induction:

\(T_P\uparrow0=\varnothing\subseteq I\);
if \(T_P\uparrow n\subseteq I\), monotonicity gives \[
T_P\uparrow(n+1)=T_P(T_P\uparrow n)\subseteq T_P(I),
\] and because \(I\) is a model, \(T_P(I)\subseteq I\).

Therefore the union of all stages is contained in every model.

title: Bottom-Up Semantics and Fixpoint Computation
section: 9.1 Example: why descending iteration may require more than \(\omega\)
text:
9.1 Example: why descending iteration may require more than \(\omega\)
Consider
r(0) :- r(0).
p(0) :- q(X).
q(s(X)) :- q(X).
The upward construction derives nothing:
\[
T_P\uparrow\omega=\varnothing.
\]
For the descending construction, \(T_P\downarrow0=B_P\) contains every ground atom over the predicates \(r\), \(p\) and \(q\). The first stages are:
\[
\begin{aligned}
T_P\downarrow1
&=\{r(0),p(0),q(s(0)),q(s(s(0))),\ldots\},\\
T_P\downarrow2
&=\{r(0),p(0),q(s(s(0))),q(s(s(s(0)))),\ldots\},\\
T_P\downarrow3
&=\{r(0),p(0),q(s(s(s(0)))),\ldots\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Each finite stage removes one more \(q\)-atom from the beginning of the chain. Their intersection is
\[
T_P\downarrow\omega=\{r(0),p(0)\}.
\]
This set is not a fixpoint:
\[
T_P(\{r(0),p(0)\})=\{r(0)\}.
\]
Applying \(T_P\) once more produces \(\{r(0)\}\), which is the greatest fixpoint. Hence the construction needs a stage after \(\omega\).



Stage
Remaining atoms, schematically




\(0\)
all atoms in \(B_P\)


\(1\)
\(r(0)\), \(p(0)\), and \(q\)-atoms from \(q(s(0))\) onward


\(2\)
\(r(0)\), \(p(0)\), and \(q\)-atoms from \(q(s(s(0)))\) onward


\(\omega\)
\(\{r(0),p(0)\}\), not a fixpoint


\(\omega+1\)
\(\{r(0)\}\), the greatest fixpoint



The asymmetry between the least and greatest fixpoints is therefore structural: upward continuity guarantees that the least fixpoint is reached at \(\omega\), while lack of downward continuity allows the greatest-fixpoint construction to continue beyond \(\omega\).
